items.text: משנת הפתיחה: עדים זוממין שאינם נעשים זוממין
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: cases where witnesses are not made zomemim in the usual way
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two cases: witnesses who say a man is a son of a divorced woman or a halutzah, or liable for exile, are not made into that status themselves but are flogged forty lashes.
items.desc: המשנה פותחת בשאלה כיצד עדים נעשים זוממין, ומביאה שני מקרים שבהם עדים זוממין אינם מקבלים את העונש שזממו להטיל אלא לוקים ארבעים: במקרה של עדות על בן גרושה או בן חלוצה, ובמקרה של עדות על חיוב גלות.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the question of how witnesses become זוממין (conspiring witnesses) and presents the first case: witnesses who testify that a man is a בן גרושה (son of a divorced woman) or a בן חלוצה (son of a חלוצה) are not made into that status themselves but receive forty lashes.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בשאלה כיצד עדים נעשים זוממין, ומביאה שני מקרים שבהם עדים זוממין אינם מקבלים את העונש שזממו להטיל אלא לוקים ארבעים: במקרה של עדות על בן גרושה או בן חלוצה, ובמקרה של עדות על חיוב גלות.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a second case: witnesses who testify that a man is liable for גלות (exile) are not exiled in his stead but receive forty lashes.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על לשון המשנה
items.text_en: Gemara's question: why does the Mishnah say 'how' instead of 'how not'?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah should have said 'how are witnesses not made zomemim', since the cases describe when they are not made zomemim, and cites a later Mishnah that contrasts these with actual zomemim.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על המשנה: כיוון שהמקרים המובאים הם מקרים שבהם אין עדים נעשים זוממין, היה צריך לשאול 'כיצד אין העדים נעשים זוממין'? ועוד, מהמשנה המאוחרת (ה ע"א) נראה שאלה אינם זוממין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says 'how are witnesses made zomemim' when the cases describe when they are not made zomemim, and cites a later Mishnah that contrasts these with actual zomemim.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על לשון המשנה: כיוון שהמקרים המובאים הם מקרים שבהם אין עדים נעשים זוממין, היה צריך לשאול 'כיצד אין העדים נעשים זוממין'? ועוד, מהמשנה המאוחרת (ה ע"א) נראה שאלה אינם זוממין.

items.text: תירוץ הגמרא: התנא עומד בסוף סנהדרין
items.text_en: Answer: the Tanna is standing in a broader context
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Tanna is continuing from a previous discussion about zomemim who precede the death penalty, and then introduces a category of witnesses who are only flogged, citing the Mishnah's cases as examples.
items.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהתנא עומד בסוף מסכת סנהדרין, שם נאמר שכל הזוממין מקדימין לאותה מיתה, חוץ מזוממי בת כהן ובועלה. ומכאן הוא ממשיך: ויש עדים זוממין אחרים שאין עושין בהם דין הזמה כלל אלא מלקות ארבעים, ומביא את המקרים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Tanna is standing in the context of a previous discussion about zomemim who precede the death penalty, except for the case of the daughter of a priest and her paramour.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהתנא עומד בסוף מסכת סנהדרין, שם נאמר שכל הזוממין מקדימין לאותה מיתה, חוץ מזוממי בת כהן ובועלה, שמקדימין למיתה אחרת.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna introduces a category of witnesses who are only flogged, citing the Mishnah's cases as examples.
sub.desc: התנא ממשיך ומפרט שיש עדים זוממין אחרים שאין עושין בהם דין הזמה כלל אלא מלקות ארבעים, ומביא את המקרים.

items.text: מקור הדין: 'לו' ולא לזרעו
items.text_en: Derivation from Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish: 'to him' and not to his seed
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Reish Lakish derives from the verse 'and you shall do to him as he plotted' that the punishment applies only to him, not to his offspring, and the Gemara adds that we need 'as he plotted to do' which is lacking here.
items.desc: הגמרא דורשת את הפסוק 'ועשיתם לו כאשר זמם' – 'לו' ולא לזרעו, ולכן אין פוסלים את העד ואת זרעו. ומקשה: לפסול אותו ולא את זרעו? ומתרצת שצריך 'כאשר זמם לעשות' ולא מתקיים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source for the rule that false witnesses about lineage are not made into that status, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Reish Lakish answers with a verse: 'ועשיתם לו כאשר זמם' (and you shall do to him as he plotted) — 'לו' (to him) but not to his offspring; the Gemara then objects that they should at least be disqualified themselves, but the verse requires 'כאשר זמם לעשות' (as he plotted to do), which is absent here.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן נלמד דין זה שאין עדים זוממין לוקים ואינם נפסלים.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi citing Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Reish Lakish provides the source: the verse 'ועשיתם לו כאשר זמם' (and you shall do to him as he plotted) implies 'לו' (to him) but not to his offspring; the Gemara then objects that they should at least be disqualified themselves, but the verse requires 'כאשר זמם לעשות' (as he plotted to do), which is absent here.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן נלמד דין זה שאין עדים זוממין לוקים ואינם נפסלים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: But why not disqualify the witnesses themselves (as זוממין) and simply not disqualify their offspring? (The verse seems to address only the offspring, not the witnesses' own status.)
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן נלמד דין זה שאין עדים זוממין לוקים ואינם נפסלים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: We require the principle 'כַּאֲשֶׁר זָמַם לַעֲשׂוֹת' (as he plotted to do) — that the punishment must match the intended harm — and here, since the witnesses only intended to disqualify the offspring, not to kill or physically harm the accused, the full penalty of disqualification cannot apply.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן נלמד דין זה שאין עדים זוממין לוקים ואינם נפסלים.

items.text: קל וחומר של בר פדא וקושיית רבינא
items.text_en: Alternative derivation from Bar Pada: a kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Bar Pada offers a kal vachomer: if one who actually profanes is not profaned, then one who intended to profane but did not is certainly not profaned. Ravina objects that this would nullify the entire law of zomemim.
items.desc: בר פדא דורש קל וחומר: אם המחלל עצמו אינו מתחלל, הבא לחלל ולא חילל אינו דין שלא יתחלל? רבינא מקשה שאם כן ביטלת תורת עדים זוממין.

sub.desc_en: Bar Pada offers a different source using a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if one who actually profanes (a חלל) is not himself profaned, then one who merely intended to profane but did not is certainly not profaned.
sub.desc: בר פדא דורש קל וחומר: אם המחלל עצמו אינו מתחלל, הבא לחלל ולא חילל אינו דין שלא יתחלל?

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects to Bar Pada's argument, arguing that if this קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) were accepted, it would nullify the entire law of zomemim witnesses.
sub.desc: בר פדא דורש קל וחומר: אם המחלל עצמו אינו מתחלל, הבא לחלל ולא חילל אינו דין שלא יתחלל?

items.text: Source for conspiring witnesses not being exiled
items.text_en: Source for conspiring witnesses not being exiled
items.desc_en: The Gemara first attempts a kal vachomer to exempt conspiring witnesses from exile, but rejects it because the witnesses need atonement. It concludes that the source is Reish Lakish's derivation from the verse 'hu yanus' – he, but not conspirators.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) to exempt conspiring witnesses from exile, but notes it was already rejected as a mere clarification.
Reish Lakish derives from the verse 'הוּא יָנוּס' (he shall flee) that the conspiring witnesses themselves are excluded from exile.
Rabbi Yochanan offers a different kal vachomer to exempt conspiring witnesses from exile.
The Gemara objects that the kal vachomer fails because the witnesses need atonement through exile, unlike the intentional killer.
The Gemara concludes that the true source is Reish Lakish's derivation, not the kal vachomer.

items.text: Source for conspiring witnesses receiving lashes
items.text_en: Source for conspiring witnesses receiving lashes
items.desc_en: Ulla asks for a hint in the Torah that conspiring witnesses receive lashes. The Gemara cites the verse 'vehitzdiku et hatzaddik vehirshiu et harasha' and explains it refers to witnesses who made a righteous person guilty, then other witnesses made him righteous and the first witnesses wicked. It rejects the derivation from 'Lo ta'aneh' because that is a prohibition without action.

sub.desc_en: Ulla asks for a hint in the Torah that conspiring witnesses receive lashes, clarifying that the explicit verse 'וַעֲשִׂיתֶם לוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁר זָמַם' already establishes the punishment, so he seeks a source for lashes specifically.

The Gemara cites the verse 'וְהִצְדִּיקוּ אֶת הַצַּדִּיק וְהִרְשִׁיעוּ אֶת הָרָשָׁע' and explains it refers to witnesses who made a righteous person guilty, then other witnesses made him righteous and the first witnesses wicked, leading to lashes.
The Gemara objects: why not derive the lashes from the prohibition 'לֹא תַעֲנֶה' (do not bear false witness)?
The Gemara resolves that the prohibition 'לֹא תַעֲנֶה' is a לאו שאין בו מעשה (a prohibition without an action), which does not incur lashes, so the verse is needed.

items.text: Baraita: Four things about conspiring witnesses
items.text_en: Baraita: Four things about conspiring witnesses
items.desc_en: A baraita lists four things that do not apply to conspiring witnesses: they cannot become a ben gerushah or ben chalutzah, they are not exiled to cities of refuge, they do not pay kofer, and they are not sold as a Hebrew slave. Rabbi Akiva adds that they do not pay on their own admission. The Gemara explains the first two as previously stated, and the third because kofer is atonement and they are not fit for atonement.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing four halachic rules that do not apply to conspiring witnesses.
Rabbi Akiva adds a fifth rule: conspiring witnesses do not pay restitution based on their own admission.
The Gemara explains the first three rules: the first two as previously stated, and the third because kofer is atonement and these witnesses are unfit for atonement.

items.text: Debate on the nature of kofer: ransom or atonement
items.text_en: Debate on the nature of kofer: ransom or atonement
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda identifies the Tanna who holds kofer is atonement as Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, based on a dispute about whether kofer is assessed by the value of the injured party or the injurer. Rav Papa argues that all agree kofer is atonement, but they dispute whether valuation is based on the injured or the injurer. The Gemara then explains the reasoning of the Rabbis and Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna who holds that kofer (ransom) is atonement, and Rav Chisda answers that it is Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka.
The baraita cites the dispute: the Rabbis interpret 'פדיון נפשו' (redemption of his soul) as the value of the injured party, while Rabbi Yishmael interprets it as the value of the injurer.
The Gemara infers that the dispute is about whether kofer is monetary restitution or atonement.
Rav Papa rejects the inference, arguing that all agree kofer is atonement, but they dispute whether valuation is based on the injured party or the injurer.

The Gemara explains the Rabbis' reasoning: a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between the 'imposition' stated below (Exodus 21:30) and above (Exodus 21:22) teaches that valuation is based on the injured party.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yishmael derives from 'פדיון נפשו' (redemption of his soul) that valuation is based on the injurer, while the Rabbis agree that the phrase indicates atonement but still assess based on the injured party.

items.text: Why conspiring witnesses are not sold as Hebrew slaves
items.text_en: Why conspiring witnesses are not sold as Hebrew slaves
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna initially suggests that the rule applies only when the witnesses have assets, but Rava rejects this, arguing that the witnesses can say 'if you had assets, would you be sold?' Rava concludes that the verse 'venimkar bignevato' teaches that a thief is sold for his theft, not for his conspiracy.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that conspiring witnesses are not sold as Hebrew slaves.
Rav Hamnuna initially suggests that the rule applies only when the falsely accused has assets, but if he lacks assets, the witnesses are sold even if they have assets.
Rava objects that the witnesses can argue that if the accused had assets, he would not be sold, so they too should not be sold.
Rav Hamnuna revises his proposal: the rule applies only when either the accused or the witnesses have assets, but if neither has assets, the witnesses are sold.
Rava rejects the revised proposal, citing the verse 'ונמכר בגנבתו' (and he shall be sold for his theft) to teach that a thief is sold for his theft, not for his conspiracy.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's reason for not paying on own admission
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's reason for not paying on own admission
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva holds that the payment is a fine (knas), and one does not pay a fine on his own admission. Rabba and Rav Nachman offer supporting proofs from the fact that they are killed and pay, or that the money is in the hands of the owners and they pay.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Akiva's reason for the ruling that witnesses do not pay on their own admission.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva holds the payment is a fine (קנס), and one does not pay a fine on his own admission.
Rabba offers supporting proof: since the witnesses did not actually perform the act yet they are killed and pay, this shows the payment is a fine.
Rav Nachman offers another supporting proof: since the money is already in the hands of the owners and they pay, this indicates it is a fine.

items.text: Clarification of Rav Nachman's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of Rav Nachman's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of Rav Nachman's statement about witnesses who did not perform an action, noting it seems identical to Rabbah's view, and suggests the correct version is 'And so said Rav Nachman'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rav Nachman's statement about witnesses who did not perform an action means, noting it seems identical to Rabbah's view.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by suggesting the correct version of Rav Nachman's statement is 'And so said Rav Nachman'.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's statement about divided payment
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's statement about divided payment
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav states that a conspiring witness pays according to his share. The Gemara questions this, arguing that if it means each pays half, that contradicts the rule that monetary payments are divided but lashes are not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav stating that a conspiring witness pays according to his share.
The Gemara asks what 'pays according to his share' means, suggesting it might mean each pays half.
The Gemara objects that this interpretation contradicts the established rule that monetary payments are divided but lashes are not.

items.text: Alternative explanation and objection
items.text_en: Alternative explanation and objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the statement refers to a case where only one witness was disqualified, so he pays his half. But an objection is raised from a baraita that a conspiring witness does not pay until both are disqualified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the statement refers to a case where only one witness was disqualified, so he pays his half.
An objection is raised from a baraita that a conspiring witness does not pay until both are disqualified.

items.text: Rava's first answer and rejection
items.text_en: Rava's first answer and rejection
items.desc_en: Rava suggests the case is where the witness says 'I testified falsely'. The Gemara objects that once a witness has testified, he cannot retract and testify again.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers that the case is where the witness says 'I testified falsely', thereby admitting perjury.
The Gemara objects that a witness cannot retract his testimony once given, so his self-incrimination is ineffective.

items.text: Second answer and disagreement with Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Second answer and disagreement with Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the case is where the witness says 'We testified and were disqualified in court'. This view is not in accordance with Rabbi Akiva, who holds that one does not pay based on his own admission.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the case is where the witness says 'We testified and were disqualified in a certain court', shifting the basis of liability.
The Gemara notes that this view disagrees with Rabbi Akiva, who holds that one does not pay based on his own admission.

items.text: Final resolution and conclusion
items.text_en: Final resolution and conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the case is where the witness says 'We testified and were disqualified in court and were obligated to pay money'. The Gemara explains that one might think since he cannot obligate his fellow, he himself is not obligated, so the teaching comes to inform us otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the case as one where the witness says 'We testified and were disqualified in court and were obligated to pay money'.
The Gemara explains that one might think since he cannot obligate his fellow, he himself is not obligated, so the teaching comes to inform us otherwise.

items.text: Mishnah: False testimony about divorce and ketubah
items.text_en: Mishnah: False testimony about divorce and ketubah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where witnesses falsely testify that a man divorced his wife without paying her ketubah. The court assesses how much a person would pay for the ketubah, considering the risks of widowhood, divorce, or the husband inheriting if she dies.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a case of witnesses falsely testifying that a man divorced his wife without paying her ketubah, noting that he will eventually have to pay it.
The Mishnah concludes that the court assesses how much a person would pay for the ketubah, considering the risks of widowhood, divorce, or the husband inheriting if she dies.

items.text: Gemara: How to assess the value
items.text_en: Gemara: How to assess the value
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses how to assess the value. Rav Chisda says it is assessed based on the husband. Rav Natan bar Oshaya says based on the wife. Rav Pappa says based on both the wife and her ketubah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the court assesses the value of the ketubah for the purpose of damages.
Rav Chisda answers that the assessment is based on the husband's financial standing.
Rav Natan bar Oshaya answers that the assessment is based on the wife's financial standing.
Rav Pappa answers that the assessment is based on both the wife's standing and the value of her ketubah.

items.text: Mishnah: False testimony about a loan with different terms
items.text_en: Mishnah: False testimony about a loan with different terms
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where witnesses testify that a man owes 1000 zuz to be paid within 30 days, but the defendant says within 10 years. The court assesses how much a person would pay to have 1000 zuz in hand for either 30 days or 10 years.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where witnesses testify about a loan of 1000 zuz with a 30-day term, but the defendant claims a 10-year term, and the court assesses the value of the time difference.

items.text: Gemara: Sabbatical year and long-term loans
items.text_en: Gemara: Sabbatical year and long-term loans
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel states that one who lends to another for ten years – the Sabbatical year cancels the debt.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel that a loan for ten years is canceled by the Sabbatical year.

items.text: Gemara's first question and Rava's answer on a ten-year loan
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and Rava's answer on a ten-year loan
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana challenges the view that a ten-year loan is not canceled by shemittah, citing a mishnah that assesses the value of having money for different periods. Rava answers that the mishnah deals with a loan on a pledge or where the documents were handed to the court, which are not canceled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that although the verse 'lo yigosh' (he shall not oppress) does not currently apply to a ten-year loan, it may eventually lead to its violation.
Rav Kahana objects by citing a mishnah that assesses the value of having money for different periods, arguing that if shemittah cancels a ten-year loan, all periods would require repayment.
Rava answers that the mishnah deals with a loan on a pledge or where documents were handed to the court, which are not canceled by shemittah.

items.text: Alternative version: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, and Rav Kahana's objection
items.text_en: Alternative version: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, and Rav Kahana's objection
items.desc_en: An alternative tradition quotes Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that a ten-year loan is not canceled by shemittah. Rav Kahana objects with the same mishnah, and Rava again answers with the same distinction of a loan on a pledge or court documents.

sub.text: Alternative version: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Alternative version: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that a ten-year loan is not canceled by shemittah, since currently the verse 'lo yigosh' does not apply.
Rav Kahana again objects with the same mishnah, arguing that if shemittah cancels the loan, all periods would require repayment.
Rava repeats his answer that the mishnah refers to a loan on a pledge or where documents were given to the court.

items.text: Stipulation against shemittah and the principle of overriding Torah law
items.text_en: Stipulation against shemittah and the principle of overriding Torah law
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that if one stipulates 'on condition that you not cancel me by shemittah,' the loan is still canceled. The Gemara questions whether this implies Shmuel holds that a condition against Torah law is void, and resolves it by distinguishing between a condition about the person and one about the law itself.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that if one stipulates 'on condition that shemittah not cancel my debt,' shemittah still cancels it, raising the question of whether Shmuel holds that a condition against Torah law is void.
A supporting baraita is cited: regarding a stipulation against the law of ona'ah (fraud), Rav says the condition is void, while Shmuel says it is valid.

Rav Anan clarifies from Shmuel himself that the distinction is between 'on condition that you have no claim of ona'ah against me' (valid) and 'on condition that there is no ona'ah in this transaction' (void).
The Gemara applies the same distinction: 'on condition that you not cancel my debt in the shemittah year' (valid) versus 'on condition that shemittah not cancel my debt' (void).

items.text: The minimum period for a loan: thirty days
items.text_en: The minimum period for a loan: thirty days
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a lender cannot demand repayment of a standard loan within thirty days. Rabbah bar bar Chanah initially limits this to loans with a document, but Rav corrects him that it applies to oral loans as well. Shmuel asks Rav Matna for the source, who derives it from the verse 'the year of release is near,' interpreting that thirty days is considered a year.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that one who lends to another without specifying a term may not demand repayment within less than thirty days.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah before Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah before Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah initially limits the baraita to loans with a document (שטר), reasoning that one would not bother writing a document for less than thirty days.
Rav corrects Rabbah bar bar Chanah, stating that the rule applies equally to loans with a document and oral loans.
A supporting baraita confirms Rav's position, explicitly stating the rule applies to both written and oral loans.
Shmuel urgently asks Rav Matna for the scriptural source of the rule that a standard loan cannot be demanded within thirty days.
Rav Matna derives the rule from the verse 'קרבה שנת השבע שנת השמטה' (the year of release is near), interpreting that thirty days in a year is considered a year.

items.text: Digression: Opening a jar on Shabbat
items.text_en: Digression: Opening a jar on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav rules that opening a jar's seal on Shabbat incurs a sin-offering. Rav Kahana questions the distinction between this and opening a barrel's lid, and is answered that one is a permanent connection and the other is not.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that one who opens a neck-opening (a sealed garment) on Shabbat is liable to bring a sin-offering.
Rav Kahana objects by comparing this to opening a barrel-stopper, and the answer is that the neck-opening is attached (חיבור) while the stopper is not.
Rav answers that the jar's seal is a permanent connection (חִבּוּר) while the barrel's lid is not, explaining the distinction.

items.text: Digression: Wine in water affecting a mikveh
items.text_en: Digression: Wine in water affecting a mikveh
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav rules that three log of water mixed with a drop of wine that looks like wine does not invalidate a mikveh. Rav Kahana compares it to dye water that does invalidate, and Rava distinguishes them. A baraita from Rabbi Chiya seems to contradict, and Rava resolves it by attributing the views to different Tannaim.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that three log of water mixed with a kortov of wine, whose appearance is like wine, does not invalidate a mikveh.
Rav Kahana objects by comparing this case to dye water, which according to Rabbi Yosei does invalidate a mikveh in three log.
Rava distinguishes: there the mixture is called dye water, here it is called diluted wine, so the halakhic status differs.
A baraita taught by Rabbi Chiya states that such a mixture does invalidate the mikveh, contradicting Rav's ruling.
Rava resolves the contradiction: Rav's ruling follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, while the baraita follows the Rabbis, as cited in the mishna.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Three logs of drawn water and the rule of appearance
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Three logs of drawn water and the rule of appearance
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if three logs of water are missing a kortov and wine or milk is added, the mikveh is not invalidated. Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says everything follows the appearance.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first case: a mikveh missing a kortov of water, into which wine or milk falls and changes the appearance, does not invalidate the mikveh.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri rules that everything follows the appearance of the water, overriding the quantity rule.

items.text: Rav Pappa's dilemma about Rav's version of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's dilemma about Rav's version of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa raises a dilemma: does Rav teach the Mishnah with 'missing a kortov' at the beginning, implying that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri disputes the first case, or does Rav not teach it that way, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri only disputes the latter case, with Rav agreeing with everyone?

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks whether Rav taught the Mishnah with the phrase 'missing a kortov' at the beginning, implying a dispute only on the second case, or without it, implying a broader dispute.
Rav Pappa offers the alternative: perhaps Rav does not teach 'missing a kortov' at the beginning, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri only disputes the latter case, with Rav agreeing with everyone.

items.text: Rava's resolution and Rav Yosef's tradition
items.text_en: Rava's resolution and Rav Yosef's tradition
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that while Rav Pappa is uncertain, Rava is certain. Rav Yosef says he did not hear this ruling, but Abaye reports that Rav Yosef himself had said that Rav does not teach 'missing a kortov' at the beginning, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri disputes only the latter case, with Rav agreeing with everyone.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara contrasts Rav Pappa's uncertainty with Rava's certainty regarding the dispute.

Abaye reminds Rav Yosef that he himself had taught that Rav does not teach 'missing a kortov' at the beginning, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri disputes only the latter case, with Rav agreeing with everyone.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling about a barrel that fell into the Great Sea
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling about a barrel that fell into the Great Sea
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in Rav's name that if a barrel full of water falls into the Great Sea, one who immerses there does not fulfill his obligation, because we suspect three logs of drawn water may be concentrated in one place. A baraita supports this with a case of wine, and the Gemara explains the need for the additional case of terumah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name that if a barrel full of water falls into the Great Sea, one who immerses there does not fulfill his obligation, because we suspect three logs of drawn water may be concentrated in one place, and this applies only to the Great Sea, not to an ordinary river.
A baraita supports Rav's ruling with a case of a barrel of wine that fell into the Great Sea, and adds that a loaf of תרומה (priestly portion) that falls there becomes ritually impure.

The Gemara explains the need for the additional case of תרומה (priestly portion): one might have thought that only a person's immersion is invalid due to a חזקה (presumption) of impurity, but the baraita teaches that the same applies to the loaf of תרומה (priestly portion).

items.text: New Mishnah: Conspiring witnesses who testify about monetary or lashes liability
items.text_en: New Mishnah: Conspiring witnesses who testify about monetary or lashes liability
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two cases: witnesses who say a person owes 200 zuz and are found conspiring are flogged and pay (Rabbi Meir) or only pay (Sages); witnesses who say a person is liable for forty lashes are flogged eighty (Rabbi Meir) or only forty (Sages).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the first case: witnesses who conspired to obligate a person for 200 zuz are flogged and pay, according to Rabbi Meir.
The Sages respond that anyone who pays is not flogged, rejecting Rabbi Meir's dual penalty.
The Mishnah presents the second case: witnesses who conspired to obligate a person for forty lashes are flogged eighty, according to Rabbi Meir, citing two verses.
The Sages respond that they are flogged only forty lashes, rejecting Rabbi Meir's double penalty.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's source for lashes and payment
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's source for lashes and payment
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Meir holds that one is both flogged and pays, unlike the Rabbis who derive from 'kedei rish'ato' that one is punished for only one offense. Ulla answers that Rabbi Meir learns from motzi shem ra, where one is flogged and pays, and holds like Rabbi Akiva that edim zomemim is a fine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Meir holds that one is both flogged and pays, given the Rabbis' derivation from 'kedei rish'ato' that one is punished for only one offense.
Ulla answers that Rabbi Meir learns from motzi shem ra, where one is flogged and pays, and holds like Rabbi Akiva that edim zomemim is a fine.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's view on a prohibition without action
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's view on a prohibition without action
items.desc_en: An alternative version applies Ulla's statement to a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda holds that a prohibition without a physical action is punishable by lashes, while Rabbi Akiva disagrees. The Gemara asks for Rabbi Yehuda's source, and Ulla again cites motzi shem ra, but the objection is raised that motzi shem ra involves both lashes and payment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative version that applies Ulla's statement to a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda holds that a prohibition without action is not lashed, citing the verse about leftover offerings.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Akiva disagrees, arguing the prohibition lacks action, and asks from where Rabbi Yehuda derives that a prohibition without action is lashed.
Ulla answers that Rabbi Yehuda derives the rule from motzi shem ra (the false bridegroom), but the objection is raised that motzi shem ra involves both lashes and payment, making it a special case.

items.text: Reish Lakish's derivation from edim zomemim
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's derivation from edim zomemim
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish proposes learning from edim zomemim, which is a prohibition without action and incurs lashes, but the objection is that edim zomemim does not require warning. Motzi shem ra is then brought as a counterexample, and the common denominator between them is established: both are prohibitions without action that incur lashes.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish proposes deriving the rule that all prohibitions without action incur lashes from the case of edim zomemim (conspiring witnesses).
The Gemara objects that edim zomemim is not a perfect parallel because they do not require warning (התראה), unlike other prohibitions.

The Gemara brings motzi shem ra as a counterexample that does require warning, and establishes a common denominator (צד השווה) between edim zomemim and motzi shem ra: both are prohibitions without action that incur lashes.

items.text: Refutation of the common denominator
items.text_en: Refutation of the common denominator
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the common denominator includes a fine, but this is not a problem because Rabbi Yehuda does not hold like Rabbi Akiva. Another objection is raised that both have a stringent aspect, but Rabbi Yehuda does not refute based on a stringent aspect.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the common denominator includes a fine (קנס), which would undermine the derivation.
The Gemara answers that this is not a problem because Rabbi Yehuda does not hold like Rabbi Akiva that fines are involved.
The Gemara raises a second objection: both sources have a stringent aspect (צד חמור), which could also undermine the derivation.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yehuda does not refute a common denominator based on a stringent aspect (צד חמור).

items.text: The Rabbis' interpretation of 'lo ta'aneh' and Rabbi Meir's source
items.text_en: The Rabbis' interpretation of 'lo ta'aneh' and Rabbi Meir's source
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis derive from the verse 'lo ta'aneh b're'akha ed shaker', and answers that it is needed for a warning to edim zomemim. Rabbi Meir derives this warning from 'vehannish'arim yishme'u veyira'u', and the Rabbis use that verse for something else.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Rabbis derive from the verse 'lo ta'aneh b're'akha ed shaker' (do not bear false witness against your neighbor).
The Gemara answers that the verse is needed as a warning (אזהרה) for edim zomemim (conspiring witnesses).
The Gemara asks from where Rabbi Meir derives the warning for edim zomemim.
Rabbi Yirmeya answers that Rabbi Meir derives the warning from the verse 'vehannish'arim yishme'u veyira'u' (and the rest shall hear and fear and no longer continue).

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Meir's view
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Meir's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Meir derives the requirement for proclamation from the verse 'yishme'u veyira'u'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Meir derives the requirement for proclamation (הכרזה) from the verse 'יִשְׁמְעוּ וְיִרָאוּ' (they shall hear and fear).

items.text: Mishnah: Division of fines and lashes
items.text_en: Mishnah: Division of fines and lashes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that monetary fines are divided among false witnesses, but lashes are not divided; each witness receives the full forty lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that monetary penalties are divided among false witnesses, but lashes are not divided; each witness receives the full forty lashes.

items.text: Gemara: Source for no division of lashes
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for no division of lashes
items.desc_en: Abaye derives from a verbal analogy that just as capital punishment is not divided, lashes are not divided. Rava offers an alternative derivation from the verse 'ka'asher zamam la'asot le'achiv', noting that monetary fines can be combined but lashes cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (that lashes are not divided) derived?
Abaye derives from a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) on the word 'רשע' (wicked) that just as capital punishment is not divided, lashes are not divided.

Rava offers an alternative derivation: the verse 'כאשר זמם לעשות לאחיו' (as he conspired to do to his brother) requires the punishment to match the intended harm, and since the conspirators intended to cause a single set of lashes, they cannot be divided.
The Gemara objects: If so, the same reasoning should apply to monetary fines, which also require the punishment to match the intended harm, yet the Mishnah states that monetary fines are divided.
Rava resolves: Monetary fines can be combined (since the total amount can be paid jointly), but lashes cannot be combined (each person must receive the full punishment individually).

items.text: Mishnah: Conditions for becoming zomemin
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conditions for becoming zomemin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that witnesses become zomemin only when they are disqualified by their own testimony (e.g., 'you were with us'). If others disqualify them, all are executed. Rabbi Yehuda limits execution to the first group.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that witnesses become zomemin only when they disqualify themselves.
The Mishnah illustrates: if the accused say 'you were with us', the witnesses are not zomemin; but if they say 'you were with us', they are zomemin and executed.
The Tanna Kamma rules that if others disqualify the witnesses, even up to a hundred groups, all are executed.
Rabbi Yehuda argues that this is a 'conspiracy' and only the first group is executed.

items.text: Gemara: Source for self-disqualification
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for self-disqualification
items.desc_en: Rav Adda and the school of Rabbi Yishmael derive from verses that the witnesses must be disqualified by the core of their testimony itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (that witnesses are rendered conspiring only if the body of the testimony is impeached) derived?

Rav Adda answers: The verse 'וְהִנֵּה עֵד שֶׁקֶר הָעֵד שֶׁקֶר עָנָה' (and behold the witness is a false witness; he testified falsely) teaches that the witnesses are not rendered conspiring until the body of the testimony itself is rendered false.

The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught a supporting source: the verse 'לַעֲנוֹת בּוֹ סָרָה' (to bear perverted witness) indicates that the witnesses are not rendered conspiring until the body of the testimony is rendered perverted.

items.text: Rava's cases: Distance and time
items.text_en: Rava's cases: Distance and time
items.desc_en: Rava presents cases where witnesses claim the event occurred in one place or time, and the alibi places them elsewhere. The court assesses whether it was physically possible for them to be at both locations; if not, they are zomemin. The Gemara notes that these rulings are obvious but necessary to counter concerns about unusual travel or camels.

sub.desc_en: Rava presents a case: witnesses testify to a murder east of a building, others claim they were west; if the west cannot see the east, they are conspiring witnesses.
The Gemara asks why this ruling is not obvious, and answers that it was necessary to counter a concern about unusually good eyesight.

items.text: Rava's case: Different day for murder vs. verdict
items.text_en: Rava's case: Different day for murder vs. verdict
items.desc_en: Rava discusses a case where witnesses claim murder on one day, but the alibi places them elsewhere on that day; they are executed because at the time they testified, the defendant was not liable for death. The Gemara compares this to a known Mishnah and notes a distinction for the final verdict.

sub.desc_en: Rava presents a case: witnesses claim murder in Sura on Sunday morning, but alibi places them in Neharde'a that evening; they are conspiring witnesses only if travel between the locations is impossible.
The Gemara asks: Isn't this obvious? Rava's ruling is necessary only to reject a concern about a flying camel.

Rava presents another case: witnesses claim murder on Sunday, but alibi places them elsewhere on Sunday, and the murder actually occurred on Monday or Shabbat eve; the first witnesses are executed because at the time of their testimony the defendant was not yet liable for death.
The Gemara asks: What is Rava teaching us? It cites a known Mishnah that already states that conspiring witnesses are executed even if the accused was guilty.

The Gemara answers: Rava's novel point is the latter clause regarding the verdict — if the witnesses testify after the defendant was already sentenced, they are not executed, because at that time the man was already liable for execution.

items.text: Application to fines and Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Application to fines and Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: The same logic applies to fines for theft and slaughter. If the alibi places the witnesses elsewhere at the time of the act, they pay; but if the alibi relates to the verdict, they do not pay. Rabbi Yehuda repeats his view that only the first group is executed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that the same halakha applies to payments of a fine.

The Gemara presents a case: if witnesses testify that the accused stole and slaughtered on Sunday, and others say the witnesses were with them on Sunday but the act occurred on Monday, the witnesses pay the fine, because at the time of their testimony the accused was not yet liable for payment.

The Gemara presents a contrasting case: if witnesses testify that the accused stole, slaughtered, and was sentenced on Sunday, and others say the witnesses were with them on Sunday but the sentencing was on Shabbat eve, the witnesses do not pay, because at the time of their testimony the accused was already liable for payment.
Rabbi Yehuda repeats his view that this situation is a conspiracy, and only the first set of witnesses is executed.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling about multiple groups of witnesses
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling about multiple groups of witnesses
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that if there are multiple groups of witnesses, only the first group is executed. Rava explains that the Mishnah means: if there is only one group, they are executed; if there are more, they are not. The Gemara objects that the Mishnah explicitly says 'only' (בלבד), implying a different meaning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah's ruling is absolute, even the first group should not be executed.
Rabbi Abahu answers that the Mishnah refers to a case where the first group already executed the defendant.
The Gemara rejects Rabbi Abahu's answer, arguing that if they already killed, the discussion is moot.
Rava explains that the Mishnah means: if there is only one group, they are executed; if more, they are not.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah explicitly says 'only' (בלבד), contradicting Rava's interpretation.

items.text: The case of the woman who brought multiple sets of witnesses
items.text_en: The case of the woman who brought multiple sets of witnesses
items.desc_en: A story is told of a woman who brought witnesses who were disqualified, then brought other witnesses who were not. Reish Lakish ruled that this woman is established as a habitual litigant. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan objected, arguing that if she is established, are all of Israel established? Rabbi Yochanan later realized that Rabbi Elazar had heard this from Reish Lakish and rebuked him for not attributing it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story of a woman who brought witnesses who were disqualified, then brought other witnesses who were not disqualified.
Reish Lakish rules that this woman is established as a habitual litigant (הוחזקה).
Rabbi Elazar objects: if she is established, are all of Israel established?

The Gemara recounts that later, when a similar case came before Rabbi Yochanan, Reish Lakish repeated his ruling, Rabbi Yochanan objected, and then Rabbi Yochanan realized Rabbi Elazar had heard this from Reish Lakish and rebuked him for not attributing it.

items.text: Attribution of Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's positions to Tannaitic opinions
items.text_en: Attribution of Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's positions to Tannaitic opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Reish Lakish follows Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yochanan follows the Rabbis. Reish Lakish explains that even the Rabbis would agree here because the woman is actively seeking witnesses. Rabbi Yochanan explains that even Rabbi Yehuda would agree here because the witnesses know the testimony, unlike the case of the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Reish Lakish follows Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yochanan follows the Rabbis.
Reish Lakish explains that even the Rabbis would agree here because the woman is actively seeking witnesses.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that even Rabbi Yehuda would agree here because the witnesses know the testimony, unlike the case of the Mishnah.

items.text: Mishnah: Timing of execution for conspiring witnesses
items.text_en: Mishnah: Timing of execution for conspiring witnesses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that conspiring witnesses are not executed until the verdict is finalized, contrary to the Sadducees who say until the defendant is executed. The Sages derive this from the verse 'and you shall do to him as he plotted to do to his brother' – his brother is still alive. The verse 'life for life' teaches that they are not executed until the verdict is complete.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that perjured witnesses are not executed until the verdict is finalized, citing the Sadducees' view.
The Sages respond with a verse and a hermeneutic derivation that the witnesses are not executed until the verdict is complete.

items.text: Gemara: Baraita of Rabbi's son and the principle that punishment is not derived through a fortiori reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara: Baraita of Rabbi's son and the principle that punishment is not derived through a fortiori reasoning
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that Rabbi's son ruled: if the witnesses did not kill, they are executed; if they killed, they are not. His father objected with a kal vachomer. The son replied that we learned from his father that we do not punish based on a fortiori reasoning, citing the derivation for the prohibition of a half-sister. The Gemara then derives lashes and exile from the same principle.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states Rabbi's son's ruling: if the witnesses did not kill the accused, they are executed; if they killed, they are not.
Rabbi objects with a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: if witnesses who did not kill are executed, those who killed should certainly be executed.
Rabbi's son replies that his father taught the principle that punishment is not derived through a fortiori reasoning (אין עונשין מן הדין).

A baraita is cited showing that for the prohibition of a half-sister, the Torah itself wrote an explicit verse rather than relying on a קל וחומר, establishing the principle that punishment is not derived through a fortiori reasoning.
The Gemara notes that the warning (אזהרה) for the half-sister is also derived from an explicit verse, not from a קל וחומר, extending the principle to warnings as well.
The Gemara derives that those liable for lashes (חייבי מלקיות) are also subject to the same principle, using a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the word 'רָשָׁע' (wicked).
The Gemara derives that those liable for exile (חייבי גליות) are also subject to the same principle, using a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the word 'רֹצֵחַ' (murderer).

items.text: The story of Rabbi Yehuda ben Tabai and Shimon ben Shetach
items.text_en: The story of Rabbi Yehuda ben Tabai and Shimon ben Shetach
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Tabai said he executed a conspiring witness to refute the Sadducees. Shimon ben Shetach rebuked him for shedding innocent blood, as the Sages require both witnesses to be disqualified. Rabbi Yehuda accepted not to rule without Shimon ben Shetach. He prostrated on the witness's grave, and his voice was heard; he explained it was his own voice. Rav Acha bar Rava questioned whether he might have argued with him in court or appeased him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Tabai declares that he executed a conspiring witness (עֵד זוֹמֵם) to refute the Sadducees, who claimed such witnesses are only executed after the accused is killed.
Shimon ben Shetach rebukes Rabbi Yehuda ben Tabai for shedding innocent blood, citing the Sages' rule that conspiring witnesses are only executed when both are disqualified.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Tabai accepts not to rule without Shimon ben Shetach, prostrates on the witness's grave, and explains that the voice heard is his own, not the dead man's.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava questions whether Rabbi Yehuda ben Tabai might have argued with the witness in court or appeased him, rather than truly executing him.

items.text: Mishnah: Comparison of two and three witnesses
items.text_en: Mishnah: Comparison of two and three witnesses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah derives from the verse 'on the testimony of two or three witnesses' that three witnesses can disqualify two, and two can disqualify three, and even a hundred. Rabbi Shimon requires all witnesses to be disqualified. Rabbi Akiva says the third comes to be stringent, and derives reward for joining a mitzvah. If one witness is found invalid, the entire testimony is void.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah derives from the verse that three witnesses can disqualify two, and even a hundred, via the word 'עדים'.
The Mishnah opens by citing the verse and deriving that three witnesses can disqualify two, two can disqualify three, and even a hundred.
Rabbi Shimon states that just as two witnesses are not executed unless both are disqualified, so too three require all three to be disqualified, and the same applies to a hundred.
Rabbi Shimon rules that all witnesses must be disqualified for execution, even up to a hundred.
Rabbi Akiva says the third witness comes not to leniency but to stringency, making his law like the others.
Rabbi Akiva says the third witness comes to be stringent, not lenient, making his law like the others.
Rabbi Akiva derives a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if the Torah punishes one who joins transgressors, how much more will it reward one who joins those performing a מצוה (commandment).
The Mishnah draws a קל וחומר (a fortiori) that if the Torah punishes those who join sinners, it certainly rewards those who join doers of מצוות (commandments).
The Mishnah concludes: just as with two witnesses, if one is found related or invalid the testimony is void, so too with three or even a hundred.
The Mishnah rules that if one witness is a relative or invalid, the entire testimony is void, even up to a hundred.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Yosei holds that in capital cases, if some witnesses are found to be relatives or invalid, the testimony is void, but in monetary cases it stands with the remaining witnesses. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi argues that both capital and monetary cases are treated the same. The Mishnah then asks: if the witnesses were not warned, what can two brothers who saw a murder do?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei states that the rule about invalid witnesses applies only in capital cases, but in monetary cases the testimony stands with the remaining witnesses.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi argues that both monetary and capital cases are treated the same regarding invalid witnesses.
The Mishnah asks: if the witnesses were not warned, what can two brothers who saw a murder do?

items.text: Gemara: Rava's condition of 'within the time of speech'
items.text_en: Gemara: Rava's condition of 'within the time of speech'
items.desc_en: Rava states that the Mishnah's ruling applies only when all witnesses testified within the time it takes to speak (tokh kedei dibbur). Rav Acha from Difti asks Ravina to define this interval, and Ravina explains it is the time for a student to greet his teacher. They then clarify that each witness must testify within the time of speech of the previous one.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that the Mishnah's rule applies only when all witnesses testified within כדי דיבור (the time it takes to speak a short phrase).
Rav Acha midifti asks Ravina: what is the measure of כדי דיבור (the time it takes a student to greet a rabbi)?
Ravina answers that each witness must testify within כדי דיבור (the speaking time) of the other.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Akiva's statement and the principle of 'yekum davar'
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Akiva's statement and the principle of 'yekum davar'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Akiva's statement that a third witness does not join to disqualify the others. Rav Pappa asks Abaye: if so, could the victim himself save the murderer? Abaye answers that this applies when the victim was killed from behind. Similarly, the one who was raped could save the rapist? Again, when the rape was from behind. When Rav Pappa asks about a murderer and a rapist saving each other, Abaye is silent. Rava later explains that the verse 'yekum davar' (the matter shall stand) refers to those who establish the matter, not the accused.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Akiva's statement that a third witness does not disqualify the testimony of two valid witnesses.
Rav Pappa asks Abaye: if so, could the victim himself testify to save the defendant?
Abaye answers that the victim cannot testify because the murderer struck him from behind, so he did not see the act.
Rav Pappa asks: could the victim of bestiality testify to save the animal?
Abaye answers that the victim did not see the act because it happened from behind.
Rav Pappa asks: could the murderer or the one who engaged in bestiality testify to save themselves?
Abaye is silent, unable to answer.
Rava resolves the difficulty by citing the verse 'יָקוּם דָּבָר' (the matter shall be established), which refers to those who establish the matter, not the accused.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's question about two brothers
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's question about two brothers
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: how do we address the two brothers who saw a murder? Rava explains that we ask them: did you come to see or to testify? If they say they came to testify, and one is found to be a relative or invalid, their testimony is void. If they say they came to see, then what can two brothers do who saw a murder?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: how do we address the two brothers who saw a murder?
Rava explains that we ask the brothers: did you come to testify or just to see? If they came to testify, their testimony is void; if to see, they are permitted.

items.text: Conclusion: Ruling on the dispute
items.text_en: Conclusion: Ruling on the dispute
items.desc_en: It is stated: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei. Rav Nachman says the halakha follows Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Nachman states that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Combined testimony and Rabbi Yosei's requirement
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Combined testimony and Rabbi Yosei's requirement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where two pairs of witnesses see the defendant from different windows, with a single warning in the middle. If the pairs can see each other, they form one testimony; if not, they are two separate testimonies. Rabbi Yosei argues that the defendant is never executed unless two witnesses warn him, citing the verse 'על פי שנים עדים'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of two pairs of witnesses seeing the defendant from different windows with a single warning in between, and rules that if they can see each other they form one testimony, otherwise two, with consequences for false testimony.
Rabbi Yosei argues that the defendant is never executed unless two witnesses warn him, citing the verse 'על פי שנים עדים', and adds that the court must not hear testimony through an interpreter.

items.text: Gemara's derivation of 'unified testimony'
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation of 'unified testimony'
items.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya quotes Rav: The source for disqualifying 'unified testimony' (where witnesses see the act but not each other) is the verse 'לֹא יוּמַת עַל פִּי עֵד אֶחָד', interpreted as 'one at a time' (אחד אחד).

sub.text: Rav Zutra bar Toviya citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Zutra bar Toviya in Rav's name opens by asking the source for disqualifying 'unified testimony' (עדות מיוחדת).
The Gemara questions the meaning of 'עֵד אֶחָד' (one witness) in the verse, noting that if it means a literal single witness, that was already derived earlier.
The Gemara answers that 'אֶחָד' means 'one at a time' (אחד אחד), disqualifying witnesses who see the event separately.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav and Rav Pappa's question
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav and Rav Pappa's question
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav's interpretation, stating that two witnesses seeing from different windows without seeing each other do not combine, and even if they see sequentially through one window they do not combine. Rav Pappa asks Abaye: if separate windows (where each sees the whole act) do not combine, then sequential viewing (where each sees only part) certainly should not? Abaye responds that the baraita's case is needed for the case of one who has intercourse with a forbidden relative (בועל את הערוה).

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav's interpretation, stating that two witnesses seeing from different windows without seeing each other do not combine, and even sequential viewing through one window does not combine.
Rav Pappa asks Abaye: if separate windows (where each sees the whole act) do not combine, then sequential viewing (where each sees only part) certainly should not?
Abaye responds that the baraita's case is needed specifically for the case of one who has intercourse with a forbidden relative (בועל את הערוה).

items.text: Rava's rulings on warning and combined testimony
items.text_en: Rava's rulings on warning and combined testimony
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if the witnesses see the one who warns, or the warner sees them, they combine into one testimony. He also states that the warning (hatra'ah) can be given even by the defendant himself or even by a demon.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if the witnesses see the warner or the warner sees them, they combine into one testimony.
Rava states that the warning (hatra'ah) can be given even by the defendant himself or even by a demon.

items.text: Rav Nachman: Unified testimony valid in monetary cases
items.text_en: Rav Nachman: Unified testimony valid in monetary cases
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that unified testimony is valid in monetary cases, as the verse 'לֹא יוּמַת' applies only to capital cases. Rav Zutra objects: if so, in capital cases such testimony should acquit, but the Mishnah says the defendant and the false witnesses are executed. The objection remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that unified testimony is valid in monetary cases, deriving from the verse 'לֹא יוּמַת' that the disqualification applies only to capital cases.

Rav Zutra objects: if unified testimony is invalid only for capital cases, then in capital cases it should acquit, but the Mishnah rules that the defendant and false witnesses are executed, leaving the objection unresolved.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's view on warning and the identity of the Tanna
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's view on warning and the identity of the Tanna
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: Does Rabbi Yosei really hold that warning is always required? But a Mishnah states Rabbi Yosei says a 'hater' (sonei) is executed because he is considered warned. Abaye answers that the latter is Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, who holds that a scholar (chaver) needs no warning, as warning was only given to distinguish between intentional and unintentional acts.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye whether Rabbi Yosei truly holds that warning is always required, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Yosei says a 'hater' (שונא) is executed because he is considered already warned.

Abaye answers that the Mishnah's ruling is from Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, who holds that a scholar (חבר) needs no warning, since warning was only given to distinguish between intentional and unintentional acts.

items.text: The court not hearing through an interpreter: Rava's practice
items.text_en: The court not hearing through an interpreter: Rava's practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Mishnah's second teaching: the court should not hear testimony through an interpreter. It relates that when certain 'la'ozei' (foreigners) came before Rava, he placed an interpreter between them. The Gemara questions this, and explains that Rava understood what they said but could not respond fluently.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah's second teaching is cited: the court should not hear testimony through an interpreter.
The Gemara relates that when certain foreigners (לָעוֹזֵי) came before Rava, he placed an interpreter between them.
The Gemara objects: how could Rava act this way, given the Mishnah's ruling that the court should not hear through an interpreter?
The Gemara resolves: Rava understood what they said but could not respond fluently, so the interpreter was only for his reply, not for receiving testimony.

items.text: Opening anecdote about witnesses
items.text_en: Opening anecdote about witnesses
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa considers whether distant relatives of the borrower and lender are valid witnesses, but Rav Huna bar Yehoshua objects that the lender always pursues the guarantor if the borrower lacks funds.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces Il'a and Toviya as relatives of the guarantor, and Rav Pappa considers them distant from the borrower and lender.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua objects to Rav Pappa that if the borrower lacks funds, the lender always pursues the guarantor, making the witnesses relevant to the lender.

items.text: Mishnah: Verdicts and Sanhedrin
items.text_en: Mishnah: Verdicts and Sanhedrin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a condemned person flees and returns to the same court, the verdict is not reopened; witnesses can testify to the verdict anywhere. It then discusses the Sanhedrin's jurisdiction in and outside the Land, and differing views on how often a court should execute.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that if a condemned person flees and returns to the same court, the verdict is not reopened, and witnesses can testify to the verdict anywhere.
The Mishnah states that the Sanhedrin functions both in and outside the Land, and a court that executes once a week is called destructive.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Azaryah says a court that executes once every seventy years is called destructive.
Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva say that if they had been on the Sanhedrin, no person would ever have been executed.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that such a court would increase murderers in Israel.

items.text: Gemara: Reopening verdicts in different courts
items.text_en: Gemara: Reopening verdicts in different courts
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah implies a verdict is reopened only before a different court, but the later clause allows witnesses to testify anywhere. Abaye resolves this by distinguishing between courts in the Land of Israel and those outside, citing a baraita of Rabbi Yehuda ben Dosteai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction: the Mishnah's first clause implies a verdict is only reopened before a different court, but the later clause allows witnesses to testify anywhere, implying the verdict can be reopened even before the same court.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between courts in the Land of Israel and those outside the Land.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Yehuda ben Dosteai
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Yehuda ben Dosteai
sub.desc_en: A baraita citing Rabbi Yehuda ben Dosteai in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Shatach supports Abaye's distinction: one who flees from the Land to outside has his verdict upheld, but from outside to the Land the verdict is reopened due to the merit of the Land of Israel.

items.text: Source for Sanhedrin outside the Land
items.text_en: Source for Sanhedrin outside the Land
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from a verse that the Sanhedrin functions both in the Land and outside, but the verse 'in your gates' limits the requirement to appoint courts in every district and city only within the Land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the Mishnah's statement that the Sanhedrin functions both in the Land and outside.
The baraita cites the verse 'וְהָיוּ אֵלֶּה לָכֶם לְחֻקַּת מִשְׁפָּט לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם' to derive that the Sanhedrin functions both in the Land and outside.

The Tanna Kamma resolves the apparent contradiction: the verse 'בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ' limits the requirement to appoint courts in every district and city only within the Land, while outside the Land courts are appointed only in every district.

items.text: Inquiry on 'destructive' court
items.text_en: Inquiry on 'destructive' court
items.desc_en: A query is raised whether a court that executes once in seventy years is called 'destructive' or whether that is normal practice; the issue remains unresolved (תיקו).

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises a question: is a Sanhedrin that kills once in seventy years called 'חוֹבְלָנִית' (destructive), or is that a normal practice?
The question remains unresolved (תֵּיקוּ).

items.text: How Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva would avoid executions
items.text_en: How Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva would avoid executions
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva would prevent executions: by questioning witnesses about details that could show the victim was a treifa or the wound was in a vulnerable spot. For adultery, they would ask if the act was as visible as a stylus in a tube, while the Sages follow Shmuel's approach of judging adulterers by their behavior.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva would have avoided executions, given their claim that if they had been on the Sanhedrin no one would ever have been executed.
Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar answer that they would ask the witnesses whether the victim was a טריפה (a person with a fatal condition) or physically intact, to find grounds for acquittal.
Rav Ashi adds that even if the victim was intact, the witnesses might be asked whether the fatal wound was in a vulnerable spot (מקום סייף), where a small wound could kill.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva would have avoided executions in cases of adultery with a forbidden relative.
Abaye and Rava answer that they would ask the witnesses whether the act of adultery was as visible as a stylus in a tube (כמכחול בשפופרת), a standard of visibility required for conviction.

The Gemara notes that the Sages (רבנן) judged adulterers according to Shmuel's approach: they are convicted from the moment they appear like adulterers (משֶׁיִּרְאוּ כמנאפים), i.e., when their behavior clearly indicates adultery.

items.text: Transition and new Mishnah on manslaughter
items.text_en: Transition and new Mishnah on manslaughter
items.desc_en: The daf concludes the previous chapter and begins a new Mishnah listing cases of inadvertent killers who are exiled, distinguishing between actions that are typical (e.g., lowering a barrel) and those that are unusual (e.g., pulling a wheel).

sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes the previous chapter with the standard formula 'we return to you, How the Witnesses...'.
The Mishnah opens a new topic listing cases of inadvertent killers who are exiled, beginning with typical actions like rolling a wheel or lowering a barrel that cause death.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rule of descent
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rule of descent
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one was ascending a ladder and fell upon another and killed him, he is not exiled. The general rule: any killing through a downward motion (דרך ירידתו) requires exile, but not through an upward motion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule of descent: a killing through a downward motion requires exile, but not through an upward motion.

items.text: Gemara: Source for the rule
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for the rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the Mishnah's rule. Samuel answers that the verse 'and he fell upon him and died' implies a fall in the manner of falling (דרך נפילה), i.e., downward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters derived?
Shmuel answers that the verse 'וַיַּפֵּל עָלָיו וַיָּמֹת' (and he fell upon him and he died) implies a fall in the manner of falling.

items.text: Derashot on 'בשגגה' and 'בבלי דעת'
items.text_en: Derashot on 'בשגגה' and 'בבלי דעת'
items.desc_en: The Tanna derives from 'בשגגה' that it excludes an intentional killer, and from 'בבלי דעת' that it excludes one who intended to kill. Rava clarifies that 'בשגגה' excludes one who thinks it is permitted, and Abaye objects that such a person is an ones (forced). Rava responds that one who thinks it is permitted is close to intentional. Rabba explains that 'בבלי דעת' excludes one who intended to kill an animal, a gentile, or a non-viable fetus but killed a person, an Israelite, or a viable child.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna derives from the verses 'בשגגה' and 'בבלי דעת' that the unintentional killer excludes an intentional killer and one who intended to kill.
The Gemara objects that the exclusion of an intentional killer is obvious, since he is liable for capital punishment.
Rava reinterprets the exclusion as referring to one who thought the act was permitted, not an obvious intentional killer.
Abaye objects that one who thinks it is permitted is considered an ones (forced) and should not be excluded.
Rava rejects the objection, asserting that one who thinks it is permitted is close to an intentional killer and thus excluded.
The Gemara again objects that the exclusion of one who intended to kill is obvious, since he is liable for capital punishment.
Rabba explains that the exclusion refers to one who intended to kill an animal, a gentile, or a non-viable fetus but killed a person, an Israelite, or a viable child.

items.text: Derashot on additional verses
items.text_en: Derashot on additional verses
items.desc_en: The Tanna expounds verses: 'אם בפתע' excludes a corner (קרן זוית); 'בלא איבה' excludes an enemy; 'הדפו' means pushing with his body; 'או השליך עליו' includes a descent that is necessary for ascent; 'בלא צדיה' excludes one who intended for one side but it went to another; 'ואשר לא צדה' excludes one who intended to throw two but threw four; 'ואשר יבא את רעהו ביער' teaches that just as the forest is a place where both the injured and the injurer have permission to enter, so too any place where both have permission.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna expounds a series of verses from the Torah to derive specific exclusions and inclusions regarding the laws of accidental killing and exile.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's question to Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's question to Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu asks Rabbi Yochanan: if one was ascending a ladder and a rung slipped from under him and fell and killed someone, is this considered an ascent or a descent? Rabbi Yochanan answers: you have already touched upon a descent that is necessary for ascent (ירידה שהיא צורך עלייה).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu asks Rabbi Yochanan: if one was ascending a ladder and a rung slipped from under him and fell and killed someone, is this considered an ascent or a descent?
Rabbi Yochanan answers: you have already touched upon a descent that is necessary for ascent (יְרִידָה שֶׁהִיא צוֹרֶךְ עֲלִיָּה).

items.text: Objection and resolution with the butcher (קצב)
items.text_en: Objection and resolution with the butcher (קצב)
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the Mishnah's general rule: the phrase 'שלא בדרך ירידתו' must come to include something, perhaps this case? It then argues that 'בדרך ירידתו' comes to include a butcher (קצב). The Gemara resolves contradictory baraitot about a butcher: one says if he cuts in front of him he is liable, behind him exempt; another says the opposite; another says both are liable; another says both are exempt. The resolution: these refer to different scenarios of descent and ascent relative to the butcher's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from the Mishnah's general rule: the phrase 'שלא בדרך ירידתו' must come to include this case of a rung falling during ascent.
The Gemara counters: by your reasoning, what does the phrase 'בדרך ירידתו' come to include?
The Gemara answers: the phrase 'בדרך ירידתו' comes to include a butcher (קצב), and similarly here it comes to include a butcher.
The Gemara cites four contradictory baraitot about a butcher's liability when cutting in front of or behind him.
The Gemara resolves the first two baraitot: one refers to a descent in front of him and an ascent behind him, the other to an ascent in front and a descent behind.
The Gemara resolves the remaining two baraitot: one refers to a descent both in front and behind, the other to an ascent both in front and behind.

items.text: Dispute among Tannaim about the ladder case
items.text_en: Dispute among Tannaim about the ladder case
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that a dispute among Tannaim about the ladder case (one says liable, another says exempt) reflects a disagreement over whether it is a descent or ascent. It rejects this, saying all agree it is an ascent, but the dispute is about damages vs. exile. Alternatively, both are about exile but differ on whether the rung was worm-eaten (אתלע) or not, or whether it was checked (מיהדק) or not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute among Tannaim about the ladder case (one liable, one exempt) reflects a disagreement over whether it is a descent or an ascent.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion, stating that all agree it is an ascent, and the dispute is about damages vs. exile.
The Gemara offers an alternative: both cases deal with exile, but differ on whether the rung was worm-eaten (אתלע) or not.
The Gemara offers another alternative: both cases involve a non-worm-eaten rung, but differ on whether it was checked (מיהדק) or not.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on the axe head
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on the axe head
items.desc_en: The Mishnah: if the iron (axe head) slipped from its handle and killed, Rabbi says he is not exiled, but the Sages say he is exiled. If it split from the wood (the handle), Rabbi says he is exiled, and the Sages say he is not. The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi argues with the Sages based on the verse 'ונשל הברזל מן העץ'. Rav Chiyya bar Ashi says in the name of Rav that both derive from the same verse: Rabbi holds 'יש אם למסורת' (the written form 'ונשל' is read as 'ונשל' meaning it slipped from the wood), while the Rabbis hold 'יש אם למקרא' (the reading 'ונשל' means it was knocked off). The Gemara questions whether Rabbi indeed holds 'יש אם למסורת'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents two cases: if the iron slipped from its handle, Rabbi exempts and the Sages obligate exile; if it split from the wood, Rabbi obligates and the Sages exempt.

A baraita records Rabbi's argument to the Sages: the verse says 'מִן הָעֵץ' (from the wood), not 'from its handle', and a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from the upper 'עֵץ' to the lower 'עֵץ' shows it refers to a split piece of wood.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi reports in Rav's name that both Rabbi and the Sages derive from the same verse: Rabbi holds 'יש אם למסורת' (the written form 'ונשל' means it slipped from the wood), while the Sages hold 'יש אם למקרא' (the reading 'ונשל' means it was knocked off).
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi indeed holds the principle of 'יש אם למסורת' (the written form is authoritative).

items.text: Gemara's citation of Rav Yitzchak's statement about 'yesh em la-mikra'
items.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rav Yitzchak's statement about 'yesh em la-mikra'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi, Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz, Beit Shammai, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Akiva all hold the principle that the text has a parent (yesh em la-mikra). This is the basis for the earlier statement 've'od' (and furthermore).

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef
sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a statement from Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan.
Rabbi Yochanan lists Rabbi, Rabbi Yehuda ben Roetz, Beit Shammai, Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Akiva, all of whom hold the principle that the text has a parent (yesh em la-mikra).
The Gemara concludes that this is the basis for the earlier statement 've'od' (and furthermore).

items.text: Rav Pappa's case of indirect causation and the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's case of indirect causation and the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa presents a case where one throws a stone at a palm tree, dislodging dates that then kill someone. This falls under the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis regarding indirect causation (ko'ach kocho). The Gemara clarifies that this is not obvious, as one might think it is considered like ko'ach kocho, but the teaching shows otherwise. It then explains how ko'ach kocho applies according to Rabbi, using a case of a stone hitting a bone that then hits a clod of earth that dislodges dates.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa presents a case of indirect causation (throwing a clod at a palm tree, dislodging dates that kill) and states it falls under the dispute between Rabbi and the Rabbis.
The Gemara questions why this case is not obvious, as it seems identical to the dispute.
The Gemara explains that the teaching is necessary lest one think the case is like ko'ach kocho (a force generated by a force) and exempt; Rav Pappa teaches that it is not.
