The Gemara asks how one can find a case of ko'ach kocho according to Rabbi that would be exempt from exile.
The Gemara provides an example: one throws a clod that hits a branch, which then hits a cluster of dates, dislodging dates that kill; this is ko'ach kocho.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of throwing a stone and the exemption for the victim intercepting
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of throwing a stone and the exemption for the victim intercepting
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who throws a stone into the public domain and kills is liable to exile. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov exempts if the victim put his head out after the stone was thrown. If one throws into his own courtyard, liability depends on whether the victim had permission to enter. Abba Shaul derives from the verse 'as one goes into the forest' that only a place where both have permission qualifies, excluding a father hitting his son, a teacher disciplining his student, and a court agent.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the ruling that one who throws a stone into the public domain and kills is liable to exile.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov states that if the victim placed his head out after the stone left the thrower's hand, the thrower is exempt.

The Mishnah rules that if one throws a stone into his own courtyard, liability depends on whether the victim had permission to enter, deriving from the verse 'as one goes into the forest' that both must have equal access.

Abba Shaul adds that just as the cutting of wood in the verse is optional, so too all cases of exile involve optional acts, excluding a father striking his son, a teacher disciplining his student, and a court agent.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the case of throwing into the public domain
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the case of throwing into the public domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how throwing into the public domain can be unintentional, as it seems intentional. Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak answers that it is when one is demolishing his wall. The Gemara objects that he should have looked, so it is refined to demolishing at night. Still an objection, so it is refined to demolishing into a garbage dump. The Gemara then analyzes the nature of the dump: if frequented by many, he is negligent; if not, it is an accident. Rav Pappa resolves that it is a dump used at night but not by day, and occasionally someone is there, so it is neither fully negligent nor fully accidental.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how throwing into the public domain can be unintentional, as it seems intentional.
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak answers that it is when one is demolishing his wall.
The Gemara objects that he should have looked.
The Gemara refines the case to demolishing at night.
The Gemara objects that even at night he should have looked.
The Gemara refines further to demolishing into a garbage dump.
The Gemara analyzes the nature of the dump.
The Gemara distinguishes: if the dump is frequented by many, he is negligent; if not, it is an accident.
Rav Pappa resolves that it is a dump used at night but not by day, and occasionally someone is there, so it is neither fully negligent nor fully accidental.

items.text: Derivation of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's exemption from 'u'matza'
items.text_en: Derivation of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's exemption from 'u'matza'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the word 'u'matza' (and finds) an exclusion for one who brings himself to be found (i.e., intercepts the stone). This is the source of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's ruling. The Gemara then questions whether 'matza' always implies something that exists from the outset, citing a contradiction from the laws of redemption of a field. Rava resolves that the meaning is determined by context: in the redemption case, it parallels 'his hand reaches' (present), while in the golah case, it parallels 'forest' (something that exists from the outset).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the word 'וּמָצָא' (and finds) an exclusion for one who brings himself to be found, establishing Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's ruling that if the victim intercepts the stone after it leaves the thrower's hand, the thrower is exempt.

The Gemara questions whether 'וּמָצָא' (and finds) always implies something that exists from the outset, citing a contradiction from the laws of redemption of a field where 'וּמָצָא' is interpreted as an exclusion for something that is already present (not newly acquired).

Rava resolves that the meaning of 'וּמָצָא' is determined by context: in the redemption case it parallels 'וְהִשִּׂיגָה יָדוֹ' (his hand reaches), implying present tense, while in the golah case it parallels 'יַעַר' (forest), implying something that exists from the outset.

items.text: Discussion of Abba Shaul's derivation from 'chatavat eitzim'
items.text_en: Discussion of Abba Shaul's derivation from 'chatavat eitzim'
items.desc_en: A certain Sage questions Rava: how do we know that 'chatavat eitzim' (wood cutting) in the verse refers to a permitted act? Perhaps it refers to the wood for the sukkah or the arrangement, and even so the Torah says he is exiled. Rava answers that since if one finds already cut wood he does not cut, it is not a mitzvah, so here too it is not a mitzvah. Ravina then objects with the cases of father, teacher, and court agent: there too, if the child had already learned, there is no mitzvah to hit, yet they are exempt. Rava responds that even if the child is learned, it is still a mitzvah, as per the verse 'discipline your son and he will give you rest'.

sub.text: A certain Sage's question to Rava
sub.text_en: A certain Sage's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: A certain Sage questions Rava: how do we know that 'chatavat eitzim' (wood cutting) in the verse refers to a permitted act? Perhaps it refers to wood for the sukkah or the arrangement, and even so the Torah says he is exiled.
Rava answers that since if one finds already cut wood he does not cut, it is not a mitzvah, so here too it is not a mitzvah.
Ravina objects with the cases of father, teacher, and court agent: there too, if the child had already learned, there is no mitzvah to hit, yet they are exempt.
Rava responds that even if the child is learned, it is still a mitzvah, as per the verse 'discipline your son and he will give you rest'.

items.text: Rava's retraction and the final proof from 'asher'
items.text_en: Rava's retraction and the final proof from 'asher'
items.desc_en: Rava retracts his previous statement, arguing that the forest is a place where one may enter or not, but if it were a mitzvah, one would be obligated to enter. Rav Ada bar Ahava challenges this, pointing out that the word 'asher' (who) does not always imply volition, citing the case of one who becomes impure from a corpse (a mitzvah) where the verse still uses 'asher'. The Gemara concludes with a partial verse, indicating the discussion continues.

sub.desc_en: Rava retracts his previous statement, arguing that the forest is a place where one may enter or not, but if it were a mitzvah, one would be obligated to enter.

Rav Ada bar Ahava challenges Rava, pointing out that the word 'asher' (who) does not always imply volition, citing the case of one who becomes impure from a corpse (a mitzvah) where the verse still uses 'asher'.
The Gemara begins to respond with a distinction, but the verse is cut off, indicating the discussion continues.

items.text: Clarifying the source for the exemption of a tevul yom and mechusar kippurim
items.text_en: Clarifying the source for the exemption of a tevul yom and mechusar kippurim
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the derivation from 'tamei yihyeh' and explains that it is needed for other halakhot. The speaker clarifies that he was referring to the phrase 'od tumato'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the phrase 'tamei yihyeh' can exempt a tevul yom and mechusar kippurim, since it seems to include all cases.
The answer explains that the phrase 'tamei yihyeh' is needed for other halakhot, and the speaker clarifies he was referring to the phrase 'od tumato'.

items.text: Debate on the verse 'becharish uva'katzir tishbot' and the nature of plowing and reaping
items.text_en: Debate on the verse 'becharish uva'katzir tishbot' and the nature of plowing and reaping
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael dispute the meaning of the verse. A rabbi questions Rava about whether plowing is always a permitted act, and Rava responds. Ravina challenges Rava with a baraita about a father striking his son, and Rava retracts his earlier statement.

sub.text: Tannaic dispute (Rabbi Akiva vs. Rabbi Yishmael)
sub.text_en: Tannaic dispute (Rabbi Akiva vs. Rabbi Yishmael)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael dispute the meaning of the verse 'becharish uva'katzir tishbot' regarding the prohibition of plowing and reaping in the Sabbatical year.

sub.text: A certain rabbi's question to Rava
sub.text_en: A certain rabbi's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: A certain rabbi questions Rava: how do we know that plowing is a permitted act (reshut) and not a mitzvah like the plowing of the omer?
Rava answers that since if one finds a field already plowed he does not plow again, it shows plowing is not a mitzvah.
Ravina challenges Rava with a baraita about a father striking his son, a teacher disciplining his student, and a court agent, arguing that even if the act could be avoided, it is still a mitzvah.
Rava distinguishes the case of the father and teacher, noting that even if the son is already learned, the act remains a mitzvah as per the verse 'yaser binkha veyanichekha'.

Rava retracts his earlier statement, arguing that reaping is analogous to plowing: if one finds the field already reaped, he does not reap, but for the omer, one must reap and bring it, proving it is a mitzvah.

items.text: Mishnah: Who may be exiled by whom
items.text_en: Mishnah: Who may be exiled by whom
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a father is exiled by his son, a son by his father, and all are exiled by Israelites except for a ger toshav, who is only exiled by another ger toshav.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules of exile: a father is exiled by his son, a son by his father, all are exiled by Israelites except a ger toshav who is only exiled by another ger toshav.

items.text: Gemara: Reconciling the Mishnah with the earlier baraita about a father striking his son
items.text_en: Gemara: Reconciling the Mishnah with the earlier baraita about a father striking his son
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a father can be exiled by his son if a father who strikes his son is exempt. It answers that the exemption applies only when the father is teaching his son a trade, but here the son was not learning a trade.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah can state that a father is exiled by his son, given the earlier baraita that exempts a father who strikes his son, and answers that the baraita refers to a case where the son was learning a trade.

The Gemara clarifies that the exemption applies only when the father is teaching his son the craft of carpentry, which is a מצוה (commandment), but here the son was learning a different trade, so the father is liable.

items.text: Resolving a contradiction about a son who kills his father
items.text_en: Resolving a contradiction about a son who kills his father
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between the Mishnah and a verse excluding one who strikes his father. Rav Kahana resolves it by attributing the views to Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis. Rava offers an alternative explanation that the verse excludes one who wounds his father accidentally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says a son goes into exile for killing his father, but a verse excludes one who strikes his father.
Rav Kahana resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Shimon and the verse to the Rabbis.

It explains that according to Rabbi Shimon, who holds strangulation is more severe than decapitation, an accidental killing by decapitation is atoned for by exile, but accidental killing by strangulation is not.

It explains that according to the Rabbis, who hold decapitation is more severe than strangulation, killing one's father accidentally is a case of accidental decapitation, which is atoned for by exile.
Rava offers an alternative explanation: the verse excludes one who accidentally wounds his father (without killing him), teaching that only killing, not wounding, triggers exile.

items.text: Clarifying the inclusion of a slave and Cuthean in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Clarifying the inclusion of a slave and Cuthean in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'all are exiled by Israelites' includes a slave and a Cuthean. It then questions how an Israelite can be flogged by a Cuthean, and resolves the issue by discussing cases of false testimony or a blow that does not require exile.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'all are exiled by Israelites' comes to include.
The Gemara answers that it comes to include a slave and a Cuthean.
A baraita is cited that explicitly states a slave and Cuthean are exiled and flogged by an Israelite, and vice versa.
The Gemara objects: while a slave or Cuthean can be flogged by an Israelite for cursing him, how can an Israelite be flogged by a Cuthean?
The Gemara rejects the possibility of flogging for cursing, citing the verse 'and a prince among your people you shall not curse' — only one who acts like your people.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that the case is where the Cuthean testified against the Israelite and was found to be a conspiring witness (edim zomemim).
The Gemara objects: if the same logic applies to a slave, is a slave even eligible to testify?

sub.text: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika answers that we are dealing with a case where the Cuthean struck the Israelite a blow that does not require exile.

items.text: Opening statement: a blow worth less than a perutah
items.text_en: Opening statement: a blow worth less than a perutah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami quoting Rabbi Yochanan states that one who strikes another with a blow worth less than a perutah is lashed, and we do not compare the blow to a curse.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who strikes another with a blow worth less than a perutah is lashed, and we do not compare a blow to a curse.

items.text: Contradiction about ger toshav's status
items.text_en: Contradiction about ger toshav's status
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised: the mishnah says a ger toshav is excluded from exile when killed by a Jew, implying he is a gentile, but the seifa says a ger toshav is exiled for killing another ger toshav. Rav Kahana resolves: the first case is a ger toshav who killed a Jew, the second is a ger toshav who killed another ger toshav. Another contradiction is raised from verses about cities of refuge, and Rav Kahana resolves similarly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the mishnah's exclusion of a ger toshav from exile when killed by a Jew implies he is a gentile.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from the seifa, which states that a ger toshav is exiled for killing another ger toshav, implying he is not a gentile.
Rav Kahana resolves the contradiction: the first clause refers to a ger toshav who killed a Jew, the seifa to a ger toshav who killed another ger toshav.
Another contradiction is raised from verses: one verse includes the ger toshav in cities of refuge, another excludes him.
Rav Kahana resolves similarly: the exclusion applies to a ger toshav who killed a Jew, the inclusion to a ger toshav who killed another ger toshav.

items.text: Baraita: ger and gentile who kill are executed
items.text_en: Baraita: ger and gentile who kill are executed
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a ger and a gentile who kill are executed, comparing the ger to a gentile: just as a gentile is executed whether he kills a fellow gentile or a Jew, so too a ger is executed in both cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that states a ger and a gentile who kill are executed, comparing the ger to a gentile: just as a gentile is executed whether he kills a fellow gentile or a Jew, so too a ger is executed in both cases.

items.text: Rav Chisda's resolution: descending vs. ascending
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's resolution: descending vs. ascending
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction: if the ger killed in a descending manner (where a Jew would be exiled), he is exiled; if in an ascending manner (where a Jew is exempt), he is executed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda resolves: the baraita refers to killing דרך ירידה (in a downward motion), where a Jew would be exiled, so the ger is also exiled; the mishnah refers to killing דרך עלייה (in an upward motion), where a Jew is exempt, so the ger is executed.

items.text: Rava's objection: kal vachomer
items.text_en: Rava's objection: kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Rava objects with a kal vachomer: if in a descending case where a Jew is exiled, the ger is also exiled, then in an ascending case where a Jew is exempt, the ger should certainly be executed?

sub.desc_en: Rava objects with a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if for a downward motion, where a Jew is exiled, the ger is also exiled, then for an upward motion, where a Jew is exempt, the ger should certainly be exempt, not executed.

items.text: Rava's answer: omer mutar
items.text_en: Rava's answer: omer mutar
items.desc_en: Rava answers that the case is where the ger says the act is permitted (omer mutar). Abaye objects that an omer mutar is an ones (unwilling). Rava responds that an omer mutar is considered close to intentional.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves: the case is where the killer claims it was permitted (אומר מותר), i.e., he mistakenly thought the act was allowed.
Abaye objects: one who says it was permitted is considered an אונס (an unavoidable accident), and should be exempt from execution.
Rava responds: one who says it was permitted is considered קרוב למזיד (close to intentional), and therefore liable for execution.

items.text: Supporting dispute: Rava vs. Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Supporting dispute: Rava vs. Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rava and Rav Chisda follow their respective views in a dispute about one who thought a person was an animal or a gentile was a ger toshav: Rava says liable (omer mutar is close to intentional), Rav Chisda says exempt (omer mutar is an ones).

sub.desc_en: The gemara notes that Rava and Rav Chisda follow their respective positions in a parallel dispute: one who thought he was killing an animal and found it was a man, or a gentile and found it was a ger toshav.
Rava rules: he is liable, because one who says it was permitted is קרוב למזיד (close to intentional).
Rav Chisda rules: he is exempt, because one who says it was permitted is an אונס (unavoidable accident).

items.text: Challenges and responses from Avimelech and Abraham
items.text_en: Challenges and responses from Avimelech and Abraham
items.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Chisda from the verse 'Behold you are dead because of the woman' (Avimelech), suggesting it was by human hands. Rav Chisda deflects that it was by heaven. Rava counters with a kal vachomer from 'I have sinned against God'. Abaye challenges Rava from 'Will you slay a righteous nation?' and the Gemara explains the context.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Chisda from the verse 'הנך מת על האשה' (Behold you are dead because of the woman), suggesting that Avimelech's death sentence was to be carried out by human hands.
Rav Chisda deflects that the death was by heaven, not by human hands, and supports this from the verse 'מחטוא לי' (from sinning against Me).

Rava counters with a kal vachomer (קל וחומר) from Abraham's statement 'וחטאתי לאלהים' (I have sinned against God), arguing that since Abraham's sin was against God but his judgment was handed over to humans, so too Avimelech's judgment was by human hands.
Abaye challenges Rava from the verse 'הגוי גם צדיק תהרוג' (Will you slay a righteous nation?), questioning whether Avimelech's death was by human hands.

The Gemara explains that the context there is that they were trying to persuade Avimelech to return Sarah, as the verse continues 'ועתה השב אשת האיש כי נביא הוא' (Now return the man's wife, for he is a prophet).

items.text: Gemara's conclusion about the Noahide's liability
items.text_en: Gemara's conclusion about the Noahide's liability
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the earlier question about Avimelech's argument by citing Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani: Avimelech was told to return Sarah, and his claim that Abraham said 'she is my sister' was answered by noting that Abraham was a prophet who learned from Avimelech's own conduct—a guest is asked about food and drink, not about his wife's identity. From here it is derived that a Noahide is executed if he could have learned but did not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the principle that a prophet's wife must be returned applies only to a prophet, implying that for a non-prophet she would not be returned.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani explains that Avimelech was told to return Sarah unconditionally, and his claim about Abraham's statement was answered by noting that Abraham, as a prophet, learned from Avimelech's own conduct—a guest is asked about food and drink, not about his wife's identity.
The Gemara concludes that from this episode it is derived that a Noahide (בן נח) is executed if he could have learned the law but did not.

items.text: Mishnah: Who is exiled?
items.text_en: Mishnah: Who is exiled?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents disputes: Rabbi Yehuda says a blind person is not exiled; Rabbi Meir says he is exiled. An enemy is not exiled; Rabbi Yosei says an enemy is executed because he is considered forewarned. Rabbi Shimon distinguishes: some enemies are exiled, some are not—the rule is that one who could claim he killed intentionally is not exiled, but one who killed unintentionally is exiled.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the laws of exile for accidental killing, listing the positions of Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon regarding a blind person, an enemy, and the general rule.
Rabbi Meir counters that a blind person is exiled.
The Mishnah states the general rule that an enemy is not exiled.
Rabbi Yosei says an enemy is executed because he is considered forewarned (מוּעָד).
Rabbi Shimon distinguishes: some enemies are exiled, some are not.
Rabbi Shimon's rule: one who could claim he killed intentionally is not exiled, but one who killed unintentionally is exiled.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation for the blind person
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation for the blind person
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda derives from 'without seeing' that a blind person is excluded; Rabbi Meir derives from the same phrase that a blind person is included. The Gemara explains their reasoning: Rabbi Yehuda uses the verse 'and he goes into the forest' to include a blind person, then 'without seeing' excludes him. Rabbi Meir uses two exclusions ('without seeing' and 'without knowledge') to include the blind person via the principle that multiple exclusions teach inclusion. Rabbi Yehuda uses 'without knowledge' to exclude one who intends.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda derives from 'without seeing' that a blind person is excluded, while Rabbi Meir derives from the same phrase that a blind person is included.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning: the verse 'and he goes into the forest' includes a blind person, then 'without seeing' excludes him.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Meir's reasoning: two exclusions ('without seeing' and 'without knowledge') form a מיעוט אחר מיעוט (multiple exclusions) which teaches inclusion of the blind person.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's use of 'without knowledge'
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's use of 'without knowledge'
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda uses 'without knowledge' to exclude one who intends to kill, not to include the blind person.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Yosei's statement about the enemy
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Yosei's statement about the enemy
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how an enemy can be executed without warning, and answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, who holds that a 'chaver' (learned person) does not require warning, since warning was only given to distinguish between unintentional and intentional.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yosei can say an enemy is executed, since no warning (התראה) was given to him.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, who holds that a colleague (חבר) does not require warning, since warning was only given to distinguish between an unintentional and intentional sinner.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Shimon's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Shimon's distinction
items.desc_en: A baraita explains Rabbi Shimon's rule: if the axe-head slipped from the handle, he is exiled; if it slipped from his hand, he is not exiled. The Gemara notes a contradiction from another baraita where Rabbi Shimon says he is never exiled unless his tool slips from his hand. The contradiction is resolved: the first case is about a friend, the second about an enemy. Another contradiction about 'slipped from his hand' is resolved: one is Rabbi's view, the other is the Rabbis' view.

sub.desc_en: A baraita explains Rabbi Shimon's rule: if the axe-head slipped from the handle (נפסק), he is exiled; if it slipped from his hand (נשמט), he is not exiled.

The Gemara raises a contradiction: another baraita says Rabbi Shimon rules he is never exiled unless the tool slips from his hand, contradicting both the 'slipped from the handle' and 'slipped from his hand' rulings.
The contradiction about 'slipped from the handle' is resolved: one case refers to a friend (אוהב), the other to an enemy (שונא).
The contradiction about 'slipped from his hand' is resolved: one is Rabbi's view, the other is the Rabbis' view.

items.text: Mishnah: Where do they flee?
items.text_en: Mishnah: Where do they flee?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the cities of refuge are three on the other side of the Jordan and three in Canaan, and they only function when all six are established simultaneously. Roads are prepared between them. Two Torah scholars are appointed to accompany the killer lest he be killed on the way, and they speak to him. Rabbi Meir adds that the killer himself may speak, citing the verse 'this is the word of the killer'. Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says that initially both intentional and unintentional killers are sent to the cities, then the court brings them back; those liable for death are executed, those not liable are freed, and those liable for exile are returned.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the killer flees to the six cities of refuge, which only function when all six are established simultaneously.
The Mishnah adds that roads were prepared between the cities, citing the verse 'תָּכִין לְךָ הַדֶּרֶךְ' (prepare the way).

The Mishnah states that two Torah scholars accompany the killer to protect him, and Rabbi Meir adds that the killer himself may speak, citing the verse 'וְזֶה דְּבַר הָרֹצֵחַ' (this is the word of the killer).

Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says that initially both intentional and unintentional killers are sent to the cities, then the court brings them back: those liable for death are executed, those not liable are freed, and those liable for exile are returned.

items.text: Gemara: Arrangement of the cities and Abaye's comment
items.text_en: Gemara: Arrangement of the cities and Abaye's comment
items.desc_en: A baraita describes how Moses' three cities across the Jordan were aligned with Joshua's three in Canaan like two rows in a vineyard, and the requirement that the distances between them be equal. The Gemara questions why three were needed in Transjordan when murderers were common there, and Abaye answers that murderers were indeed common in Gilead.

sub.desc_en: A baraita describes how Moses' three cities of refuge across the Jordan were aligned with Joshua's three in Canaan like two rows in a vineyard, with equal distances between them.
The Gemara questions why three cities were needed in Transjordan when murderers were common there, implying that fewer should suffice.
Abaye answers that murderers were indeed common in Gilead, justifying the need for three cities there as well.

items.text: Why Shechem is not a city of refuge
items.text_en: Why Shechem is not a city of refuge
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Shechem, which is centrally located, is not a city of refuge. Abaye explains that murderers were common in Shechem, citing a verse that describes priests conspiring to murder there, similar to how priests gather to divide terumot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse about Gilead and asks what 'עקובה מדם' means, with Rabbi Elazar explaining it refers to those who ambush to murder.
The Gemara questions why Shechem, being centrally located, is not a city of refuge like other central cities.
Abaye answers that Shechem also had murderers, citing a verse and Rabbi Elazar's explanation that priests conspired to murder there like priests gathering to divide terumot.

items.text: Difference between Levite cities and cities of refuge
items.text_en: Difference between Levite cities and cities of refuge
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that there are forty-two Levite cities, but only six cities of refuge. Abaye explains that the Levite cities absorb both intentional and unintentional killers, while the cities of refuge only absorb unintentional killers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Are there no more cities of refuge? But the verse mentions forty-two Levite cities.
Abaye answers that the Levite cities absorb both intentional and unintentional killers, while the cities of refuge only absorb unintentional killers.

items.text: Hebron and Kedesh as cities of refuge
items.text_en: Hebron and Kedesh as cities of refuge
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Hebron and Kedesh were cities of refuge, given that Hebron was given to Caleb and Kedesh is listed among fortified cities. Abaye explains that Hebron's fields and outskirts were given to Caleb, and Rav Yosef and Rav Ashi explain that there were two cities named Kedesh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Hebron was a city of refuge, citing the verse that it was given to Caleb.
Abaye answers that only the fields and outskirts of Hebron were given to Caleb, not the city itself.
The Gemara questions whether Kedesh was a city of refuge, citing a baraita that lists it among fortified cities which must be medium-sized towns.
Rav Yosef answers that there were two cities named Kedesh, one fortified and one a city of refuge.
Rav Ashi supports Rav Yosef's answer with an analogy of two similarly named places, Selikum and the village of Selikum.

items.text: Requirements for cities of refuge
items.text_en: Requirements for cities of refuge
items.desc_en: The baraita details the physical and social requirements for cities of refuge: they must be medium-sized towns, located near water and markets, with a large population. They must not sell weapons or traps, and Rabbi Yitzchak derives from a verse that the city must provide a livelihood for the refugee.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that cities of refuge must be medium-sized towns, located near water and markets, with a large population, and if the population decreases, it must be supplemented.

Rabbi Nechemya adds that weapons and traps may not be sold in these cities, while the Sages permit it; both agree that nets and ropes may not be spread there to avoid the presence of the blood avenger.
Rabbi Yitzchak derives from the verse 'וְנָס אֶל אַחַת מִן הֶעָרִים הָאֵל וָחָי' (and he shall flee to one of these cities and live) that the city must provide a livelihood for the refugee.

items.text: Exile of the rabbi and Torah as refuge
items.text_en: Exile of the rabbi and Torah as refuge
items.desc_en: The Gemara teaches that if a student is exiled, his rabbi must go with him, and if a rabbi is exiled, his yeshiva goes with him. Rabbi Yochanan states that words of Torah provide refuge, and the Gemara resolves a contradiction by distinguishing between when one is engaged in Torah study and when not.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna teaches that if a student is exiled, his rabbi is exiled with him, citing the verse 'וָחַי' (and he shall live) to provide life, and Rabbi Ze'ira derives from here that one should not teach an unworthy student.
Rabbi Yochanan states that if a rabbi is exiled, his yeshiva is exiled with him.
The Gemara objects: Did Rabbi Yochanan not say that words of Torah themselves provide refuge, citing the verse about 'בֶּצֶר' (Bezer) and 'וְזֹאת הַתּוֹרָה' (and this is the Torah)?
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: when one is engaged in Torah study, the Torah itself provides refuge; when not engaged, the rabbi or yeshiva provides refuge.

items.text: Torah protects from the Angel of Death
items.text_en: Torah protects from the Angel of Death
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is given that Torah protects from the Angel of Death, illustrated by the story of Rav Chisda who was so engrossed in study that the Angel of Death could not approach him until he paused.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation that the Torah protects from the Angel of Death.
The Gemara cites the story of Rav Chisda, who was so engrossed in study that the Angel of Death could not approach him until he paused.

items.text: Aggadic teachings on refuge and Torah study
items.text_en: Aggadic teachings on refuge and Torah study
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents several aggadic teachings: why Reuven is mentioned first in rescue, that Moses 'shined a sun' for murderers by establishing cities of refuge, and interpretations of verses about loving to learn or teach in public, with praise for those who teach the masses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Tanchum bar Chanilai asks why Reuven merited to be mentioned first in rescue, answering that he initiated the rescue of Joseph.
Rabbi Simlai interprets the verse about Moses setting aside cities of refuge, explaining that God told Moses to 'shine a sun' for murderers.
Rabbi Simai interprets 'lover of silver' as Moses, who knew the three cities beyond the Jordan would not absorb until three were chosen in Canaan, yet fulfilled the commandment.
Rabbi Elazar explains that it is fitting for one whose entire 'produce' (Torah) is his to teach the masses, and similarly one who can fully express God's praise should recount His might.
Rabbana (or Rabbah bar Mari) states that whoever loves to teach the masses will have produce, and the Sages set their eyes on Rava son of Rabbah.

items.text: Further teachings on learning and teaching
items.text_en: Further teachings on learning and teaching
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi and Ravina offer interpretations of the verse about loving to learn or teach in public, with Rav Ashi citing a teaching about scholars who study alone becoming foolish, and Ravina citing Rabbi's statement about learning more from students. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that Jerusalem's gates and the anticipation of the Temple caused David to rejoice, and the baraita concludes with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's teaching.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a mnemonic for the following teachings: Rav Ashi on learning and Ravina on teaching.
Rav Ashi teaches that one who loves to learn in public will have produce, citing Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's interpretation of a verse about scholars who study alone becoming foolish and sinful.

Ravina teaches that one who loves to teach in public will have produce, citing Rabbi's statement that he learned more from his teachers, even more from his colleagues, and most of all from his students.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's first teaching
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's first teaching
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that the verse 'our feet stood within your gates, Jerusalem' means that the gates of Jerusalem, where people studied Torah, caused their feet to stand firm in war.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's second teaching
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's second teaching
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that David rejoiced when people said they would go to the Temple, and God told David that one day of his Torah study is better than a thousand burnt offerings Solomon would bring.
The Gemara transitions to a baraita citing Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's teaching about the paths being directed.

items.text: Preparing the road to the city of refuge
items.text_en: Preparing the road to the city of refuge
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that 'refuge' was written at crossroads. Rav Kahana cites a verse to show that one must prepare the way for the manslayer.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that 'refuge' was written at crossroads so the manslayer would recognize and turn there.
Rav Kahana cites the verse 'תָּכִין לְךָ הַדֶּרֶךְ' to show that one must prepare the way for the manslayer.

items.text: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina's homily on the path of sinners
items.text_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina's homily on the path of sinners
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina opens the parashah with a verse about God teaching sinners the way, concluding that if He does so for sinners, certainly for the righteous.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina opens the parashah with a verse about God teaching sinners the way, concluding that if He does so for sinners, certainly for the righteous.

items.text: Reish Lakish's parable of two killers
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's parable of two killers
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish interprets a verse about two men who killed, one accidentally and one intentionally, without witnesses. God brings them to the same inn, and the intentional killer is killed by the accidental one, who then goes into exile.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish opens the section by citing a verse about two killers and the proverb 'from the wicked, wickedness goes forth'.

Reish Lakish explains the verse as a parable: two killers, one intentional and one accidental, are brought by God to the same inn; the intentional killer is killed by the accidental one, who then goes into exile.

items.text: The principle: a person is led on the path they wish to go
items.text_en: The principle: a person is led on the path they wish to go
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna in the name of Rav Huna (or Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Elazar) states that from Torah, Prophets, and Writings, a person is led on the path they wish to go. Prooftexts are cited for each.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna / Rav Huna / Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna / Rav Huna / Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna in the name of Rav Huna (or Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Elazar) states the principle that a person is led on the path they wish to go, citing support from Torah, Prophets, and Writings.
The gemara cites three prooftexts: from Torah (Balaam's story), from Prophets (Isaiah 48:17), and from Writings (Proverbs 3:34), demonstrating the principle.

items.text: Rav Huna: the blood redeemer who kills the manslayer in the city of refuge is exempt
items.text_en: Rav Huna: the blood redeemer who kills the manslayer in the city of refuge is exempt
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if the blood redeemer finds the manslayer in the city of refuge and kills him, he is exempt, interpreting 'he has no judgment of death' as referring to the blood redeemer. This is challenged by a baraita that interprets the verse as referring to the manslayer, but Rav Huna follows another tanna who agrees with him.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if the blood redeemer kills the manslayer in the city of refuge, the redeemer is exempt, interpreting the verse 'וְלוֹ אֵין מִשְׁפַּט מָוֶת' as referring to the blood redeemer.
The Gemara challenges Rav Huna by citing a baraita that interprets the same verse as referring to the manslayer, not the blood redeemer.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Huna follows a different tanna who interprets the verse as referring to the blood redeemer.

items.text: The escort of two Torah scholars and their speech to the blood redeemer
items.text_en: The escort of two Torah scholars and their speech to the blood redeemer
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that two Torah scholars are given to the manslayer to prevent the blood redeemer from killing him on the way. The Gemara clarifies that they speak appropriate words to him, not a warning. Rabbi Meir adds that the manslayer speaks for himself, citing a verse, but the Sages say that many missions are accomplished.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the phrase 'they speak to him' in the mishnah means they warn him that if he kills, he is liable to death.
The Gemara rejects the warning interpretation and explains that they speak appropriate words to him, telling him not to act like a murderer since the act came about accidentally.
Rabbi Meir adds that the manslayer himself speaks on his own behalf, citing the verse 'וְזֶה דְּבַר הָרֹצֵחַ' (and this is the matter of the manslayer).
The Sages object to Rabbi Meir, saying that many missions are accomplished (by the Torah scholars' speech, not the manslayer's own words).

items.text: Clarification: the act came to him accidentally
items.text_en: Clarification: the act came to him accidentally
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why it is necessary to state that the act came accidentally, since if it were intentional he would not be exiled. It answers that indeed it is obvious.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita needs to state that the act came to the killer accidentally, since if it were intentional he would not be exiled.
The Gemara answers that indeed it is obvious, and the statement is merely a clarification.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi about initial procedure
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi about initial procedure
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda says that initially both intentional and accidental killers are sent to cities of refuge, and the court brings them back; those liable for death are executed, those not liable are freed, and those liable for exile are returned. Rabbi says they go on their own, thinking the cities absorb both, but they do not know that only the accidental killer is absorbed.

sub.text: Baraita citation: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
sub.text_en: Baraita citation: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda
sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's position that initially both intentional and accidental killers are sent to cities of refuge, and the court brings them back.

sub.text: Baraita continues: Scriptural support for execution
sub.text_en: Baraita continues: Scriptural support for execution
sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'וְשָׁלְחוּ זִקְנֵי עִירוֹ...' to show that those liable for death are executed.

sub.text: Baraita continues: Scriptural support for acquittal
sub.text_en: Baraita continues: Scriptural support for acquittal
sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'וְהִצִּילוּ הָעֵדָה...' to show that those not liable are freed.

sub.text: Baraita continues: Scriptural support for exile
sub.text_en: Baraita continues: Scriptural support for exile
sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verse 'וְהֵשִׁיבוּ אֹתוֹ הָעֵדָה...' to show that those liable for exile are returned to the city of refuge.
Rabbi states that the killers go on their own, thinking the cities absorb both, but they do not know that only the accidental killer is absorbed.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar: a city with a majority of murderers does not absorb
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar: a city with a majority of murderers does not absorb
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that a city where most inhabitants are murderers does not serve as a city of refuge, based on a verse requiring the elders to speak to the manslayer, implying their words are not equal to his.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that a city where most inhabitants are murderers does not serve as a city of refuge, based on a verse requiring the elders to speak to the manslayer, implying their words are not equal to his.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar and the dispute about a city without elders
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and the dispute about a city without elders
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says a city without elders does not absorb, requiring 'elders of the city'. Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi dispute: one says it does not absorb, the other says it does, the latter viewing the requirement as merely a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that a city without elders does not absorb an accidental killer, because the verse requires 'elders of the city'.
The gemara records a dispute between Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi: one says the city does not absorb (requiring elders), the other says it does (viewing the requirement as merely a מצוה (commandment)).

items.text: Dispute about a stubborn and rebellious son in a city without elders
items.text_en: Dispute about a stubborn and rebellious son in a city without elders
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi dispute whether a stubborn and rebellious son can be judged in a city without elders. One says no, requiring 'elders of his city', the other says yes, viewing it as a mere mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi about whether a stubborn and rebellious son can be judged in a city without elders.

sub.text: First opinion (Rabbi Ammi or Rabbi Assi)
sub.text_en: First opinion (Rabbi Ammi or Rabbi Assi)
sub.desc_en: One sage argues that a stubborn and rebellious son cannot be judged in a city without elders because the Torah requires 'elders of his city' (זקני עירו).

sub.text: Second opinion (Rabbi Ammi or Rabbi Assi)
sub.text_en: Second opinion (Rabbi Ammi or Rabbi Assi)
sub.desc_en: The other sage argues that a stubborn and rebellious son can be judged even without elders, because the requirement of elders is merely a מצוה (a mitzvah) and not an essential condition.

items.text: Dispute about the heifer whose neck is broken in a city without elders
items.text_en: Dispute about the heifer whose neck is broken in a city without elders
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi dispute whether a city without elders brings the heifer whose neck is broken. One says no, requiring 'elders of that city', the other says yes, viewing it as a mere mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi regarding whether a city without elders brings the heifer whose neck is broken (עגלה ערופה).
The gemara explains that the one who says the city does not bring the heifer requires the verse 'elders of that city' (זקני העיר ההיא), which is absent.
The gemara explains that the one who says the city does bring the heifer views the requirement as merely a mitzvah (מצוה בעלמא), not a strict biblical requirement of elders.

items.text: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina's question about the parashah of murderers
items.text_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina's question about the parashah of murderers
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina asks why the parashah of murderers was stated, beginning a new discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chama bar Chanina asks why the parashah of murderers was stated, initiating a new discussion.

items.text: Why Joshua spoke harshly about cities of refuge
items.text_en: Why Joshua spoke harshly about cities of refuge
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Joshua spoke harshly when commanding the Israelites about the cities of refuge, and explains that 'דיבר' implies harsh language, while 'ידבר' implies gentle language.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Joshua spoke harshly (בלשון עז) when commanding about the cities of refuge, and answers that it is because they are matters of Torah.
The Gemara objects that not all 'דיבור' (speech) is harsh, citing a baraita that 'ידבר' implies gentle language, and resolves that 'דבר' (harsh) and 'ידבר' (gentle) are distinct forms.

items.text: Siman for the following disputes
items.text_en: Siman for the following disputes
items.desc_en: A mnemonic sign is given for the upcoming disputes between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The gemara provides a mnemonic sign (סימן) for the upcoming disputes between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.

items.text: Dispute about why Joshua wrote the cities of refuge
items.text_en: Dispute about why Joshua wrote the cities of refuge
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis disagree about why Joshua wrote the cities of refuge: one says because they were delayed, the other says because they are from the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis, with one opinion stating that Joshua wrote the cities of refuge because they were delayed.
The second opinion states that Joshua wrote the cities of refuge because they are from the Torah.

items.text: Dispute about what Joshua wrote in the Torah
items.text_en: Dispute about what Joshua wrote in the Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya disagree about what Joshua added to the Torah: one says eight verses, the other says the cities of refuge. The Gemara explains the scriptural support for each view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse about Joshua writing in the Torah scroll and introduces the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemya.
One opinion (Rabbi Yehuda) says Joshua wrote eight verses of the Torah.
The other opinion (Rabbi Nechemya) says Joshua wrote the cities of refuge.
The Gemara explains that according to the view of eight verses, the phrase 'in the book of God's Torah' is understood literally.
The Gemara explains that according to the view of cities of refuge, the verse means Joshua wrote in his own book the things that are written in the Torah scroll.

items.text: Dispute about sewing a Torah scroll with linen threads
items.text_en: Dispute about sewing a Torah scroll with linen threads
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir disagree about whether a Torah scroll sewn with linen threads is valid. The Gemara explains the reasoning: one derives from tefillin that it must be sewn with sinews, the other limits the comparison. Rav concludes that the halakha does not follow the one who permits linen.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir about whether a Torah scroll sewn with linen threads is valid.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation for the one who invalidates
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation for the one who invalidates
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the one who invalidates derives from the verse 'לְמַעַן תִּהְיֶה תּוֹרַת ה׳ בְּפִיךָ' that all Torah scrolls are compared to תפילין (phylacteries), which by הלכה למשה מסיני (a law given to Moses at Sinai) must be sewn with sinews.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation for the one who permits
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation for the one who permits
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the one who permits limits the comparison: the verse only compares Torah to תפילין regarding what is permitted in your mouth (i.e., the material of the parchment), not regarding its halachic details like sewing with sinews.
Rav concludes that although he saw the תפילין of the house of Ḥavivi sewn with linen, the halakha does not follow the one who permits linen.

items.text: Mishnah: Who returns the murderer to the city of refuge
items.text_en: Mishnah: Who returns the murderer to the city of refuge
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that an anointed high priest, one who served in many garments, or one who passed from his anointing, returns the murderer. Rabbi Yehuda adds the priest anointed for war. Therefore, the mothers of priests provide sustenance to the murderers so they won't pray for their sons' deaths.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the high priests who return the murderer to the city of refuge: the anointed, the one with many garments, the one who passed from his anointing, and according to Rabbi Yehuda, the priest anointed for war.
The Mishnah explains that the mothers of priests provide sustenance and clothing to the murderers so that they will not pray for the priests' sons to die.

items.text: Gemara: Source for the high priest returning the murderer
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for the high priest returning the murderer
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana derives from verses that the murderer returns upon the death of the high priest. Rabbi Yehuda adds a verse for the priest anointed for war, but the Rabbis say that verse refers to one of the other high priests.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters (that the high priest returns the murderer) derived?
Rav Kahana answers by citing three verses that repeat the phrase 'until the death of the high priest' to derive the halacha.
Rabbi Yehuda adds another verse that omits 'the great' to include the priest anointed for war.
The Rabbis respond that the verse without 'the great' refers to one of the other high priests already mentioned, not the priest anointed for war.

items.text: Why the mothers' prayers might cause death
items.text_en: Why the mothers' prayers might cause death
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mothers' prayers would cause death, given that a curse without cause does not come. An elder answers that they should have prayed for their generation but did not. A second version says the mothers prayed that their sons not die, but the problem is that the innocent suffer for the guilty. The elder's answer is repeated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mothers' prayers would cause death, given the principle that a curse without cause does not come.
An elder answers that the mothers should have prayed for their generation but did not, so their curse was justified.
An alternative version states that the mothers prayed that their sons not die, shifting the premise.
The Gemara asks why the sons would die if the mothers did not pray, since the sons are innocent and the guilty are the murderers.
The Gemara cites two proverbs illustrating that the innocent sometimes suffer for the guilty.
The elder repeats that the mothers should have prayed for their generation, citing a story about a man eaten by a lion near Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.

items.text: The curse of a sage even if unwarranted
items.text_en: The curse of a sage even if unwarranted
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav teaches that a sage's curse comes even if unwarranted, from the story of Achitofel. David wrote God's name on a potsherd to stop the flood, and Achitofel reasoned that if the name can be erased for peace, it can be used for this. Nevertheless, Achitofel was later hanged.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that a sage's curse comes even if unwarranted, and asks for the source from Achitofel.
The gemara recounts the story of David digging the foundations and the flood threatening the world, leading to David's curse that anyone who knows a solution and withholds it should be choked.
Achitofel reasons with a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) that if God's name can be erased for peace between a man and his wife, surely it can be used to save the world.
David permits the act, Achitofel writes the name on a potsherd and casts it into the deep, the flood subsides, yet Achitofel is later hanged, showing the curse came even though unwarranted.

items.text: A sage's curse even on condition
items.text_en: A sage's curse even on condition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu teaches that a sage's curse comes even if conditional, from Eli who cursed Samuel if he hid anything. Samuel told him everything, yet Eli's sons still did not follow his ways.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abahu states that a sage's curse comes even if conditional, citing Eli's conditional curse against Shmuel.
The gemara notes that even though Shmuel told Eli everything, the verse shows Eli's sons did not walk in his ways, proving the curse took effect despite the condition being met.

items.text: Gemara's opening: Nidui on condition requires annulment, derived from Judah's bones
items.text_en: Gemara's opening: Nidui on condition requires annulment, derived from Judah's bones
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that a conditional ban of excommunication requires annulment. The Gemara derives this from Judah, whose bones were rolling in the ark for forty years until Moses prayed for him, citing verses about Judah's role in Reuben's confession.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states in the name of Rav that a conditional ban of excommunication (נידוי על תנאי) requires annulment.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive this? From Judah, as it is written: 'If I do not bring him to you...'

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan explains the verse 'Let Reuben live and not die... and this for Judah' as referring to Judah's bones rolling in the ark.
The Gemara narrates that for forty years in the wilderness, Judah's bones were rolling in the ark until Moses prayed for mercy.
Moses argues before God: who caused Reuben to confess? Judah — and then cites the verse 'And this for Judah... Hear, Lord, the voice of Judah.'

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the prayer's effect
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the prayer's effect
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Moses' prayer addressed Judah's three deficiencies: his limbs were disjointed, he could not enter the heavenly academy, and he could not engage in halachic debate — and the prayer resolved them.

items.text: Question: Does the murderer return upon the death of all High Priests or one?
items.text_en: Question: Does the murderer return upon the death of all High Priests or one?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the murderer returns from exile upon the death of all High Priests or only one. It attempts to answer from a mishnah: if his trial concluded without a High Priest, he never leaves, implying that if there were a High Priest, he would leave upon his death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the murderer returns from exile upon the death of all High Priests or only one.

The Gemara attempts to answer from a mishnah: if his trial concluded without a High Priest, he never leaves, implying that if there were a High Priest, he would leave upon his death, but the answer is rejected because the case lacks a High Priest entirely.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of the murderer's release and permanent exile
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of the murderer's release and permanent exile
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that if the High Priest dies after the trial is concluded, the murderer does not go into exile. If the High Priest dies before the trial and another is appointed, the murderer returns upon the second's death. If the trial concluded without a High Priest, or the murderer killed a High Priest, or a High Priest killed, he never leaves. He also cannot leave for any testimony, even for a great leader like Yoav.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens with the law that if the High Priest dies after the trial is concluded, the murderer does not go into exile.
The mishnah states that if the High Priest dies before the trial and another is appointed, the murderer returns upon the second's death.
The mishnah states that if the trial concluded without a High Priest, or the murderer killed a High Priest, or a High Priest killed, he never leaves.

The mishnah rules that the murderer cannot leave the city of refuge for any testimony, even for a great leader like Yoav, citing the verse 'there shall be his dwelling, there his death, there his burial'.

items.text: Mishnah: The city's boundary and the avenger's rights
items.text_en: Mishnah: The city's boundary and the avenger's rights
items.desc_en: The mishnah teaches that the city's boundary also provides refuge. If the murderer leaves the boundary and the blood avenger finds him, Rabbi Yose HaGelili says it is a mitzvah for the avenger to kill him, and permission for anyone. Rabbi Akiva says it is only permission for the avenger, and others are liable.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating that the city's boundary (תחום) also provides refuge, just as the city itself does.

The mishnah presents Rabbi Yose HaGelili's view: if the murderer leaves the boundary and the blood avenger finds him, it is a מצוה (commandment) for the avenger to kill him, and permission for anyone else.
The mishnah presents Rabbi Akiva's opposing view: it is only permission for the blood avenger to kill him, and anyone else who kills him is liable (חייב).

items.text: Gemara: Reason for the mishnah's first clause
items.text_en: Gemara: Reason for the mishnah's first clause
items.desc_en: Abaye explains the mishnah's first clause with a kal vachomer: if one who already went into exile leaves now (upon the High Priest's death), then one who never went into exile should not go at all. The Gemara objects that exile itself might not atone; rather, the High Priest's death atones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reason for the mishnah's first clause that a killer whose trial concluded after the High Priest's death does not go into exile.
Abaye answers with a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if one who already went into exile leaves now (upon the High Priest's death), then one who never went into exile should not go at all.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the one who already went into exile has achieved atonement (כפרה) through exile, while the one who never went has not, so the kal vachomer is invalid.
The Gemara rejects the objection: does exile itself atone? No, it is the death of the High Priest (מיתת כהן) that atones, so the kal vachomer stands.

items.text: Gemara: Source for the mishnah's second clause
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for the mishnah's second clause
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana derives from a verse that the High Priest referred to is the one anointed in the murderer's days. The Gemara then asks what the murderer should have done, answering that he should have prayed for a favorable verdict, but he did not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the mishnah's rule that the High Priest referred to is the one anointed in the murderer's days.
Rav Kahana derives from the verse 'וְיָשַׁב בָּהּ עַד מוֹת הַכֹּהֵן הַגָּדֹל אֲשֶׁר מָשַׁח אֹתוֹ' that the High Priest is the one anointed in the murderer's days, not the one who anointed him.
The Gemara asks what the murderer should have done to avoid the situation where the High Priest dies before his trial is completed.
The Gemara answers that the murderer should have prayed for a favorable verdict before the High Priest died, but he did not.

items.text: Gemara: Burial of the murderer's bones
items.text_en: Gemara: Burial of the murderer's bones
items.desc_en: Abaye states that if the murderer died after the trial, his bones are brought to the city of refuge for burial, as derived from a verse. A baraisa adds that if he died before the High Priest, his bones are brought to his ancestral burial place.

sub.desc_en: Abaye states that if the murderer died after the trial, his bones are brought to the city of refuge for burial, as derived from the verse 'לָשׁוּב לָשֶׁבֶת בָּאָרֶץ'.
A baraita adds that if the murderer died before the High Priest, his bones are brought to his ancestral burial place, as derived from the verse 'יָשׁוּב הָרֹצֵחַ אֶל אֶרֶץ אֲחֻזָּתוֹ'.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute about a High Priest who is a ben gerushah or ben chalutzah
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute about a High Priest who is a ben gerushah or ben chalutzah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha disagree about a High Priest who is disqualified: one says his priesthood 'died' (retroactively invalid), the other says it 'ceased' (from now on). The Gemara links this to a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua about sacrifices offered by such a priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha about a High Priest who becomes a בן גרושה (son of a divorced woman) or בן חלוצה (son of a chalutzah) after his trial is concluded.
One sage says the priesthood 'died' (retroactively invalid), the other says it 'ceased' (from now on).
The Gemara asks whether this dispute corresponds to the earlier dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua.
The Gemara cites a baraita: if a priest was offering sacrifices and was discovered to be a בן גרושה or בן חלוצה, Rabbi Eliezer invalidates all his sacrifices, while Rabbi Yehoshua validates them.
The Gemara resolves: the one who says 'died' aligns with Rabbi Yehoshua (sacrifices valid retroactively), and the one who says 'ceased' aligns with Rabbi Eliezer (sacrifices invalid retroactively).

items.text: Clarification of the dispute regarding the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Clarification of the dispute regarding the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua is only according to Rabbi Yehoshua's opinion. One who says the animal died follows Rabbi Yehoshua, while one who says it was nullified holds that Rabbi Yehoshua would agree here because the verse 'bless his strength' applies even to blemished animals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua is only according to Rabbi Yehoshua's opinion, and that one who says the animal died follows Rabbi Yehoshua, while one who says it was nullified holds that Rabbi Yehoshua would agree here because the verse 'bless his strength' applies even to blemished animals.

items.text: Yoav's two mistakes regarding the altar
items.text_en: Yoav's two mistakes regarding the altar
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav that Yoav made two mistakes: he thought the altar's horns provided refuge, but only the roof does; and he thought the altar in Shiloh provided refuge, but only the permanent Temple altar does. Abaye adds a third mistake: the altar only protects a priest performing the service, but Yoav was a non-priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Yehuda quoting Rav that Yoav made two mistakes when he fled to the sanctuary, and Abaye adds a third mistake.
Abaye adds a third mistake: the altar only protects a priest performing the service, but Yoav was a non-priest (זר).

items.text: The future three mistakes of Rome's prince
items.text_en: The future three mistakes of Rome's prince
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that the prince of Rome will make three mistakes: he will flee to Botzra, but only Betzer is a city of refuge; he is willful, but only an unintentional killer is protected; and he is an angel, but only a human is protected.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that the angelic prince of Rome will make three mistakes regarding the city of refuge.

items.text: Cities of refuge not for burial
items.text_en: Cities of refuge not for burial
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu states that the open spaces of the cities of refuge were not given for burial, as the verse says they are for livestock and property, i.e., for the living. An objection is raised from a baraita that says 'there' includes burial, but the Gemara distinguishes: a murderer is different because the Torah explicitly provides for his burial there.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu states that cities of refuge were not given for burial, based on the verse that their open spaces are for livestock and property.
A baraita is cited that states 'there' shall be his dwelling, his death, and his burial, contradicting Rabbi Avahu.
The Gemara resolves that a murderer is different, as the Torah explicitly includes burial for him.

items.text: The city's boundary for refuge and dwelling
items.text_en: The city's boundary for refuge and dwelling
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised: the Mishnah says the city's outskirts are like the city, but a verse says 'he shall dwell in it' implying only the city itself. Abaye resolves: one verse is for refuge (the outskirts also protect), the other is for dwelling (one may not live in the outskirts). Rav Sheshet adds that the ruling is needed for caves (underground dwellings).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says the outskirts of the city are like the city for refuge, but a verse states 'he shall dwell in it' (וְיָשַׁב בָּהּ) — implying only the city itself, not its outskirts.
Abaye resolves the contradiction: one verse refers to refuge (the outskirts also protect the killer), the other to dwelling (one may not live in the outskirts).
The Gemara objects: if dwelling is prohibited in the outskirts, that is already known from the rule that one may not convert a field into a migrash (open space) or vice versa.
Rav Sheshet explains that the ruling about dwelling is needed specifically for caves (underground dwellings) in the outskirts, which are not covered by the general rule.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva on the blood redeemer
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva on the blood redeemer
items.desc_en: A baraita states: if the blood redeemer kills the murderer, it is a mitzvah for the redeemer; if there is no redeemer, it is permitted for anyone (Rabbi Yose HaGelili). Rabbi Akiva says it is merely permitted for the redeemer, and anyone else is liable. The Gemara asks the scriptural basis: Rabbi Yose HaGelili notes the verse does not say 'if the redeemer kills', while Rabbi Akiva notes it does not say 'he shall kill'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Yose HaGelili says it is a mitzvah for the blood redeemer to kill the murderer, and if there is no redeemer it is permitted for anyone; Rabbi Akiva says it is merely permitted for the redeemer, and anyone else is liable.

The Gemara asks the scriptural basis for each opinion: Rabbi Yose HaGelili notes the verse does not say 'if the redeemer kills', implying it is not exclusive; Rabbi Akiva notes it does not say 'he shall kill', implying it is not obligatory.

items.text: Mar Zutra's ruling and its source in a Tanna
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's ruling and its source in a Tanna
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Toviya said in the name of Rav: if a murderer leaves the boundary and the blood redeemer kills him, the redeemer is executed. This follows neither Rabbi Yose HaGelili nor Rabbi Akiva, but rather Rabbi Eliezer, who derives from 'until he stands before the congregation for judgment' that the redeemer may not kill immediately. Rabbi Yose and Rabbi Akiva use that verse for a different law: that a Sanhedrin that saw a murder may not execute until they stand before another court.

sub.text: Mar Zutra bar Toviya in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra bar Toviya in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra bar Toviya states in the name of Rav that if a murderer leaves the boundary and the blood redeemer kills him, the redeemer is executed.
The Gemara asks: whose opinion does this ruling follow, since it aligns with neither Rabbi Yose HaGelili nor Rabbi Akiva?
The Gemara answers that Mar Zutra's ruling follows Rabbi Eliezer, who derives from the verse 'עַד עׇמְדוֹ לִפְנֵי הָעֵדָה לַמִּשְׁפָּט' that the redeemer may not kill the murderer immediately.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva use the same verse for a different law: that a Sanhedrin that saw a murder may not execute until they stand before another court.

items.text: The verse 'if the murderer goes out' and the dispute about 'the Torah speaks in human language'
items.text_en: The verse 'if the murderer goes out' and the dispute about 'the Torah speaks in human language'
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'if the murderer goes out' applies even to an unintentional killer. Another baraita says that if one kills the murderer, if intentional the killer is executed, if unintentional he goes into exile. The Gemara resolves this by attributing the views to the dispute over whether the Torah speaks in human language. Abaye supports the view that it does, so that the end is not stricter than the beginning.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'if the murderer goes out' applies even to an unintentional killer.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from another baraita that says if one kills the murderer, if intentional the killer is executed, if unintentional he goes into exile.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the views to the dispute over whether the Torah speaks in human language.
Abaye supports the view that the Torah speaks in human language, so that the end is not stricter than the beginning.

items.text: Contradictory baraitot on a son as blood redeemer for his father
items.text_en: Contradictory baraitot on a son as blood redeemer for his father
items.desc_en: One baraita says a son can be a blood redeemer for his father, another says he cannot. The Gemara initially suggests this reflects the dispute between Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva, but rejects this because even according to the view that it is a mitzvah, a son cannot strike or curse his father. The resolution: one baraita refers to the son, the other to the grandson.

sub.desc_en: Two contradictory baraitot are cited: one says a son becomes a blood redeemer for his father who killed, the other says he does not.
The Gemara suggests that the contradiction reflects the dispute between Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva.

The Gemara rejects this suggestion, arguing that even according to the view that it is a mitzvah, a son is not permitted to strike or curse his father, citing Rabba bar Rav Huna and the school of Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Huna / Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna / Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The principle is cited that a son never acts as an agent to strike or curse his father, except for a mesit (one who incites to idolatry), as the Torah says 'you shall not spare nor conceal him'.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one baraita refers to the son himself, the other to the grandson.

items.text: The Mishnah on a tree's foliage and the Gemara's resolution of contradictions
items.text_en: The Mishnah on a tree's foliage and the Gemara's resolution of contradictions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that for a tree within the boundary but with foliage outside, or vice versa, the law follows the foliage. The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about maaser sheni that distinguishes based on the wall. The Gemara answers that maaser depends on the wall, while cities of refuge depend on dwelling (the foliage is where one dwells). Another contradiction between maaser and cities of refuge is resolved by attributing the views to Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that for a tree whose trunk is inside the boundary but foliage extends outside, or vice versa, the law follows the foliage.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about maaser sheni that distinguishes based on the wall, not the foliage.
The Gemara answers that maaser depends on the wall, while cities of refuge depend on dwelling (the foliage is where one dwells).
The Gemara raises another contradiction between two baraitot about maaser sheni and cities of refuge, both following the foliage.
Rav Kahana resolves the contradiction by attributing the views to Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis, as cited in a baraita.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that for a cave, one follows its entrance; for a tree, one follows its foliage. This sets up the discussion about the boundaries of the cities of refuge.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda rules that for a cave one follows its entrance, and for a tree one follows its foliage.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Applying Rabbi Yehuda's rule to ma'aser vs. cities of refuge
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Applying Rabbi Yehuda's rule to ma'aser vs. cities of refuge
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes Rabbi Yehuda's rule applies to ma'aser for stringency, but then questions its application to cities of refuge. If the trunk is inside and foliage outside, the go'el hadam could kill the murderer, which is problematic since the murderer is inside.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes Rabbi Yehuda's rule applies to ma'aser (tithe) only for stringency (לחומרא), explaining both cases where the trunk is outside or inside.

The Gemara objects that applying Rabbi Yehuda's rule to cities of refuge (ערי מקלט) leads to a contradiction: if the trunk is inside and foliage outside, the go'el hadam (blood redeemer) could kill the murderer, but the murderer is inside.

items.text: Rava's resolution: The dispute is about the trunk being a step for the foliage
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: The dispute is about the trunk being a step for the foliage
items.desc_en: Rava clarifies that everyone agrees that if the murderer stands at the trunk he cannot be killed, and if he stands in the foliage he can be killed with arrows. The dispute is only whether the trunk is considered a step to the foliage, affecting the status of the trunk.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that everyone agrees that if the murderer stands at the trunk he cannot be killed.
Rava states that everyone agrees that if the murderer stands in the foliage he can be killed with arrows and stones.
Rava explains that the dispute is only whether the trunk is considered a step to the foliage, with one opinion holding it is and the other holding it is not.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative interpretation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative interpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that Rabbi Yehuda's phrase 'after the foliage' means 'even after the foliage,' implying that the foliage extends the city's protection.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that 'after the foliage' means 'even after the foliage,' expanding the rule.

items.text: Mishnah: Murderer who kills within the city
items.text_en: Mishnah: Murderer who kills within the city
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a murderer kills within the city of refuge, he is exiled from one neighborhood to another, and a Levite is exiled from one city to another.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one kills within the same city, he goes into exile from one neighborhood to another, and a Levite goes from city to city.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation that Levites go from district to district
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation that Levites go from district to district
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that derives from the verse that Israelites were exiled in the wilderness to the Levite camp. From this, it is said that a Levite who kills goes from district to district, and if he goes to his own district, it absorbs him. Rav Acha bar Rav Ika provides the scriptural support.

sub.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verse 'ושמתי לך מקום' to teach that Israel exiled in the wilderness to the camp of the Levites.
