sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's statement
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's statement
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika derives from the verse 'כי בעיר מקלטו ישב' that a Levite who killed goes from district to district, and his own district absorbs him.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's scriptural support
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's scriptural support
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika provides the scriptural support from the verse 'כִּי בְעִיר מִקְלָטוֹ יֵשֵׁב', meaning the city that already absorbed him.

items.text: Mishnah: The murderer's humility and acceptance of honor
items.text_en: Mishnah: The murderer's humility and acceptance of honor
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if the townspeople wish to honor the exiled murderer, he must say 'I am a murderer,' but if they insist, he may accept, as the verse says 'and this is the word of the murderer.'

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a killer who goes to a city of refuge and is honored by its residents must say 'I am a killer,' but if they insist, he may accept, as per the verse 'וזה דבר הרוצח'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about Levites' wages and return to office
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about Levites' wages and return to office
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda holds that Levites were paid wages for their work in the cities of refuge, while Rabbi Meir disagrees. Additionally, Rabbi Meir holds that the Levite returns to his previous position, while Rabbi Yehuda disagrees.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Yehuda's position that Levites were paid wages for their work in the cities of refuge.
Rabbi Meir disputes, asserting that Levites were not paid wages.
Rabbi Meir states that the Levite returns to his previous position of authority.
Rabbi Yehuda counters that the Levite does not return to his previous position.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute: Rav Kahana and Rava's interpretations
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute: Rav Kahana and Rava's interpretations
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana explains that the dispute is specifically about the six cities of refuge, based on differing interpretations of the word 'לָכֶם'. Rava objects, arguing that 'לָכֶם' implies all needs, and instead reinterprets the dispute as being about the additional forty-two cities, based on the phrase 'וַעֲלֵיהֶם תִּתְּנוּ'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana explains that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir is specifically about the six cities of refuge, based on differing interpretations of the word 'לָכֶם' (for you), but regarding the additional forty-two cities, all agree that wages were paid.
Rava objects to Rav Kahana's interpretation, arguing that the word 'לָכֶם' (for you) clearly implies all needs, not just refuge.

Rava reinterprets the dispute as being about the additional forty-two cities, based on the phrase 'וַעֲלֵיהֶם תִּתְּנוּ' (and upon them you shall give), while regarding the six cities of refuge, all agree that wages were not paid.

items.text: Baraita on returning to ancestral inheritance
items.text_en: Baraita on returning to ancestral inheritance
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses the verse 'וְשָׁב אֶל מִשְׁפַּחְתּוֹ', with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir disputing whether one returns only to his family or also to his ancestral property. The same dispute is applied to the returning murderer, with a verbal analogy (גזירה שוה) of 'שיבה'.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the verse 'וְשָׁב אֶל מִשְׁפַּחְתּוֹ' and presents Rabbi Yehuda's position that one returns only to his family, not to ancestral property.
Rabbi Meir counters that one also returns to ancestral property, citing the phrase 'אֶל אֲחֻזַּת אֲבוֹתָיו' to equate the returnee with his ancestors.
The baraita extends the same dispute to the returning murderer, using the word 'יָשׁוּב' to include him.
The Gemara asks what the phrase 'וְכֵן בַּגּוֹלָה' means.
The Gemara answers by citing a baraita that applies the same dispute to the murderer, with Rabbi Meir deriving the rule via a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) of 'שיבה' from the earlier verse.

items.text: Conclusion of previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous chapter
items.desc_en: The standard closing formula 'הֲדַרַן עֲלָךְ' marks the end of the previous chapter.

sub.desc_en: The standard closing formula 'הדרן עלך' marks the end of the previous chapter.

items.text: Mishnah: Those liable for lashes
items.text_en: Mishnah: Those liable for lashes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists various transgressions punishable by lashes, including forbidden sexual relations, eating sacred food while impure, and other prohibitions. It also includes a dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages about the minimum amount of untithed produce (טבל) that incurs liability.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the categories of forbidden sexual relations that incur lashes.
The Mishnah clarifies that a woman who is both an widow and a divorcee incurs liability under two distinct prohibitions, while a divorcee who is also a חלוצה (halutza) incurs only one.

The Mishnah lists additional prohibitions punishable by lashes: an impure person eating sacred food, entering the Temple while impure, and eating forbidden fats, blood, leftover offerings, piggul, and impure offerings.

The Mishnah continues listing prohibitions: slaughtering and offering outside the Temple, eating leaven on Passover, eating or working on Yom Kippur, compounding anointing oil or incense, anointing with sacred oil, and eating neveilot, treifot, and creeping things.
The Mishnah adds liability for eating טבל (untithed produce), first tithe from which תרומה (priestly portion) was not removed, and second tithe or consecrated property that was not redeemed.
The Mishnah asks: how much טבל (untithed produce) must one eat to be liable for lashes?
Rabbi Shimon answers that any amount, even the smallest, incurs liability.
The Sages answer that one must eat at least a כזית (olive's bulk) to be liable.
Rabbi Shimon objects by asking whether the Sages agree that one who eats an ant is liable for any amount, implying a parallel to טבל (untithed produce).
The Sages respond that an ant is liable in any amount because it is a complete creature (כברייתה), unlike a grain of wheat.
Rabbi Shimon counters that a single wheat grain is also a complete entity (כברייתה), so the same logic should apply to טבל (untithed produce).

items.text: Gemara's question: Why only karet offenses?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why only karet offenses?
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah lists only those liable for karet, not those liable for court-imposed death penalties. It identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Akiva, who equates karet and death penalty offenses in this context.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah lists only those liable for karet (כרת), not those liable for court-imposed death penalties, and asks why.
The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Akiva, who equates karet and death penalty offenses in this context, as cited in a baraita.

items.text: Opening dispute: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva on lashes for karet and death penalties
items.text_en: Opening dispute: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva on lashes for karet and death penalties
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael states that only those liable for lashes are included in the category of forty lashes, excluding karet and death penalties. Rabbi Akiva argues that those liable for karet are included because repentance leads to divine forgiveness, but those liable for court-imposed death are excluded because earthly courts cannot forgive.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael states that only those liable for lashes are included in the category of forty lashes, excluding those liable for karet or court-imposed death.

Rabbi Akiva argues that those liable for karet are included because repentance leads to divine forgiveness, but those liable for court-imposed death are excluded because earthly courts cannot forgive.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's explanation of karet's exclusion
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's explanation of karet's exclusion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains that karet was originally included in the general category of lashes, but the Torah explicitly singled out the case of one who has relations with his sister to teach that he is punished with karet and not lashes.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that those liable for כרת (karet) were included in the general category of lashes, but the Torah singled out the case of one who has relations with his sister to teach that he is punished with karet and not lashes.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives Rabbi Yishmael's position from the verse 'if you do not observe' and the word 'wondrous' (הפלאה), which is interpreted as lashes. It then addresses potential objections: that positive commandments would also be included (answered by the principle of 'הִשָּׁמֶר, פֶּן, אַל' indicating negative commands), that a prohibition without an action would be included (answered by 'לַעֲשׂוֹת'), and that a prohibition that can be rectified by a positive command would be included (answered by comparing to the prohibition of muzzling an animal). Finally, the Gemara concludes that all these cases are analogous to the prohibition of muzzling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Yishmael's reasoning for including prohibitions punishable by lashes.
The Gemara derives Rabbi Yishmael's position from the verse 'if you do not observe' and the word 'wondrous' (הפלאה), interpreted as lashes.
The Gemara objects that positive commandments would also be included by this derivation.

sub.text: Gemara's answer citing Rabbi Avin quoting Rabbi Ilai
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer citing Rabbi Avin quoting Rabbi Ilai
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the verse says 'if you do not observe', and citing Rabbi Avin quoting Rabbi Ilai, the terms 'הִשָּׁמֶר, פֶּן, אַל' indicate only negative commandments.
The Gemara objects that a prohibition without an action would also be included.
The Gemara answers that the verse says 'לַעֲשׂוֹת' (to do), excluding prohibitions without an action.
The Gemara objects that a prohibition that can be rectified by a positive command would also be included.
The Gemara answers that it is analogous to the prohibition of muzzling an animal, which is a negative command that cannot be rectified by a positive command.
The Gemara concludes that all these cases are analogous to the prohibition of muzzling an animal.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Akiva's reasoning and a challenge
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Akiva's reasoning and a challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Akiva's position from the verse 'according to his wickedness' (כְּדֵי רִשְׁעָתוֹ), meaning one is punished for one transgression, not two. Rabbi Yishmael distinguishes between death and monetary fines (or lashes and monetary fines) versus death and lashes, where death is considered a prolonged form of lashes. The Gemara then challenges Rabbi Akiva: if so, why are those liable for karet included? The response is that they are included because they can repent, but the Gemara objects that currently they have not repented.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Akiva's reasoning, and answers that he derives from the verse 'כְּדֵי רִשְׁעָתוֹ' (according to his wickedness) that one is punished for one transgression, not two.
Rabbi Yishmael explains that his principle applies only to death and monetary fines or lashes and monetary fines, but death and lashes are considered a single prolonged form of lashes.
The Gemara objects to Rabbi Akiva: if so, why are those liable for karet included, since they have not yet repented at the time of punishment?

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's derivation and subsequent debate
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's derivation and subsequent debate
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu derives from a verbal analogy that the Torah explicitly includes karet liabilities in lashes. Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects that the same analogy would include death penalties. The Gemara responds that the analogy is limited to 'לְעֵינֵי' and not 'מֵעֵינֵי'. A further objection is raised based on the principle that similar words can be used for analogy even if not identical. The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak accepted the objection, explaining that the verse 'according to his wickedness' refers specifically to a transgression that is under the jurisdiction of a court.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu asserts that the Torah explicitly includes those liable to כרת (karet) in lashes, derived by a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'לְעֵינֵי' (before the judges) to 'לְעֵינֶיךָ' (before your eyes).

Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects that the same verbal analogy would also include those liable to death penalties, since the Torah uses 'מֵעֵינֵי' (from before the judges) which could be derived from 'לְעֵינֶיךָ'.
The Gemara responds that the analogy is limited to the exact phrase 'לְעֵינֵי' (before the judges) and not to the variant 'מֵעֵינֵי' (from before the judges).

The Gemara objects that the distinction between 'לְעֵינֵי' and 'מֵעֵינֵי' is meaningless, citing the school of Rabbi Yishmael that similar words (like 'וְשָׁב' and 'וּבָא') can be used for analogy even if not identical.

Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak accepts the objection and resolves it by citing the verse 'כְּדֵי רִשְׁעָתוֹ' (according to his wickedness), explaining that the Torah speaks only of a transgression that is under the jurisdiction of a court, excluding death penalties.

items.text: Rava's distinction and further discussion on karet
items.text_en: Rava's distinction and further discussion on karet
items.desc_en: Rava explains that all agree that if one is warned for death, he does not receive lashes. The dispute is when warned for lashes: Rabbi Yishmael holds that a prohibition that serves as a warning for court-imposed death is punishable by lashes, while Rabbi Akiva disagrees. The Gemara then challenges Rabbi Akiva regarding karet, which also has a warning. Rav Mordechai quotes Avimi from Hagronya in the name of Rava that karet liabilities do not require a warning, as seen with Passover and circumcision where punishment applies even without warning. The Gemara objects that perhaps the warning is for a sacrifice, but Passover and circumcision have no warning and thus no sacrifice. The Gemara concludes that the reason is that all commandments are compared to idolatry, which is a negative command, excluding positive commands.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that all agree that if one is warned for death, he does not receive lashes.

Rava explains that the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva is when warned for lashes: Rabbi Yishmael holds that a prohibition that serves as a warning for court-imposed death is punishable by lashes.
Rava states that Rabbi Akiva disagrees and holds that a prohibition that serves as a warning for court-imposed death is not punishable by lashes.
The Gemara objects that according to Rabbi Akiva, those liable for karet (כרת) should also be exempt from lashes, since their prohibition serves as a warning for karet.

sub.text: Rav Mordechai quoting Avimi from Hagronya in the name of Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Mordechai quoting Avimi from Hagronya in the name of Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Mordechai tells Rav Ashi that Avimi from Hagronya said in the name of Rava that those liable for karet do not require a warning, as seen with Passover (פסח) and circumcision (מילה), where punishment applies even without warning.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the warning for karet is for a sacrifice, but Passover and circumcision have no warning and thus no sacrifice.
The Gemara resolves that the reason is that all commandments are compared to idolatry (עבודה זרה), which is a negative command, excluding positive commands.

items.text: Ravina's alternative explanation (incomplete)
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative explanation (incomplete)
items.desc_en: Ravina begins an alternative explanation, but the text is cut off, leaving the argument incomplete.

sub.desc_en: Ravina begins an alternative explanation, but the text is cut off, leaving the argument incomplete.

items.text: Continuation of the previous sugya: the case of repentance
items.text_en: Continuation of the previous sugya: the case of repentance
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues its earlier discussion, stating that if sinners repent, the heavenly court forgives them, and the threat of karet is not absolute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the earlier issue by stating that if sinners repent, the heavenly court forgives them, and the threat of karet is not absolute.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's view: karet for a sister excludes lashes
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's view: karet for a sister excludes lashes
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak argues that those liable for karet were included in the general category of lashes, but the Torah specified karet for one's sister to teach that he is punished by karet and not lashes.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that those liable for karet were included in the general category of lashes, but the Torah specified karet for one's sister to teach that he is punished by karet and not lashes.

items.text: The Rabbis' view: karet for a sister teaches division of liability
items.text_en: The Rabbis' view: karet for a sister teaches division of liability
items.desc_en: The Rabbis explain that the mention of karet for a sister is needed to teach that one is liable separately for each forbidden act, as per Rabbi Yochanan's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis explain that the mention of karet for a sister is needed to teach division of liability, so that one is liable separately for each forbidden act, as per Rabbi Yochanan's principle.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's source for division and the Rabbis' alternative
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's source for division and the Rabbis' alternative
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks where Rabbi Yitzchak derives the principle of division; he learns it from the verse about a menstruating woman. The Rabbis agree that this verse could also teach division, but they need the karet for a sister to teach liability for multiple relationships involving the same woman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where Rabbi Yitzchak derives the principle of division (חילוק) to make one liable separately for each prohibited act.

The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yitzchak derives the principle from the verse 'וְאֶל אִשָּׁה בְּנִדַּת טֻמְאָתָהּ' (and to a woman in her menstrual impurity), which teaches liability for each woman separately.
The Gemara objects that the Rabbis could also derive division from the same verse, so why do they need the karet for a sister?
The Gemara concedes that indeed the Rabbis could derive division from that verse as well.
The Gemara then asks what purpose the karet for a sister serves for the Rabbis if division is already derived from elsewhere.
The Gemara answers that the karet for a sister is needed to make one liable for a sister who is also a paternal aunt and a maternal aunt (a single woman with multiple prohibited relationships).

items.text: Clarification: liability for a woman who is both sister and aunt
items.text_en: Clarification: liability for a woman who is both sister and aunt
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the need for a verse to teach liability for separate relationships, since they are distinct bodies and names. It explains that the verse is needed for a case where a woman is one's sister, father's sister, and mother's sister simultaneously, i.e., a wicked person born of a wicked person.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a verse is needed to teach liability for separate relationships, since they are distinct bodies and names.
The Gemara explains that the verse is needed for a case where a woman is one's sister, father's sister, and mother's sister simultaneously, i.e., a wicked person born of a wicked person.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's derivation via a kal vachomer and its refutation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's derivation via a kal vachomer and its refutation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak derives the liability for multiple relationships from a kal vachomer based on the case of five menstruating women. The Rabbis reject this kal vachomer because the bodies are distinct in the case of menstruation, unlike here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where does Rabbi Yitzchak derive the principle of liability for multiple relationships?

The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yitzchak derives it from a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) based on the case of five menstruating women, as cited in a baraita where Rabbi Akiva asked Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua about a man who has relations with his sister who is also his father's sister and mother's sister.

The Rabbis object that the קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) is refutable: the case of menstruation is different because the bodies of the women are distinct, unlike here where the same body is involved.

items.text: Alternative derivation: from the second mention of 'sister'
items.text_en: Alternative derivation: from the second mention of 'sister'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yitzchak derives the law from the second mention of 'sister' in the verse. The Rabbis use that mention to teach that punishment is not derived from logical inference. The Gemara concludes with two alternative explanations for Rabbi Yitzchak's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that for the other opinion (Rabbi Yitzchak) as well, this a fortiori inference is certainly refuted.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yitzchak derives the law from the phrase 'his sister' in the latter clause of the verse.
The Gemara asks: And for the other opinion (the Rabbis), why do I need the phrase 'his sister' in the latter clause of the verse?

The Gemara answers: It teaches to render him liable for his sister who is the daughter of his father and the daughter of his mother, to say that one does not administer punishment from a logical inference.

The Gemara asks: And for the other opinion (Rabbi Yitzchak), from where does he derive the liability for a woman who is both his father's daughter and his mother's daughter? The Gemara answers: If you wish, say he derives the punishment from the prohibition; if you wish, say he derives it from the verse.

items.text: Clarifying the source for karet on the one who anoints or compounds the anointing oil
items.text_en: Clarifying the source for karet on the one who anoints or compounds the anointing oil
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the verse 'his sister' is needed for the list of karet punishments. One opinion derives from it the division of karet for the one who compounds or anoints with the anointing oil, while another rejects this and derives the division from a principle of Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Hoshaya. A third alternative derives it from the verse about a man lying with a menstruating woman, which is then used for Rabbi Yochanan's teaching about the source of a woman's impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the source for the word 'his sister' in the opening verse.
One opinion answers that the verse is needed to divide karet for the one who compounds or anoints with the anointing oil.
Another opinion rejects the first and instead follows Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Hoshaya, who holds that wherever there are two prohibitions and one karet, they are divided for a sacrifice.
A third alternative derives the division from the verse about a man lying with a menstruating woman.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse about a menstruating woman is needed for Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that a woman is not impure until her discharge exits through her sexual organ.

items.text: The problem: finding a warning for a tamei who eats kodashim
items.text_en: The problem: finding a warning for a tamei who eats kodashim
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for a tamei person entering the Temple, both the punishment (karet) and the warning (prohibition) are explicit in the Torah. However, for a tamei person eating kodashim, while the punishment is explicit, the source for the warning is not clear, prompting the question.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for a tamei person entering the Temple, both the punishment (karet) and the warning (prohibition) are explicit, but for a tamei person eating kodashim, while the punishment is explicit, the source for the warning is not clear, prompting the question.

items.text: Two derivations for the warning: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Two derivations for the warning: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish derives the warning from the verse 'Do not touch any holy thing.' Rabbi Yochanan, citing a baraita of Bardela, uses a gezeirah shavah (verbal analogy) between 'tum'ato' here and 'tum'ato' in the context of a zav, where both punishment and warning are stated, to derive the warning for eating kodashim.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish derives the warning for a טמא (impure person) who eats קודש (sacred food) from the verse 'בכל קדש לא תגע' (Do not touch any holy thing).

Rabbi Yochanan, citing a baraita of Bardela, uses a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between 'טומאתו' here and 'טומאתו' in the context of a זב (zav), where both punishment and warning are stated, to derive the warning for eating קודש (sacred food).

items.text: Analysis of the dispute: why each rejects the other's derivation
items.text_en: Analysis of the dispute: why each rejects the other's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Reish Lakish does not accept Rabbi Yochanan's gezeirah shavah because he does not know it. Rabbi Yochanan rejects Reish Lakish's derivation because he interprets the verse 'Do not touch any holy thing' as a warning for terumah, not for kodashim. Reish Lakish derives the warning for terumah from a different verse, and the Gemara notes that one verse deals with eating and the other with touching.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Reish Lakish does not accept Rabbi Yochanan's gezeirah shavah because he does not know it.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yochanan rejects Reish Lakish's derivation, and answers that Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse 'Do not touch any holy thing' as a warning for terumah.
The Gemara explains that Reish Lakish derives the warning for terumah from a different verse, and notes that one verse deals with eating and the other with touching.

items.text: The verse 'Do not touch' is needed for the case of a tamei touching kodashim
items.text_en: The verse 'Do not touch' is needed for the case of a tamei touching kodashim
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Reish Lakish's use of the verse for eating is problematic because the verse is needed for the dispute about whether a tamei who touches kodashim is liable. Reish Lakish holds he is liable, Rabbi Yochanan holds he is not, and the Gemara explains that the verse is used for the eater by analogy to the Temple.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Reish Lakish's use of the verse 'בְּכׇל קֹדֶשׁ לֹא תִגָּע' (Do not touch any holy thing) for the eater, arguing it is needed for the case of a tamei (ritually impure person) who touches kodashim (sacred offerings).

The Gemara cites the dispute: Reish Lakish holds that a tamei who touches kodashim is liable to lashes (לוקה) from this verse, while Rabbi Yochanan holds he is not liable, as the verse is an admonition for terumah (תרומה, priestly portion).

The Gemara resolves that since the Torah expressed the case of a tamei touching kodashim in the language of 'touch' (נגיעה), the admonition for the eater is derived by analogy (היקש) of kodashim to the Temple (מקדש).

items.text: The verse is also needed for the case of a tamei eating before blood sprinkling
items.text_en: The verse is also needed for the case of a tamei eating before blood sprinkling
items.desc_en: The Gemara further argues that the verse is needed for the dispute about a tamei who eats kodashim before the blood is sprinkled. Reish Lakish holds he is liable, Rabbi Yochanan holds he is not, because the verse 'tum'ato' is written after sprinkling. The Gemara concludes that the case before sprinkling is derived from 'Do not touch.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse 'בכל קדש לא תגע' is needed for the case of a טמא (impure person) who eats sacred meat before the blood is sprinkled.
Reish Lakish holds that the טמא (impure person) is liable (לוקה) whether before or after sprinkling, based on the verse 'בכל קדש לא תגע'.
Rabbi Yochanan holds that the טמא (impure person) is not liable before sprinkling, because the verse 'טומאתו' applies only after sprinkling, and the case before sprinkling is derived from 'בכל קדש'.

items.text: A baraita supports Reish Lakish's position
items.text_en: A baraita supports Reish Lakish's position
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that explicitly states that the verse 'Do not touch any holy thing' is a warning for the eater, not the toucher, by comparing kodashim to the Temple, where the prohibition involves a life-taking act (eating), not mere touching.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that explicitly supports Reish Lakish's position by interpreting the verse 'בְּכׇל קֹדֶשׁ לֹא תִגָּע' as a warning for the eater, not the toucher, through a comparison (היקש) of קודש (sacred food) to the מקדש (Temple), where the prohibition involves a life-taking act (eating), not mere touching.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's general principle: a prohibition preceded by a positive command is punishable by lashes
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's general principle: a prohibition preceded by a positive command is punishable by lashes
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah quotes Rabbi Yochanan stating a general rule: for any negative commandment that is preceded by a positive commandment, one is liable to lashes for violating it.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah quotes Rabbi Yochanan stating a general rule: for any negative commandment that is preceded by a positive commandment, one is liable to lashes for violating it.

items.text: Rabba's oath and the contradiction
items.text_en: Rabba's oath and the contradiction
items.desc_en: Rabba swears he said the ruling that a rapist who divorces must remarry and is lashed, but cites a verse and a Mishnah that imply he is not lashed. This sets up the difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rabba whether he actually said the ruling, and he denies it.
Rabba swears by God that he did say it, but then notes that a verse and a Mishnah contradict him.
Rabba cites the verse 'וִישַׁלְּחוּ מִן הַמַּחֲנֶה' and the Mishnah 'הַבָּא לַמִּקְדָּשׁ טָמֵא' as evidence that a טמא (impure person) who enters the Temple is liable, contradicting his own ruling.

items.text: The reason for Rabba's retraction: the case of an אונס
items.text_en: The reason for Rabba's retraction: the case of an אונס
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabba retracted because of a difficulty from the law of an אונס (rapist) who divorced: if he is an Israelite, he must remarry but is not lashed; if a priest, he is lashed but does not remarry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabba retracted his statement, and answers that it was due to a difficulty from the case of an אונס (rapist).
A baraita is cited: a rapist who divorced, if he is an Israelite, he must remarry and is not lashed; if a priest, he is lashed and does not remarry.

items.text: Question on the Israelite case
items.text_en: Question on the Israelite case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why an Israelite rapist who divorces is not lashed, since the prohibition is a לא תעשה preceded by a עשה, and one should be lashed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why an Israelite rapist who divorces is not lashed, since the prohibition is a לא תעשה (negative commandment) preceded by a עשה (positive commandment), and one should be lashed.

items.text: Ulla's derivation from מוציא שם רע
items.text_en: Ulla's derivation from מוציא שם רע
items.desc_en: Ulla suggests that the verse 'לו תהיה לאשה' in the case of an אונס is unnecessary for its own context, so it is applied to the case after divorce, teaching that if he divorced he must remarry. This is derived via a קל וחומר from מוציא שם רע.

sub.desc_en: Ulla proposes that the verse 'לו תהיה לאשה' in the case of an אונס (rapist) is superfluous, and derives via a קל וחומר (a fortiori) from מוציא שם רע (defamer of a bride) that the rapist must remarry if he divorced.
Ulla resolves that since the verse is not needed for its own context (the rapist's initial obligation), it is applied to the case after divorce, teaching that if he divorced he must remarry.

items.text: Refutation of the derivation from מוציא שם רע
items.text_en: Refutation of the derivation from מוציא שם רע
items.desc_en: The Gemara refutes the קל וחומר: מוציא שם רע is stricter because he is lashed and pays a fine, so the comparison fails.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara refutes the קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from מוציא שם רע (defamer of a bride) to אונס (rapist) because מוציא שם רע is stricter, as he is lashed and pays a fine.

items.text: Reverse derivation and its refutation
items.text_en: Reverse derivation and its refutation
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts the reverse: the verse is unnecessary for מוציא שם רע and is applied to the אונס after divorce. But this is refuted because the אונס did an action, making him more culpable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes the reverse derivation: the verse 'לו תהיה לאשה' is unnecessary for מוציא שם רע, so apply it to the אונס after divorce.
The Gemara refutes the reverse derivation because the אונס performed an action, making him more culpable than מוציא שם רע.

items.text: Alternative derivation and further discussion
items.text_en: Alternative derivation and further discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the verse is unnecessary for מוציא שם רע because she is already his wife, so it applies to the אונס after divorce. It then questions whether it could apply to the later part of מוציא שם רע itself to exempt him from lashes, and concludes that the אונס cannot learn from it due to the refutation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the verse 'לו תהיה לאשה' is unnecessary for מוציא שם רע since she is already his wife, so it should be applied to the אונס after divorce.
The Gemara questions whether the verse could instead be applied to the later part of מוציא שם רע itself to exempt him from lashes.
The Gemara rejects this, concluding that the אונס cannot learn from מוציא שם רע due to the refutation that מוציא שם רע did not commit an act.

items.text: Rava's ruling: all his days in standing and returning
items.text_en: Rava's ruling: all his days in standing and returning
items.desc_en: Rava states that the rapist is obligated to remarry his divorced wife all his days, and Rabbi Yochanan agrees. This resolves the issue without lashes.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the dilemma by ruling that the rapist must constantly remarry and divorce his wife, fulfilling the positive command without incurring lashes, and Rabbi Yochanan agrees.

items.text: Rav Papa's question and Rava's answer
items.text_en: Rav Papa's question and Rava's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Papa questions whether this is a לאו שניתק לעשה, and Rava responds that the additional עשה does not detract from the לאו. The Gemara then clarifies that the extra עשה is to nullify the לאו.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa questions Rava whether this prohibition is comparable to the לאו (negative commandment) of muzzling an animal, which is a לאו שניתק לעשה (a negative commandment that is remedied by a positive commandment).
Rava responds that the additional positive commandment (עשה) written by the Torah does not detract from the negative commandment; it is not a לאו שניתק לעשה.

The Gemara objects that if so, in every case of a לאו שניתק לעשה (negative commandment remedied by a positive commandment), one could similarly argue that the additional positive commandment does not detract, which would undermine the entire category.
Rava resolves that in the case of a לאו שניתק לעשה, the additional positive commandment comes specifically to nullify the negative commandment, whereas here it does not.

items.text: Dispute about nullification of the לאו
items.text_en: Dispute about nullification of the לאו
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this works for the opinion that the לאו is nullified, but for the opinion that it is not nullified, what can be said?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks that the previous explanation works for the opinion that the לאו (prohibition) is nullified, but for the opinion that it is not nullified, what can be said?

items.text: Gemara's question and the baraita before Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Gemara's question and the baraita before Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning is, given that he instructed the tanna to recite a baraita stating that one is liable only if he nullified the positive command. The baraita taught before Rabbi Yochanan distinguished between fulfilling and nullifying the positive command, but Rabbi Yochanan corrected it to focus on nullification versus non-nullification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning is, given that he instructed the tanna to recite a baraita stating liability only for nullifying the positive command.
The baraita taught before Rabbi Yochanan distinguished between fulfilling and nullifying the positive command.
Rabbi Yochanan corrects the tanna to focus on nullification versus non-nullification, not fulfillment versus non-fulfillment.

items.text: The dispute defined: uncertain warning
items.text_en: The dispute defined: uncertain warning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish disagree about whether uncertain warning is considered valid warning. One holds that uncertain warning is valid, the other that it is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: On what point do Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish disagree?
The Gemara answers: They disagree about whether uncertain warning (התראת ספק) is considered valid warning; one holds it is valid.
The Gemara adds: And the other holds that uncertain warning is not considered valid warning.

items.text: Support from a parallel dispute about oaths
items.text_en: Support from a parallel dispute about oaths
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish follow their respective views in a parallel case: one who swears to eat a loaf today and does not eat is not flogged, and Rabbi Yochanan explains that this is because the warning is uncertain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a parallel dispute about oaths to show that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish follow their respective views consistently.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that one who swears to eat a loaf today and does not eat is not flogged, consistent with his view that uncertain warning (התראת ספק) is not considered valid warning.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on the rationale for exemption
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on the rationale for exemption
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish both agree that one is not lashed for violating the prohibition of leaving over the Passover offering, but they disagree on the reason. Rabbi Yochanan holds it is because it is a prohibition without an action, while Reish Lakish holds it is because it is a doubtful warning. Both derive their positions from the same baraita about Rabbi Yehuda's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents Rabbi Yochanan's and Reish Lakish's positions on why one is not lashed for leaving over the Passover offering: Rabbi Yochanan says it is a prohibition without an action (לאו שאין בו מעשה), and Reish Lakish says it is a doubtful warning (התראת ספק).

The Gemara notes that both opinions align with Rabbi Yehuda's view, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda derives from the verse about the Passover offering that a prohibition followed by a positive commandment is not punishable by lashes.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan infers from the baraita that without the verse, one would be lashed, implying that a doubtful warning is valid; Reish Lakish infers that without the verse, one would be lashed, implying that a prohibition without an action is punishable.

items.text: Objection to Reish Lakish and resolution via another baraita
items.text_en: Objection to Reish Lakish and resolution via another baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Reish Lakish's case is clearly one of doubtful warning, so how can he claim it is a prohibition without action? It answers that Reish Lakish follows a different tanna's version of Rabbi Yehuda's opinion, where a doubtful warning is still considered a valid warning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Reish Lakish's case is clearly one of doubtful warning (התראת ספק), so how can he claim it is a prohibition without action?
The Gemara resolves that Reish Lakish follows a different tanna's version of Rabbi Yehuda's opinion, where a doubtful warning is still considered a valid warning.

items.text: Objection to Rabbi Yochanan and resolution via a tradition from Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
items.text_en: Objection to Rabbi Yochanan and resolution via a tradition from Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan's case is clearly a prohibition without action, so how can he claim it is a doubtful warning? It answers that Rabbi Yochanan follows a tradition from Rabbi Yosei HaGelili that lists exceptions to the rule that prohibitions without action are not lashed, including swearing, exchanging, and cursing one's fellow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan's case is clearly a prohibition without action (לאו שאין בו מעשה), so how can he claim it is a doubtful warning?

sub.text: Resolution via Rav Idi bar Avin's tradition
sub.text_en: Resolution via Rav Idi bar Avin's tradition
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan follows a tradition from Rabbi Yosei HaGelili listing exceptions (swearing, exchanging, cursing) to the rule that prohibitions without action are not lashed.

items.text: Reconciliation of contradictions in Rabbi Yehuda's statements
items.text_en: Reconciliation of contradictions in Rabbi Yehuda's statements
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two statements of Rabbi Yehuda. It resolves that for Reish Lakish, there are two different tannaic versions of Rabbi Yehuda's opinion, while for Rabbi Yochanan, the contradiction is between his own view and that of his teacher.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two statements of Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara resolves that for Reish Lakish there are two tannaic versions of Rabbi Yehuda's opinion, while for Rabbi Yochanan the contradiction is between his own view and that of his teacher.

items.text: The principle of a negative commandment with a positive fulfillment
items.text_en: The principle of a negative commandment with a positive fulfillment
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah about one who takes a mother bird with its young, where Rabbi Yehuda says he is lashed and does not send the mother away, while the Sages say he sends and is not lashed. The rule is that any negative commandment that has a positive fulfillment is not punishable by lashes. Rabbi Yochanan says there are only two such cases: this one and another. Rabbi Elazar asks which other, and Rabbi Yochanan says to find it. He finds a baraita about a rapist who divorces: if he is an Israelite, he takes her back and is not lashed; if a priest, he is lashed and does not take her back.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah about one who takes a mother bird with its young, where Rabbi Yehuda says he is lashed and does not send the mother away, while the Sages say he sends and is not lashed.
The mishnah states the general rule that any negative commandment with a positive fulfillment is not punishable by lashes.
Rabbi Yochanan says there are only two such cases: this one and another.
Rabbi Elazar asks which other case, and Rabbi Yochanan tells him to find it.
Rabbi Yochanan finds a baraita about a rapist who divorces: if he is an Israelite, he takes her back and is not lashed; if a priest, he is lashed and does not take her back.

items.text: Discussion of the case of the rapist and the versions of the baraita
items.text_en: Discussion of the case of the rapist and the versions of the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the baraita about the rapist in light of two versions: one that says 'fulfilled and not fulfilled' and another that says 'nullified and not nullified'. It raises difficulties for the latter version regarding the case of the rapist, and resolves them by suggesting scenarios such as the woman accepting betrothal from another or being vowed by her husband in public. The Gemara concludes with a distinction between a vow made in public and one made with the knowledge of the public.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita about the rapist works smoothly for the version that says 'fulfilled and not fulfilled'.
The Gemara raises a difficulty for the version that says 'nullified and not nullified': how can the case of the rapist be found in that version?
The Gemara objects that if the rapist killed the woman, he would be liable for a more severe punishment (death), not lashes.
Rav Shimi of Mehoza suggests a scenario where the woman accepted betrothal from another man, so the rapist's nullification is ineffective.
Rav objects that if the woman appointed the other man as her agent, she herself nullifies the rapist's marriage; if not, the betrothal is invalid.
Rav Shimi of Nehardea suggests a scenario where the rapist vowed in public (ברבים) to nullify the marriage.
The Gemara objects that this works only for the opinion that a vow made in public cannot be annulled; what about the opposing opinion?
Amemar resolves the difficulty by distinguishing between a vow made in public (יש לו הפרה) and one made with the knowledge of the public (אין לו הפרה), so the scenario works for all opinions.

items.text: Additional cases and objection regarding a convert's pledge
items.text_en: Additional cases and objection regarding a convert's pledge
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if there are no other cases of negative commandments with a positive fulfillment, and suggests theft and pledge as examples, but notes that since they involve payment, one is not lashed and pays. Rabbi Zeira objects that there is the case of a pledge of a convert who dies, where the positive commandment of return does not apply, yet one is still not lashed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks if there are no other cases of negative commandments with a positive fulfillment, and suggests theft and pledge as examples.

The Gemara answers that these cases can be found in the scenario of קִיְּימוֹ וְלֹא קִיְּימוֹ (fulfilled and not fulfilled) or בִּיטְּלוֹ וְלֹא בִּיטְּלוֹ (nullified and not nullified), but since one is liable for payment, one is not lashed and pays.
Rabbi Zeira objects that there is the case of a pledge of a convert who dies, where the positive commandment of return does not apply, yet one is still not lashed.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding pe'ah
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding pe'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the case of pe'ah (corner of the field) seems to contradict the earlier principle, since one can fulfill the obligation even after the grain is harvested. It resolves that this is like Rabbi Yishmael's view, but even then it only applies if one ate the dough.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the case of pe'ah (corner of the field) seems to contradict the earlier principle, since one can fulfill the obligation even after the grain is harvested.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah showing that pe'ah can be given even after the grain is harvested, contradicting the earlier principle.
The Gemara resolves that this is like Rabbi Yishmael's view, but even then it only applies if one ate the dough.

items.text: Distinction between reshus and mitzvah for annulment of vows
items.text_en: Distinction between reshus and mitzvah for annulment of vows
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the principle 'on da'at rabbim there is no annulment' applies only to matters of reshus (optional matters), but for a mitzvah matter, annulment is possible. It brings a story about a children's teacher who was reinstated despite a ban.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the principle 'על דעת רבים אין לו הפרה' (on the consensus of the public there is no annulment) applies only to a matter of רשות (optional matter), but for a matter of מצוה (commandment) annulment is possible.

The Gemara brings a story about a children's teacher who was negligent, was banned by Rav Acha, and then reinstated by Ravina because no one else was as precise as him, illustrating that annulment is possible for a mitzvah matter.

items.text: Lashes for eating creeping creatures
items.text_en: Lashes for eating creeping creatures
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that one who eats a certain fish (binita) is lashed for violating the prohibition of 'sheretz hashoretz'. Abaye then lists the number of lashes for eating various creatures: putita (4), nemala (5), and tzir'a (6), each based on different biblical prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah listing categories of forbidden foods for which one is lashed.
Rav Yehuda rules that one who eats a binita fish from the Be Karava family is lashed for violating the prohibition of 'שרץ השורץ על הארץ' (creeping creature that swarms on the earth).
The Gemara reports that Rav Yehuda actually administered lashes to someone who ate that fish, confirming his ruling in practice.
Abaye states that one who eats a putita (a type of fish) receives four lashes.
Abaye rules that one who eats an ant receives five lashes, due to the prohibition of 'שרץ השורץ על הארץ' (creeping creature).
Abaye rules that one who eats a hornet receives six lashes, due to the prohibition of 'שרץ העוף' (swarming bird/insect).

items.text: Prohibition of delaying excretion and drinking from a craftsman's horn
items.text_en: Prohibition of delaying excretion and drinking from a craftsman's horn
items.desc_en: Rav Achai states that one who delays his bodily functions violates 'lo teshaktzu'. Rav Beivai bar Abaye adds that one who drinks from a craftsman's horn also violates this prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Rav Achai rules that one who delays his bodily functions violates the prohibition of 'לֹא תְשַׁקְּצוּ' (do not make yourselves abominable).
Rav Beivai bar Abaye adds that one who drinks from a craftsman's horn also violates the same prohibition of 'לֹא תְשַׁקְּצוּ'.

items.text: Lashes for crushed ants with a live one
items.text_en: Lashes for crushed ants with a live one
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Huna says that if one crushed nine ants and added one live ant to complete a kezayit, he receives six lashes: five for the live creature and one for a kezayit of neveila. Rava citing Rabbi Yochanan says even two ants and himself, and Rav Yosef says even one and himself, and they do not disagree—one refers to large ants, the other to small ones.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Huna states that crushing nine ants and adding one live ant to complete a kezayit (olive's bulk) incurs six lashes: five for the live creature and one for a kezayit of neveila (carcass).
Rava in the name of Rabbi Yochanan adds that even two ants plus himself (the eater) constitute a kezayit for lashes.
Rav Yosef says that even one ant plus himself suffices for a kezayit.
The gemara resolves that the opinions do not disagree: one refers to large ants, the other to small ants.

items.text: Lashes for eating tevel of ma'aser ani
items.text_en: Lashes for eating tevel of ma'aser ani
items.desc_en: Rav states that one who eats tevel of ma'aser ani is lashed. The Gemara identifies this with the view of Rabbi Yossi, who derives from a verse that the prohibition of 'lo suchal' applies even to ma'aser ani.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that one who eats tevel (untithed produce) of ma'aser ani (the poor tithe) is lashed.
The Gemara asks: In accordance with which Tanna's view does Rav rule?
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yossi derives from a verse that the prohibition of eating tevel applies even when only ma'aser ani has not been separated.
The Gemara explains the derivation: the verse 'לֹא תוּכַל' (you may not eat) is linked via a verbal analogy to the verse about ma'aser ani, establishing that the prohibition includes ma'aser ani.

items.text: Debate about calling the name on ma'aser ani of demai
items.text_en: Debate about calling the name on ma'aser ani of demai
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef frames a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding whether one must call the name on ma'aser ani of demai produce.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef frames the dispute as a Tannaitic debate, introducing Rabbi Eliezer's position.
Rabbi Eliezer rules that one need not call the name (designate the tithe) on ma'aser ani of demai produce.
The Sages disagree, holding that one must call the name on ma'aser ani of demai.

items.text: Clarifying the dispute about demai
items.text_en: Clarifying the dispute about demai
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the dispute in the Mishnah is about whether one who is certain the produce is untithed must separate terumah. Abaye rejects this, explaining that all agree that certain tevel requires separation; the dispute is about demai, where one opinion holds that amei ha'aretz are not suspected of neglecting poor man's tithe, while the other holds they are.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's dispute is about whether one who is certain the produce is untithed must separate תרומה (priestly portion).
Abaye rejects the Gemara's question, arguing that if the dispute were about certain tevel, they would have argued about that directly rather than about doubtful cases.

Abaye explains that all agree certain tevel requires separation; the dispute is about דמאי (doubtfully tithed produce), where one opinion holds that עמי הארץ (the unlearned) are not suspected of neglecting poor man's tithe, while the Sages hold they are.

items.text: Dispute about the measure for eating tevel: wheat vs. flour
items.text_en: Dispute about the measure for eating tevel: wheat vs. flour
items.desc_en: Rav Bivi citing Reish Lakish states the dispute is only about wheat, but for flour all agree the measure is a kezayit. Rabbi Yirmeya citing Reish Lakish says the dispute applies to both. The Gemara supports Rabbi Yirmeya from a baraita where Rabbi Shimon argues that a single wheat grain is significant like a whole creature, but flour is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's opening phrase about the measure for eating tevel.
Rav Bivi reports Reish Lakish's position that the dispute is only about wheat, but for flour all agree the measure is a kezayit.
Rabbi Yirmeya cites Reish Lakish saying the dispute applies to both wheat and flour.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon argues that a single wheat grain is significant like a whole creature, but flour is not, supporting Rabbi Yirmeya's view.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon was speaking according to the Sages' reasoning, conceding that wheat is significant but flour is not, while the Sages reject the significance of a single wheat grain.
A baraita is cited in support of Rabbi Yirmeya, where Rabbi Shimon states that for lashes any amount suffices, and the kezayit measure applies only to sacrificial offerings.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibitions that incur lashes
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibitions that incur lashes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where one is liable for lashes: eating first fruits without reciting the declaration, eating most holy offerings outside the courtyard, eating lesser holy offerings and second tithe outside the wall, and breaking a bone of a pure Passover offering. It also discusses the case of taking the mother bird with the young, where Rabbi Yehuda says one is lashed but does not send the mother away, while the Sages say one sends the mother away and is not lashed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists prohibitions that incur lashes: eating first fruits without reciting the declaration, eating most holy offerings outside the courtyard, eating lesser holy offerings and second tithe outside the wall, and breaking a bone of a pure Passover offering, while noting that leaving over or breaking a bone of an impure offering does not incur lashes.

The Mishnah presents the case of taking the mother bird with the young, where Rabbi Yehuda says one is lashed but does not send the mother away, while the Sages say one sends the mother away and is not lashed, concluding with the general rule that any negative commandment that includes a positive commandment does not incur lashes.

items.text: Attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan states that the Mishnah's ruling on first fruits is the view of Rabbi Akiva, but the Sages say that placing the first fruits in the Temple is essential, while recitation is not. The Gemara questions why it is not attributed to Rabbi Shimon, and explains that it teaches that Rabbi Akiva holds like Rabbi Shimon.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan attributes the Mishnah's ruling on first fruits to Rabbi Akiva, while the Sages hold that placing the first fruits in the Temple is essential but recitation is not.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah is attributed to Rabbi Akiva rather than to Rabbi Shimon, since the ruling aligns with Rabbi Shimon's view.
The Gemara answers that the attribution teaches that Rabbi Akiva holds like Rabbi Shimon on this matter.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's derivations for each offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's derivations for each offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a baraita where Rabbi Shimon derives from verses that one is lashed for eating first fruits before recitation, for eating todah and shelamim before blood sprinkling, for eating the firstborn even after sprinkling, for eating chatat and asham outside the curtains, and for eating the olah in any of these circumstances. Each derivation uses a kal vachomer from the previous category.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Shimon's statement is and introduces a baraita that identifies 'תרומת ידך' (the donation of your hand) as first fruits.

Rabbi Shimon asks what the verse comes to teach, argues that eating first fruits outside the wall is already derived by kal vachomer from second tithe, and concludes that the verse teaches that one who eats first fruits before recitation is lashed.

Rabbi Shimon identifies 'נדבותיך' (your gift offerings) as the thanks-offering and peace-offering, asks what the verse teaches, argues that eating outside the wall is derived from second tithe, and concludes that the verse teaches that one who eats these offerings before blood sprinkling is lashed.

Rabbi Shimon identifies 'בכורות' (the firstborn) as the firstborn offering, asks what the verse teaches, argues that eating outside the wall is derived from second tithe and eating before sprinkling from thanks-offering and peace-offering, and concludes that the verse teaches that a non-priest who eats the firstborn even after sprinkling is lashed.

Rabbi Shimon identifies 'בקרך וצאנך' (your herd and your flock) as the sin-offering and guilt-offering, asks what the verse teaches, argues that eating outside the wall is derived from second tithe, eating before sprinkling from thanks-offering and peace-offering, and eating by a non-priest after sprinkling from the firstborn, and concludes that the verse teaches that one who eats these offerings even after sprinkling but outside the curtains is lashed.

Rabbi Shimon identifies 'נדריך' (your vows) as the burnt-offering, asks what the verse teaches, argues that eating outside the wall is derived from second tithe, eating before sprinkling from thanks-offering and peace-offering, eating by a non-priest after sprinkling from the firstborn, and eating outside the curtains from sin-offering and guilt-offering, and begins to conclude that the verse comes to teach a unique prohibition.

items.text: Opening statement: the case of eating from the olah after sprinkling
items.text_en: Opening statement: the case of eating from the olah after sprinkling
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of one who eats from the olah after sprinkling, even inside the walls, who is liable to lashes according to Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of one who eats from the olah after sprinkling, even inside the walls, who is liable to lashes according to Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Rava's rhetorical comment
items.text_en: Rava's rhetorical comment
items.desc_en: Rava comments that if one's mother gives birth to a child like Rabbi Shimon, let her give birth; otherwise, let her not give birth, even though there are refutations to his view.

sub.desc_en: Rava declares that one whose mother gives birth to him as a follower of Rabbi Shimon should be born, otherwise not, even though there are refutations.

items.text: Series of comparisons between sacrifices
items.text_en: Series of comparisons between sacrifices
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a series of comparisons between bikurim and ma'aser, todah and shelamim and ma'aser, bechor and todah and shelamim, chatat and asham and bechor, and olah and chatat and asham, each time showing a stringency and a counter-stringency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what stringency bikurim (first fruits) have over ma'aser (tithe), answering that bikurim are forbidden to non-priests.
The Gemara counters that ma'aser is more stringent because it is forbidden to an אונן (a mourner before burial).
The Gemara asks what stringency todah (thanksgiving offering) and shelamim (peace offerings) have over ma'aser, answering that they require blood application and sacrificial portions on the altar.
The Gemara counters that ma'aser is more stringent because it requires minted silver coins for redemption.
The Gemara asks what stringency bekhor (firstborn animal) has over todah and shelamim, answering that its sanctity is from the womb.
The Gemara counters that todah and shelamim are more stringent because they require semikhah (laying of hands), libations, and the waving of the breast and thigh.
The Gemara asks what stringency chatat (sin offering) and asham (guilt offering) have over bekhor, answering that they are most holy (קדשי קדשים).
The Gemara counters that bekhor is more stringent because its sanctity is from the womb.
The Gemara asks what stringency olah (burnt offering) has over chatat and asham, answering that it is entirely consumed on the altar.
The Gemara counters that chatat and asham are more stringent because they provide atonement (כפרה).

items.text: Conclusion: all are stricter than olah
items.text_en: Conclusion: all are stricter than olah
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that all these sacrifices are stricter than the olah because they involve two acts of eating.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether all of them are stricter than olah because they involve two acts of eating.

items.text: Clarification of Rava's intent
items.text_en: Clarification of Rava's intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rava's statement refers to one who interprets the verse in a forced manner according to his own view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rava meant by his statement, and explains that Rabbi Shimon interprets the verse by reversing its plain meaning.

items.text: Question about deriving prohibitions from punishments
items.text_en: Question about deriving prohibitions from punishments
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one can derive prohibitions from punishments, noting that even those who derive punishments from logic do not derive prohibitions from logic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether warnings can be derived through logical inference, noting that even those who derive punishments from logic do not derive warnings from logic.
The Gemara resolves that the warning is merely a prohibition (איסור בעלמא), not a formal warning for lashes.

items.text: Rava's statement about five prohibitions
items.text_en: Rava's statement about five prohibitions
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rava's statement that a non-priest who eats from the olah before sprinkling outside the wall, according to Rabbi Shimon, is liable to five lashes, indicating five prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that a non-priest who eats from the olah before sprinkling outside the wall, according to Rabbi Shimon, is liable to five lashes, indicating five separate prohibitions.

items.text: Transition to the Mishnah
items.text_en: Transition to the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to quote the Mishnah listing those who are liable to lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's statement by citing the Mishnah's list of those who receive lashes.

items.text: Derivation of separate prohibitions
items.text_en: Derivation of separate prohibitions
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the extra verse 'You shall not eat them' serves to establish a separate prohibition for each forbidden item, rather than being redundant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since the Torah already wrote the general prohibition 'You shall not eat them' after the command to bring offerings to the Temple, why does it need to specify each forbidden item separately?
The Gemara answers: the extra verse comes to establish a separate prohibition (לאו) for each forbidden item individually, so that one who eats multiple forbidden items is liable for each one.

items.text: Rava's statement about a non-priest eating from the offering
items.text_en: Rava's statement about a non-priest eating from the offering
items.desc_en: Rava states that a non-priest who eats from the burnt-offering before the blood is thrown outside the wall incurs five lashes according to Rabbi Shimon. The Gemara questions why he does not also incur lashes for the prohibition 'No stranger shall eat' and for 'Flesh torn in the field', and answers that these prohibitions apply only when the meat is fit for priests or inside the permitted area, which is not the case here.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that a non-priest who eats from the burnt-offering before the blood is thrown outside the wall incurs five lashes according to Rabbi Shimon.
The Gemara asks why the non-priest does not also incur lashes for the prohibition 'No stranger shall eat, for they are holy'.
The Gemara answers that this prohibition applies only when the meat is fit for priests, which is not the case here since it is outside the wall.
The Gemara asks why the non-priest does not also incur lashes for the prohibition 'Flesh torn in the field you shall not eat', since the meat left its permitted boundary.
The Gemara answers that this prohibition applies only when the meat is fit inside the permitted area, which is not the case here since it was never fit inside.
The Gemara asks why the non-priest does not also incur lashes according to Rabbi Eliezer's teaching about the verse 'It shall not be eaten, for it is holy'.

items.text: Gemara's question on the applicability of a negative commandment to invalid sacred items
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the applicability of a negative commandment to invalid sacred items
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the principle that anything invalid in sacred matters is subject to a negative commandment for eating applies only when it was initially fit, but here it was never fit. It then suggests that the lashes should be derived from Rabbi Eliezer's teaching about items that are 'entirely burnt,' and concludes that Rava indeed derives from that verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the principle that anything invalid in sacred matters is subject to a negative commandment for eating applies only when it was initially fit, but here it was never fit.
The Gemara suggests that the lashes should be derived from Rabbi Eliezer's teaching about items that are 'entirely burnt,' and concludes that Rava indeed derives from that verse.

items.text: Rav Giddel's statement about a priest eating before sprinkling
items.text_en: Rav Giddel's statement about a priest eating before sprinkling
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel says in the name of Rav that a priest who eats from a sin-offering or guilt-offering before the sprinkling of the blood is lashed, because the verse 'And they shall eat them that atonement was made with them' implies after atonement, not before. This is a negative derived from a positive command.

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel states in the name of Rav that a priest who eats from a sin-offering or guilt-offering before sprinkling is lashed, deriving a negative command from the positive verse about eating after atonement.

items.text: Rava's objection from the laws of kosher animals
items.text_en: Rava's objection from the laws of kosher animals
items.desc_en: Rava raises an objection: The verse 'that you may eat' implies only that animal, and if the negative 'this you shall not eat' is derived from a positive command, why would another verse be needed? This challenges the previous derivation.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects: from the positive command 'that you may eat' we infer a prohibition on other animals, so why would the Torah need the explicit negative 'this you shall not eat'? This challenges the idea that a prohibition derived from a positive command is a full-fledged negative.

items.text: Revised version of Rav Giddel's statement regarding a non-priest
items.text_en: Revised version of Rav Giddel's statement regarding a non-priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a corrected version: Rav Giddel said in the name of Rav that a non-priest who eats from a sin-offering or guilt-offering before sprinkling is exempt. The reason is that the verse 'and they shall eat them that atonement was made with them' determines whether the prohibition 'no stranger shall eat holy' applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the corrected version of Rav Giddel's statement in the name of Rav: a non-priest who eats from a sin-offering or guilt-offering before sprinkling is exempt, because the prohibition for a non-priest applies only where the verse permits priests to eat after atonement.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's statement about first-fruits
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's statement about first-fruits
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Rabbi Hoshaya that for first-fruits, placement is essential but recitation is not essential.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states in the name of Rabbi Hoshaya that for first-fruits, placement is essential but recitation is not essential.

items.text: Contradiction from Rabbi Elazar's own statement and resolution via Rabbi Zeira
items.text_en: Contradiction from Rabbi Elazar's own statement and resolution via Rabbi Zeira
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: Rabbi Elazar also said that if first-fruits were set aside before Sukkot and the festival passed, they must rot. This implies recitation is essential. The Gemara resolves this with Rabbi Zeira's principle: anything fit for mixing is not hindered by lack of mixing, but what is not fit for mixing is hindered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Elazar's consistency by citing his own statement that first fruits set aside before Sukkot and left over must rot, implying recitation is essential.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by applying Rabbi Zeira's principle: what is fit for mixing is not hindered by lack of mixing, but what is not fit for mixing is hindered; similarly, recitation is only essential when it is possible.

items.text: Alternative version via Rabbi Asi and contradiction within Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Alternative version via Rabbi Asi and contradiction within Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Yaakov teaches the statement in the name of Rabbi Asi quoting Rabbi Yochanan, and a contradiction arises between two statements of Rabbi Yochanan. The Gemara notes contradictions regarding both recitation and placement.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Yaakov teaches the halakha in the name of Rabbi Asi quoting Rabbi Yochanan, and a contradiction between two statements of Rabbi Yochanan is difficult for him.

The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan indeed holds that placement invalidates first fruits but recitation does not, citing a different statement where Rabbi Yochanan rules that first fruits are permitted to priests from the time of recitation or from seeing the Temple.
The Gemara notes that there is an apparent contradiction between the two statements of Rabbi Yochanan regarding both recitation and placement.

items.text: Resolution of contradictions by attributing views to different Tannaim
items.text_en: Resolution of contradictions by attributing views to different Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradictions: the dispute about recitation is between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis, and the dispute about placement is between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis. It then explains Rabbi Yehuda's view that 'and you shall place it' refers to waving, and the opposing view of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov who derives waving for first-fruits from a verbal analogy with peace-offerings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradictions: the dispute about recitation is between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis, and the dispute about placement is between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehuda's view is, and cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda interprets 'וְהִנַּחְתּוֹ' (and you shall place it) as referring to waving, not actual placement.
The Gemara asks who disagrees with Rabbi Yehuda, and answers that it is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who holds that first fruits require waving.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov derives the requirement of waving for first fruits via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of 'hand' from peace-offerings, resulting in the priest placing his hands under the owner's hands and waving together.

items.text: Rava bar Adda's statement about first-fruits
items.text_en: Rava bar Adda's statement about first-fruits
items.desc_en: Rava bar Adda said in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak something about first-fruits, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar Adda begins a statement in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak about first fruits, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Opening question: When are they liable?
items.text_en: Opening question: When are they liable?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks from when one is liable for bikurim, answering from when they see the face of the Temple. It identifies this with Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that bikurim partially outside and inside have different statuses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from when one is liable for bikurim, and answers: from when they see the face of the Temple.
The Gemara identifies this answer with Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that bikurim partially outside and inside have different statuses.

items.text: Rav Sheishet: Hanachah is essential, keri'ah is not
items.text_en: Rav Sheishet: Hanachah is essential, keri'ah is not
items.desc_en: Rav Sheishet states that for bikurim, the placement (hanachah) is essential, but the recitation (keri'ah) is not. The Gemara seeks to align this with a baraita.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheishet states that for bikurim, the placement (הנחה) is essential, but the recitation (קריאה) is not.

items.text: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei and the hekesh between ma'aser and bechor
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Yosei and the hekesh between ma'aser and bechor
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yishmael argues that ma'aser sheni can only be eaten before the Temple, using a hekesh to bechor. The Gemara notes that if keri'ah were essential for bikurim, one could refute the analogy, but Rav Ashi explains that since keri'ah is not essential, the refutation fails.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita where Rabbi Yosei reports three things in the name of three elders, and Rabbi Yishmael begins a kal vachomer argument about ma'aser sheni.
The Gemara raises an objection to Rabbi Yishmael's kal vachomer: bechor requires blood and fats on the altar, but bikurim require placement, so the analogy is not perfect.

The baraita resolves the objection by citing a hekesh (verbal analogy) from the verse, equating ma'aser to bechor, and the Gemara notes that if keri'ah were essential for bikurim, one could refute the hekesh.

items.text: Rav Ashi: Keri'ah is a mitzvah but not essential
items.text_en: Rav Ashi: Keri'ah is a mitzvah but not essential
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that although keri'ah is not essential, it is still a mitzvah. However, the Gemara asks why one cannot refute the hekesh based on the mitzvah. Rav Ashi answers that because a convert's bikurim cannot include the phrase 'which the Lord swore to our fathers', the mitzvah of keri'ah is not absolute, so the refutation fails.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asserts that although keri'ah is not essential (עיכובא), it is still a mitzvah (מצוה).
The Gemara asks why one cannot refute the hekesh based on the mitzvah of keri'ah.
Rav Ashi answers that because a convert's bikurim cannot include the phrase 'which the Lord swore to our fathers', the mitzvah of keri'ah is not absolute, so the refutation fails.

items.text: Attempt to use a binyan av (common element)
items.text_en: Attempt to use a binyan av (common element)
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests using a 'mah ha-tzad' (common element) argument, but rejects it because each item has a unique aspect related to the altar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes reviving the argument using a 'mah ha-tzad' (common element) inference.
The Gemara rejects the proposal because each item has a unique aspect related to the altar, preventing a valid common element.

items.text: Two possibilities regarding sanctity of the Temple
items.text_en: Two possibilities regarding sanctity of the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers two views: whether the original sanctity of the Temple sanctified for its time and the future, or only for its time. Depending on this, the status of bechor after the Temple's destruction is affected.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Tanna holds regarding the sanctity of the Temple, presenting two possibilities: that the original sanctity sanctified both for its time and the future, or only for its time, and notes that either way the status of bechor would be affected.

items.text: Ravina's resolution: Bechor whose blood was sprinkled before destruction
items.text_en: Ravina's resolution: Bechor whose blood was sprinkled before destruction
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that the case involves a bechor whose blood was sprinkled before the Temple's destruction, and its meat remains. The hekesh compares the meat to the blood, and then ma'aser is learned from bechor. The Gemara questions whether something learned via hekesh can then teach via another hekesh, noting that ma'aser dagan is chullin.
