sub.desc_en: Ravina resolves the contradiction by positing that the case involves a bechor whose blood was sprinkled before the Temple's destruction, and its meat remains; the hekesh compares the meat to the blood, and then ma'aser is learned from bechor.
The Gemara objects that something learned via hekesh cannot then teach via another hekesh, noting that ma'aser dagan is chullin.

items.text: Gemara's question on the dispute about the interpretive principle
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the dispute about the interpretive principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling works for the opinion that we follow the last word (lamed), but asks what can be said for the opinion that we follow the first word (melamed).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: This works out well according to the one who says we follow the derived matter, but what can be said for the one who says we follow the teaching matter?

items.text: Answer: Blood and flesh are one matter
items.text_en: Answer: Blood and flesh are one matter
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that for the other opinion, blood and flesh are considered a single entity, so the prohibition applies to both together.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that blood and flesh are considered one matter, so the derivation is direct.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's redundancy and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's redundancy and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah repeats the case of second tithe and consecrated property that were not redeemed, since it was already taught. Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains that the first clause deals with impure second tithe and an impure person eating it in Jerusalem, while the latter clause deals with pure second tithe and a pure person eating it outside the wall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah repeats the case of second tithe and consecrated property that were not redeemed, since it was already taught.

Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains that the first clause deals with impure second tithe and an impure person eating it in Jerusalem, while the latter clause deals with pure second tithe and a pure person eating it outside the wall.

items.text: Source for liability for impurity and the unknown warning for eating
items.text_en: Source for liability for impurity and the unknown warning for eating
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon derives liability for impurity from the verse 'I have not removed it while impure', but notes that the source for the warning against eating is unknown.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that one is liable for lashes due to impurity?
Rabbi Shimon cites the verse 'I have not removed it while impure' to derive liability for impurity in both cases: person impure and produce pure, or person pure and produce impure.
Rabbi Shimon notes that the source for the warning against eating is unknown.

items.text: Derivation of the warning for impurity of the body and impurity of the item itself
items.text_en: Derivation of the warning for impurity of the body and impurity of the item itself
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that impurity of the body is explicit in the Torah, but impurity of the item itself is derived from the verse 'You may not eat in your gates', compared with another verse that permits impure and pure to eat together, implying that here it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: The impurity of the body is explicitly written, but from where is the impurity of the item itself derived?
The Gemara answers: It is derived from the verse 'You may not eat in your gates' and the later verse 'Within your gates you may eat it, the impure and the pure alike'.
A baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that impure and pure may eat together in one dish, and the Merciful One says: That impure flesh is permitted there, but here you may not eat.

items.text: Source that redemption applies even in Jerusalem and the dual derivation
items.text_en: Source that redemption applies even in Jerusalem and the dual derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar derives from 'you cannot bear it' that impure second tithe may be redeemed even in Jerusalem. Rav Bibi bar Rav Asi adds that pure second tithe may be redeemed even a step outside the wall)Skip. The Gemara resolves the apparent redundancy by showing the verse teaches both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where do we derive that impure second-tithe produce is subject to redemption?

Rabbi Elazar derives from the verse 'כִּי לֹא תוּכַל שְׂאֵתוֹ' (because you are unable to carry it) that impure second-tithe produce may be redeemed even in Jerusalem, interpreting 'שְׂאֵת' as eating.
Rav Bibi bar Rav Asi adds that pure second-tithe produce may be redeemed even one step outside the wall, but the Gemara objects that this verse is needed for Rabbi Elazar's derivation.
The Gemara resolves that the unusual term 'שְׂאֵתוֹ' teaches both laws: redemption of impure produce in Jerusalem and redemption of pure produce just outside the wall.

items.text: Inquiry about the gate of Jerusalem and the elder's answer
items.text_en: Inquiry about the gate of Jerusalem and the elder's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Chanina and Rav Hoshaya inquire about the status of one who is outside the gate while his load is inside, or vice versa. An elder from the school of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai answers with a verse implying that the prohibition applies only when the item is with you.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanina and Rav Hoshaya inquire about the status of second-tithe produce at the entrance of Jerusalem, specifically when the person is inside and the load is outside.
The Gemara clarifies that the case where the person is outside and the load is inside is obvious: the walls have admitted it. The dilemma is when the person is inside and the load is outside.

sub.text: Elder from the school of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai
sub.text_en: Elder from the school of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai
sub.desc_en: An elder from the school of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai answers by interpreting the verse 'כי ירחק ממך המקום' (for the place is too far from you) as 'from your fullness' (ממילואך), implying that if any part of the person or his burden is inside, it is considered as if he is entirely inside, so redemption is not allowed.

items.text: Rav Pappa's inquiry about carrying with a reed
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's inquiry about carrying with a reed
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks what the law is if one carries the tithe with a reed, and the Gemara concludes with 'teiku' (let it stand).

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks what the law is if one carries the tithe with a reed, and the Gemara concludes with 'teiku' (let it stand).

items.text: Rabbi Asi quoting Rabbi Yochanan on when liability begins
items.text_en: Rabbi Asi quoting Rabbi Yochanan on when liability begins
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that liability for second tithe begins from the moment it sees the face of the wall (of Jerusalem), based on the juxtaposition of verses.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan states that liability for second tithe begins from the moment it sees the face of the wall of Jerusalem.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind this ruling.

Rabbi Yochanan explains the reason: the verse 'לִפְנֵי ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ תֹאכְלֶנּוּ' (before the Lord your God you shall eat it) and the prohibition 'לֹא תוּכַל לֶאֱכֹל בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ' (you may not eat within your gates) are linked; wherever the positive command applies, the prohibition applies, and vice versa.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about Rabbi Yosei's case
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about Rabbi Yosei's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Yosei discusses a priest who designates tithes on a fig while in Jerusalem or the border, implying that the prohibition applies even before seeing the wall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Yosei discusses a priest who designates tithes on a fig while in Jerusalem or the border, implying that the prohibition applies even before seeing the wall.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Lashes for eating second tithe outside Jerusalem
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Lashes for eating second tithe outside Jerusalem
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a non-priest who eats second tithe outside Jerusalem receives two lashes, whereas if he had eaten it initially outside Jerusalem he would receive only one. The Gemara will question this distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a non-priest who eats second tithe outside Jerusalem receives two lashes, whereas if he had eaten it initially outside Jerusalem he would receive only one.
The Mishnah elaborates that a non-priest who eats the fig is flogged with two sets of lashes, but if he ate it initially before separating teruma and tithes, he is flogged with only one.

items.text: Gemara's initial inference and challenge
items.text_en: Gemara's initial inference and challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that the Mishnah's case is specifically when the tithe was brought into Jerusalem, implying that if it were outside the walls, the eater would be liable for three lashes. It then challenges this inference by asking what novelty the Mishnah teaches.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that the case is specifically when the tithe was brought into Jerusalem, implying that if it were outside the walls, the eater would be liable for three lashes, and then challenges this inference by noting that the baraita itself says the fig entered and exited Jerusalem.

items.text: First answer: The case of untithed produce
items.text_en: First answer: The case of untithed produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah deals with produce that was brought into Jerusalem while still untithed, and Rabbi Yosei holds that untithed produce is considered as if it were tithed, so the walls of Jerusalem do not 'absorb' it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the case involves untithed produce brought into Jerusalem, and Rabbi Yosei holds that untithed produce is considered as if it were tithed, so the walls do not absorb it.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda quotes Rabbi Yosei stating that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree on untithed produce that passed through Jerusalem, implying that the walls do not 'absorb' such produce. This contradicts the assumption that Rabbi Yosei considers untithed produce as tithed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda quotes Rabbi Yosei stating that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree on untithed produce that passed through Jerusalem, implying that the walls do not 'absorb' such produce.

The Gemara continues the objection, noting that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree only on produce whose labor was completed, and if untithed produce were considered tithed, the walls would have absorbed it, contradicting Beit Hillel's leniency.

items.text: Rabbah's resolution: Distinction between biblical and rabbinic absorption
items.text_en: Rabbah's resolution: Distinction between biblical and rabbinic absorption
items.desc_en: Rabbah resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the biblical requirement to eat the tithe within the walls and the rabbinic concept of the walls 'absorbing' the produce. The rabbinic decree applies only when the produce is fully tithed, not when it is untithed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the biblical requirement to eat the tithe within the walls and the rabbinic concept of the walls 'absorbing' the produce; the rabbinic decree applies only when the produce is fully tithed, not when it is untithed.

items.text: Ravina's alternative answer and connection to Rav Pappa's dilemma
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative answer and connection to Rav Pappa's dilemma
items.desc_en: Ravina offers a different answer: the case is where the person holds the tithe in a container (קניא), so it is not considered as having entered the walls. This also resolves a dilemma of Rav Pappa.

sub.desc_en: Ravina offers a different answer: the case is where the person holds the tithe in a container (קניא), so it is not considered as having entered the walls. This also resolves a dilemma of Rav Pappa.

items.text: New Mishnah: Prohibitions of baldness, rounding the head, and marring the beard
items.text_en: New Mishnah: Prohibitions of baldness, rounding the head, and marring the beard
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the prohibitions of making a bald spot, rounding the corners of the head, and marring the beard, stating that one is liable for each act. It also discusses the number of lashes for multiple acts and the opinions of Rabbi Eliezer regarding the use of scissors or tweezers.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists prohibitions: making a bald spot, rounding the head, marring the beard, and cutting incisions for the dead, stating liability for each act.
The Mishnah specifies the number of lashes for rounding the head and marring the beard, and records Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that if all edges are removed at once, only one set of lashes is given.
The Mishnah states that liability for marring the beard requires a razor, but Rabbi Eliezer holds that even tweezers or a plane render one liable.

items.text: Gemara's exposition on the verses for baldness
items.text_en: Gemara's exposition on the verses for baldness
items.desc_en: The Gemara expounds the verse 'You shall not make a bald spot' to derive that one is liable for each bald spot, and that the prohibition applies to the entire head, not just between the eyes. It then extends these laws to Israelites via a gezerah shavah, and questions the scenario of multiple bald spots.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by expounding the verse 'לֹא יִקְרְחוּ' (they shall not make a bald spot), deriving from the singular 'קׇרְחָה' that one is liable for each bald spot.
The Gemara asks why the verse adds 'בְּרֹאשָׁם' (upon their heads), and answers that it includes the entire head, not just between the eyes.
The Gemara asks how we know that Israelites are also liable for creating a bald spot, since the verse is addressed to priests.

The Gemara answers via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between the verse here (Deuteronomy 14:1) and the verse there (Leviticus 21:5), extending the laws to Israelites and limiting the prohibition to mourning for the dead.
The Gemara questions the scenario of multiple bald spots, suggesting that if they were done sequentially with separate forewarnings, liability is obvious.

items.text: Gemara's question about multiple warnings for one act
items.text_en: Gemara's question about multiple warnings for one act
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one is liable for multiple korchot if done with a single warning, citing a baraita about a nazir who drinks wine all day and is liable for each warning. It resolves that the case is where he dipped five fingers and placed them simultaneously, making each a separate warning.

items.text: Dispute over the shiur of korchah
items.text_en: Dispute over the shiur of korchah
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan dispute the minimum size of a korchah: Rav Huna says it must be visible from the head, while Rabbi Yochanan says it is the size of a gris. A baraita records a similar dispute between the Sages and Acheirim. Rav Yehuda bar Chaviva adds a third opinion of two hairs, and some replace that with a lentil.

items.text: The measure of melo pi hazug and its application to korchah
items.text_en: The measure of melo pi hazug and its application to korchah
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who takes a full cheekful on Shabbat is liable, and Rav Yehuda says the measure is two. The Gemara notes a contradiction with another baraita that says the measure for korchah is two, and resolves by saying 'and likewise for korchah it is two'. Another baraita confirms this, with Rabbi Eliezer saying one, and the Sages agreeing that picking white hairs from black is liable even for one, and is forbidden even on a weekday due to cross-dressing.

items.text: Definition of pe'at rosho
items.text_en: Definition of pe'at rosho
items.desc_en: The Rabbis taught that 'pe'at rosho' means the end of the head, which is the area that aligns the temples with the back of the ear and the forehead.

items.text: Liability of the one being rounded and the one rounding
items.text_en: Liability of the one being rounded and the one rounding
items.desc_en: A tanna taught before Rav Chisda that both the one who rounds and the one who is rounded are liable. Rav Chisda objects, comparing it to eating dates in a sieve. Rava explains it refers to one who rounds himself, and Rav Ashi says it refers to one who assists.

items.text: Definition of pe'at zekano
items.text_en: Definition of pe'at zekano
items.desc_en: The Rabbis taught that 'pe'at zekano' means the end of the beard, which is the shibbolet zakan (the tip of the beard).

items.text: Liability for incisions for the dead
items.text_en: Liability for incisions for the dead
items.desc_en: The Rabbis taught that the verse 'veseret' excludes incisions made for a collapsed house or sunken ship, limiting liability to incisions for the dead. Multiple incisions for one dead person each incur liability, and Rabbi Yosei adds that one incision for multiple dead persons also incurs liability for each soul. The Gemara notes that this derivation already excluded the cases of house and ship.

items.text: Opening statement: Rabbi Yosei's view on scratching and cutting
items.text_en: Opening statement: Rabbi Yosei's view on scratching and cutting
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei holds that scratching and cutting are the same act, and the verse for cutting mentions 'for the dead'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Yosei considers scratching and cutting to be the same act, and the verse for cutting mentions 'for the dead'.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling and challenge
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling and challenge
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that one who scratches with a utensil is liable. A baraita is cited that distinguishes scratching (by hand) from cutting (by utensil), but Shmuel follows Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that one who scratches with a utensil is liable, and the Gemara notes that Shmuel follows Rabbi Yosei's view.
The Gemara challenges Shmuel by citing a baraita that distinguishes scratching (by hand) from cutting (by utensil).
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel follows Rabbi Yosei, who equates scratching and cutting.

items.text: Tanna's teaching before Rabbi Yochanan and correction
items.text_en: Tanna's teaching before Rabbi Yochanan and correction
items.desc_en: A Tanna taught before Rabbi Yochanan that for a dead person, both hand and utensil are liable; for idolatry, hand is liable and utensil is exempt. The Gemara objects from the verse about cutting with swords and spears, and corrects: for idolatry, hand is exempt and utensil is liable.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna recites a baraita before Rabbi Yochanan: for a dead person, both hand and utensil are liable; for idolatry, hand is liable, utensil is exempt, but the Gemara objects from a verse and reverses the ruling.
The Gemara objects that the verse about cutting with swords and spears (חרבות ורמחים) implies the opposite ruling.
The Gemara corrects the teaching: for idolatry, the hand is exempt and the utensil is liable.

items.text: Liability for head and beard shaving
items.text_en: Liability for head and beard shaving
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states one is liable for the head and beard. Rav Sheishes demonstrates between the parts of the head and between the parts of the beard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that one is liable for the head, and Rav Sheishet demonstrates the boundaries between the hair sections; similarly for the beard, with two on each side and one below.
Rav Sheishes demonstrates the boundaries between the parts of the head and between the parts of the beard.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion on multiple hairs
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion on multiple hairs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer says if one removed them all at once, he is liable only once, because he holds it is a single prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer holds that if one removed the hair, he is liable, and the Gemara explains that he considers the two prohibitions as one negative commandment.

items.text: Derivation that shaving must be with a razor
items.text_en: Derivation that shaving must be with a razor
items.desc_en: The Sages derive from verses that the prohibition applies only to shaving that involves destruction, i.e., with a razor. Rabbi Eliezer argues even tweezers or a plane are liable, but the Gemara questions his consistency and resolves that he holds these also constitute shaving.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on tattooing
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on tattooing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states one is liable only if he writes and tattoos. Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says one must write the name of God. The Gemara clarifies that it means writing the name of an idol, as derived from the verse.

sub.desc_en: Mishnah: The one who writes a tattoo. If he wrote but did not tattoo, or tattooed but did not write – not liable, until he writes and tattoos with ink or anything that marks. Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon says: not liable until he writes the Name there, as the verse says 'You shall not give a tattoo, I am Hashem'.

items.text: Discussion on appearance of tattooing and names of rabbis
items.text_en: Discussion on appearance of tattooing and names of rabbis
items.desc_en: Rav Malkiya says it is forbidden to put ash on a wound because it looks like a tattoo. Rav Nachman bar Rav Ika distinguishes between names of rabbis. Rav Pappa explains the pattern. Rav Bibi bar Abaye is strict even for a fish scale, and Rav Ashi says a wound proves the intent.

sub.text: Rav Malkiya citing Rav Adda bar Ahava
sub.text_en: Rav Malkiya citing Rav Adda bar Ahava
sub.desc_en: Rav Malkiya in the name of Rav Adda bar Ahava rules that one may not put ash from a kiln on a wound because it resembles a tattoo.
Rav Nachman bar Rav Ika distinguishes between two rabbis named Rav Malkiyo and Rav Malkiya based on the topics they discuss.

Rav Pappa explains the pattern: Rav Malkiya is associated with Mishnah and baraita, while Rav Malkiyo is associated with amoraic statements, and the practical difference between them is the topic of 'shifchot' (handmaidens).
Rav Bibi bar Abaye was strict even about a fish scale on a wound, showing the severity of the tattoo-like appearance.
Rav Ashi rules that wherever there is a wound, the wound itself proves the intent is medical, not decorative, so the prohibition does not apply.

items.text: Mishnah: Multiple warnings for a single action
items.text_en: Mishnah: Multiple warnings for a single action
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that for a nazirite drinking wine, becoming impure, shaving, or wearing kilayim, if done continuously without warning, only one liability; but if warned between each act, liable for each.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: a nazirite who performs a prohibited act continuously without warning is liable only once, but if warned between each act, he is liable for each.
The Mishnah applies the same rule to a nazirite who becomes impure from corpses, with warnings between each act.
The Mishnah applies the same rule to a nazirite who shaves, with warnings between each act.
The Mishnah applies the same rule to one who wears kilayim (forbidden mixtures), with warnings between each act of putting on and removing.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Eight lashes for one furrow
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Eight lashes for one furrow
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists eight prohibitions violated by plowing a single furrow: plowing with an ox and donkey, with consecrated animals, with diverse seeds in a vineyard, during the Sabbatical year, on Yom Tov, and a priest or nazirite in a cemetery. Hananya ben Hakhinai adds wearing diverse kinds, but the Sages reject this, and he retorts that the nazirite case is also not analogous.

items.text: Gemara: Definition of wearing diverse kinds
items.text_en: Gemara: Definition of wearing diverse kinds
items.desc_en: Rav Bibi quoting Rabbi Yosei questions whether the prohibition of wearing diverse kinds applies only to actual wearing or even to inserting and removing a sleeve. Rav Acha bar Rav Ika demonstrates inserting and removing, and Rav Ashi rules that even without pausing the time to put on and take off, one is liable.

items.text: Gemara: Covering with diverse seeds
items.text_en: Gemara: Covering with diverse seeds
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai reports that the sages concluded in a group that one who covers with diverse seeds is lashed. Rabbi Yochanan objects that this is already in the Mishnah: the plowing case must involve covering the seeds as he goes.

items.text: Gemara: Praise and attribution to Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Gemara: Praise and attribution to Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan praises Rabbi Yannai for revealing a pearl under a shard. Resh Lakish says that had Rabbi Yochanan not praised him, he would have said the Mishnah follows Rabbi Akiva, who holds that maintaining diverse seeds is lashed.

items.text: Gemara: Source for Rabbi Akiva's view
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for Rabbi Akiva's view
items.desc_en: A baraita states that weeding and covering with diverse seeds incur lashes, and Rabbi Akiva adds that maintaining them also incurs lashes. The source is a verse linking the prohibition of diverse seeds to that of diverse animals, implying that maintaining is like sowing.

items.text: Gemara: Question about plowing on Yom Tov and the principle of distinct prohibitions
items.text_en: Gemara: Question about plowing on Yom Tov and the principle of distinct prohibitions
items.desc_en: Ulla asks Rav Nachman why the Mishnah does not also count a prohibition for sowing on Yom Tov. Rav Nachman answers that the Tanna omitted it. Ulla objects that the Tanna listed eight, so how could he omit? Rava explains that there is a distinction: on Shabbat different labors are distinct, but on Yom Tov they are not. Ulla accepts this.

items.text: Gemara: Abaye's objection from cooking on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Gemara: Abaye's objection from cooking on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rava's principle by citing a Mishnah: one who cooks a sciatic nerve in milk on Yom Tov and eats it incurs five lashes, showing that different prohibitions are distinct even on Yom Tov. The segment ends mid-list of the five lashes.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about burning and cooking
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about burning and cooking
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that one who burns a limb from a living animal should be liable for the prohibition of burning, but notes that he is already liable for cooking. It then proposes replacing the burning prohibition with the prohibition of eating the sciatic nerve of a neveilah. However, a baraita of Rabbi Chiyya states that one who eats such a limb receives two lashes and three for cooking, implying three for eating, so the Gemara instead replaces burning with the prohibition of using wood from an asherah, citing the verse 'וְלֹא יִדְבַּק בְּיָדְךָ'.

items.text: Rav Acha's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Acha's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava objects to Rav Ashi that one should also be liable for the prohibition 'לֹא תָבִיא תוֹעֵבָה אֶל בֵּיתֶךָ'. The Gemara resolves that the case involves cooking with wood from hekdesh, and the warning comes from the verse 'וַאֲשֵׁרֵיהֶם תִּשְׂרְפוּן... לֹא תַעֲשׂוּן כֵּן לַה׳'.

items.text: Siman
items.text_en: Siman
items.desc_en: A mnemonic sign 'שנבא״י שנ״ז' is given for the following series of challenges.

items.text: Series of challenges: additional prohibitions to count
items.text_en: Series of challenges: additional prohibitions to count
items.desc_en: A series of Amoraim challenge the Mishnah's list, each proposing another action that should be counted for lashes: Rav Hoshaya suggests sowing in a nachal eitan, Rav Chananya suggests erasing God's name, Rabbi Avahu suggests cutting off a baheret, Abaye suggests removing the choshen or the poles of the Ark, Rav Ashi suggests plowing with asherah wood, and Ravina suggests cutting down good fruit trees. Each cites a relevant verse as the warning.

items.text: Discussion of a vow not to plow on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Discussion of a vow not to plow on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Mani why a case of one who says 'Shevuah that I will not plow on Yom Tov' is not counted. Rabbi Mani explains that such a vow does not take effect because one is already bound by the Torah prohibition. Rabbi Zeira then suggests a case where the vow includes both weekdays and Yom Tov, but the Gemara concludes that since the prohibition can be annulled by a sage, it is not listed. The Gemara then questions this principle with examples of hekdesh and nazir, resolving that the Tanna does not hold of issur kolel.

items.text: Statements of Rabbi Hoshaya and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.text_en: Statements of Rabbi Hoshaya and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.desc_en: Rabbi Hoshaya states that one who causes an animal with blemished consecrated status to mate receives two lashes. Rabbi Yitzchak states that one who leads such an animal receives lashes, because the Torah treats one body as two separate bodies for the prohibitions.

items.text: Mishnah: How many lashes and the dispute
items.text_en: Mishnah: How many lashes and the dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one receives forty minus one lashes, as the verse says 'בְּמִסְפַּר אַרְבָּעִים' meaning a number close to forty. Rabbi Yehuda says he receives a full forty, and the extra lash is given between his shoulders. The Mishnah also discusses that the assessment is based on lashes that can be divided into thirds, and if assessed for forty but only receives part, he is exempt from the remainder.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Assessment of capacity for lashes
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Assessment of capacity for lashes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the court initially assessed that the person cannot receive forty lashes, he is exempt. If they assessed he could receive eighteen, but after being lashed they realize he could receive forty, he is exempt.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rava's comment
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rava's comment
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah says 'in number forty' rather than 'forty in number', and Rava criticizes those who stand for a Torah scroll but not for a great sage, noting that the Torah wrote 'forty' and the rabbis reduced it by one.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion and its scriptural basis
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion and its scriptural basis
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says the lashes are a full forty. Rabbi Yitzchak explains his reasoning from a verse about wounds, and the Rabbis interpret that verse differently, referring to schoolchildren.

items.text: Mishnah: Assessment only before lashes
items.text_en: Mishnah: Assessment only before lashes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that assessment is only done for lashes that are actually administered, implying that if he was not lashed, no assessment is needed.

items.text: Contradiction and resolution by Rav Sheishet
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution by Rav Sheishet
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised from a baraita that seems to allow assessment after lashes. Rav Sheishet resolves it by distinguishing between assessment for days (total capacity) and assessment for the next day.

items.text: Mishnah: Two prohibitions and one assessment
items.text_en: Mishnah: Two prohibitions and one assessment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a case where one violated two prohibitions; if assessed with one assessment, he is lashed and exempt; otherwise, he is lashed, heals, and is lashed again.

items.text: Contradiction and resolution by Rav Sheishet
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution by Rav Sheishet
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one assessment is not made for two prohibitions. Rav Sheishet resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between an assessment for forty-one lashes and for forty-two.

items.text: Mishnah: Procedure for lashes
items.text_en: Mishnah: Procedure for lashes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure: the person's hands are tied to a pillar, the synagogue attendant tears his clothes, a stone is behind him, and the strap is made of calf leather, folded, with two donkey straps. He is struck a third in front and two-thirds behind, while reclining. Verses are recited, and if he dies, the striker is exempt; if he adds a strap and the person dies, he is exiled. If the person becomes incontinent, he is exempt.

items.text: Gemara's question on the number of lashes
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the number of lashes
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies forty lashes less one, and answers that it is derived from the word 'ונקלה' (and he be degraded).

items.text: Four homilies of Rav Sheishet citing Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah
items.text_en: Four homilies of Rav Sheishet citing Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah
items.desc_en: Rav Sheishet delivers four homilies based on the proximity of verses: the strap must be from a calf, a yevamah who falls to a man with boils is not restrained, one who despises festivals is like an idolater, and one who speaks or accepts lashon hara or bears false witness deserves to be thrown to dogs.

items.text: Two straps: one of calf, one of donkey
items.text_en: Two straps: one of calf, one of donkey
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that the second strap is of donkey hide, as expounded by a Galilean before Rav Chisda: the ox knows its owner but the donkey knows its master's crib, so God punishes Israel who do not know.

items.text: Width of the hand and number of lashes
items.text_en: Width of the hand and number of lashes
items.desc_en: Abaye infers that the strap's width is a handbreadth, and each person is lashed according to his build. Rava objects that this would require too many straps, and explains that the strap has a knot that can be tightened or loosened.

items.text: Source for lashes given while standing and leaning
items.text_en: Source for lashes given while standing and leaning
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana derives from the verse 'והפילו השופט והכהו' that one lash is given while the convict is before the judge, and two after he is behind him.

items.text: Source that the strap is doubled
items.text_en: Source that the strap is doubled
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda citing Rabbi Yochanan derives from 'והפילו' that the strap is doubled. The Gemara questions this, and answers that the word implies both the act of falling and the doubling.

items.text: Qualifications of the flogger
items.text_en: Qualifications of the flogger
items.desc_en: A baraisa states that the flogger must be weak in strength but wise. Rabbi Yehuda says even weak in wisdom and strong in strength. Rava supports Rabbi Yehuda from the verse 'לא יוסיף... פן יוסיף', and the Rabbis respond that only one who needs warning is warned.

items.text: How the flogger raises and strikes
items.text_en: How the flogger raises and strikes
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that the flogger raises the strap with both hands but strikes with one hand, so that the blow comes from his own strength.

items.text: The reader and the number of lashes
items.text_en: The reader and the number of lashes
items.desc_en: A baraisa describes the roles: the senior judge reads, the second counts, the third says 'hit him'. If the lashes are many, he lengthens the reading; if few, he shortens. The Mishnah says he returns to the beginning if he does not finish. Another baraisa derives that even a few lashes are called 'מכה רבה' from the verse 'לא יוסיף'.

items.text: Covering the convict during flogging
items.text_en: Covering the convict during flogging
items.desc_en: A baraisa debates whether the convict is covered with a cloth or water: Rabbi Meir says both man and woman with a cloth; Rabbi Yehuda says man with cloth, woman with water; the Sages say either. A contradiction is resolved by Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak that both are equal with a cloth.

items.text: If the convict fled or the strap broke
items.text_en: If the convict fled or the strap broke
items.desc_en: Shmuel says if he was tied and fled from court, he is exempt. A challenge is raised from a baraisa about the strap breaking: if it broke on the second lash he is exempt, but on the first he is not. The Gemara distinguishes: there he did not run, here he ran.

items.text: If he became weak before or after lashes
items.text_en: If he became weak before or after lashes
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches: if they estimated he would become weak and he did, he is exempt; if he became weak after leaving court, he is lashed; even if he became weak at the start, he is lashed, as the verse says 'והכהו... ונקלה' and not that he was already weak in court.

items.text: Lashes exempt from karet and the reward for mitzvot
items.text_en: Lashes exempt from karet and the reward for mitzvot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all liable for karet who are lashed are exempt from karet, as per Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel. He adds a kal vachomer: if one who commits a sin loses his soul, one who does a mitzvah will have his soul given to him. Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse 'ונכרתו הנפשות העושות'.

items.text: Opening exposition on reward for refraining from sin
items.text_en: Opening exposition on reward for refraining from sin
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse about living by the commandments, interpreting that one who sits and does not sin receives reward like one who performs a mitzvah. Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi and Rabbi Chananya ben Akashya offer additional homilies on the great reward for avoiding sin and God's desire to merit Israel through many commandments.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'which a person shall do and live by them' and interprets that one who sits and does not sin receives reward like one who performs a mitzvah.

Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi argues from the verse about refraining from blood that if one receives reward for avoiding what is repulsive, how much more so for avoiding theft and forbidden relations which the soul desires.

Rabbi Chananya ben Akashya teaches that God wanted to merit Israel, so He multiplied Torah and commandments, citing the verse 'the Lord desired for His righteousness to magnify Torah and make it glorious.'

items.text: Dispute about lashes for karet liabilities
items.text_en: Dispute about lashes for karet liabilities
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel's colleagues disagree with him. Rav Adda bar Ahavah cites a baraita that the only difference between Shabbat and Yom Kippur is that the intentional violation of Shabbat is punishable by human court (stoning) while Yom Kippur is by karet, implying that karet is not punishable by human court. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak and Rav Ashi offer alternative explanations to reconcile the baraita with Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel's view.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel's colleagues disagree with him.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahavah citing the school of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah citing the school of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah cites a baraita that the only difference between Shabbat and Yom Kippur is that intentional violation of Shabbat is punishable by human court (stoning) while Yom Kippur is by karet (divine excision).
The Gemara objects: if Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel is correct that karet liabilities are also punishable by lashes, then both Shabbat and Yom Kippur should be punishable by human court.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that the baraita follows Rabbi Yitzchak, who holds that karet liabilities are not subject to lashes, citing the verse about a sister as a source.

Rav Ashi offers an alternative answer: even according to the rabbis (who hold that karet liabilities are subject to lashes), the baraita means that the primary punishment for Shabbat is by human court, while for Yom Kippur it is by divine hands.

items.text: Halakhic ruling and challenge
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling and challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah reports in Rav's name that the halakha follows Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel. Rav Yosef challenges this, asking how one can know what happens in heaven. Abaye responds by citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's teaching about three things the earthly court did that the heavenly court agreed to, arguing that we derive such matters from verses.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahavah in Rav's name
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah in Rav's name
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahavah reports in Rav's name that the halakha follows Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel.
Rav Yosef challenges how one can know what happens in heaven to determine the halakha.
Abaye responds by citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's teaching about three things the earthly court did that the heavenly court agreed to, arguing that we derive such matters from verses.

items.text: Three things agreed upon by heavenly court
items.text_en: Three things agreed upon by heavenly court
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi lists three enactments of the earthly court that received heavenly approval: reading the Megillah (Purim), greeting with God's name, and bringing tithes. The Gemara provides scriptural support for each: for Megillah, the verse 'kiyemu vekiblu'; for greeting, Boaz's greeting and the angel's greeting to Gideon; for tithes, Malachi's challenge to test God.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi lists three enactments of the earthly court that received heavenly approval: reading the Megillah, greeting with God's name, and bringing tithes.
The Gemara provides scriptural support for the Megillah reading from the verse 'קִיְּמוּ וְקִבְּלוּ' (they fulfilled and accepted), indicating heavenly confirmation of the earthly acceptance.
The Gemara provides scriptural support for greeting with God's name from Boaz's greeting and the angel's greeting to Gideon, addressing a potential objection that Boaz acted on his own.

The Gemara provides scriptural support for bringing tithes from Malachi's challenge to test God, and Rami bar Rav explains the phrase 'עַד בְּלִי דָי' (until there is no room) as meaning until your lips are exhausted from saying 'enough'.

items.text: Divine spirit in three courts and Rava's critique
items.text_en: Divine spirit in three courts and Rava's critique
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that the Holy Spirit appeared in three courts: Shem's, Samuel's, and Solomon's. For each, a bat kol confirmed the court's decision. Rava challenges each proof: regarding Judah, perhaps he calculated the months; regarding Samuel, perhaps the singular language refers to all Israel; regarding Solomon, the mother's compassion is obvious. He concludes these are traditions.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar teaches that the Holy Spirit appeared in three courts: Shem's, Samuel's, and Solomon's, and for each a bat kol confirmed the court's decision.

sub.text: Rava's objection to the Shem proof
sub.text_en: Rava's objection to the Shem proof
sub.desc_en: Rava challenges the proof from Shem's court: perhaps Judah simply calculated the months and knew the child was his.

sub.text: Rava's objection to the Samuel proof
sub.text_en: Rava's objection to the Samuel proof
sub.desc_en: Rava challenges the proof from Samuel's court: the singular language may refer to all Israel, not a bat kol.

sub.text: Rava's objection to the Solomon proof
sub.text_en: Rava's objection to the Solomon proof
sub.desc_en: Rava challenges the proof from Solomon's court: the mother's compassion was obvious, so no bat kol was needed.

items.text: Number of commandments and gematria
items.text_en: Number of commandments and gematria
items.desc_en: Rabbi Simlai teaches that 613 commandments were given to Moses: 365 negative commandments corresponding to the solar year, and 248 positive commandments corresponding to the limbs of a person. Rav Hamnuna notes that the gematria of 'Torah' is 611, implying that the first two commandments were heard directly from God.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Simlai teaches that 613 commandments were given to Moses: 365 negative commandments corresponding to the solar year, and 248 positive commandments corresponding to the limbs of a person.
Rav Hamnuna notes that the gematria of 'תּוֹרָה' (Torah) is 611, implying that the first two commandments were heard directly from God.

items.text: David reduces the 613 commandments to eleven
items.text_en: David reduces the 613 commandments to eleven
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the 613 commandments were heard from God at Sinai, but David reduced them to eleven principles in Psalm 15. Each phrase is interpreted as a specific virtue exemplified by a biblical figure or rabbi. The section concludes with Rabban Gamliel's concern that one must fulfill all eleven, but the Gemara argues that even one suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the 613 commandments were heard from God at Sinai, with the first two commandments heard directly from the Almighty.
The Gemara provides a mnemonic for the list of eleven principles.
David reduced the 613 commandments to eleven principles, as written in Psalm 15.
The phrase 'הוֹלֵךְ תָּמִים' (walks blamelessly) refers to Abraham, as it is written 'walk before Me and be blameless'.
The phrase 'פּוֹעֵל צֶדֶק' (works righteousness) refers to Abba Hilkiah.
The phrase 'וְדוֹבֵר אֱמֶת בִּלְבָבוֹ' (speaks truth in his heart) refers to Rav Safra.
The phrase 'לֹא רָגַל עַל לְשֹׁנוֹ' (does not slander with his tongue) refers to Jacob our father, who feared being found as a deceiver.
The phrase 'לֹא עָשָׂה לְרֵעֵהוּ רָעָה' (does no evil to his neighbor) means one does not encroach on his fellow's livelihood.

sub.text: Interpretation of 'וְחֶרְפָּה לֹא נָשָׂא עַל קְרֹבוֹ'
sub.text_en: Interpretation of 'וְחֶרְפָּה לֹא נָשָׂא עַל קְרֹבוֹ'
sub.desc_en: The phrase 'וְחֶרְפָּה לֹא נָשָׂא עַל קְרֹבוֹ' (bears no reproach against his close relative) refers to one who draws his relatives close.
The phrase 'נִבְזֶה בְּעֵינָיו נִמְאָס' (despised in his eyes is the rejected) refers to King Hezekiah, who dragged his father's bones on a rope bed.
The phrase 'וְאֶת יִרְאֵי ה׳ יְכַבֵּד' (honors those who fear the Lord) refers to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, who would rise from his throne and embrace a Torah scholar.
The phrase 'נִשְׁבַּע לְהָרַע וְלֹא יָמִר' (swears to his own hurt and does not change) refers to Rabbi Yochanan, who vowed to fast until he reached home.
The phrase 'כַּסְפּוֹ לֹא נָתַן בְּנֶשֶׁךְ' (does not put out his money at interest) applies even to interest from a gentile.

sub.text: Interpretation of 'וְשֹׁחַד עַל נָקִי לֹא לָקָח'
sub.text_en: Interpretation of 'וְשֹׁחַד עַל נָקִי לֹא לָקָח'
sub.desc_en: The phrase 'וְשֹׁחַד עַל נָקִי לֹא לָקָח' (takes no bribe against the innocent) refers to Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei.
Rabban Gamliel wept upon reaching this verse, arguing that only one who fulfills all eleven principles will not be moved, but one who fulfills only one will be moved.
The Sages answered that the verse says 'עֹשֵׂה אֵלֶּה' (does these things), not 'all these', meaning even one of them suffices, as proven by a parallel verse about impurity.

items.text: Isaiah reduces the principles to six
items.text_en: Isaiah reduces the principles to six
items.desc_en: Isaiah further reduces the principles to six, as found in Isaiah 33:15-16. Each of the six qualities is again exemplified by a biblical figure or rabbi, including Abraham, Rabbi Yishmael, and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces that Isaiah reduced the principles to six, citing Isaiah 33:15-16.
The gemara identifies 'walking righteously' as Abraham, citing the verse about commanding his household.
The gemara explains 'speaking uprightly' as one who does not embarrass another in public.
The gemara exemplifies 'despising dishonest gain' with Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha.
The gemara exemplifies 'shaking hands from bribes' with Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei.
The gemara explains 'stopping ears from hearing bloodshed' as not hearing a rabbi's humiliation, exemplified by Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.
The gemara exemplifies 'closing eyes from seeing evil' with Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, who avoids looking at women doing laundry.
The gemara concludes with the verse that such a person will dwell on high.

items.text: Micah reduces the principles to three
items.text_en: Micah reduces the principles to three
items.desc_en: Micah reduces the principles to three: justice, loving-kindness, and walking humbly with God. The Gemara explains that walking humbly includes even public acts like funerals and weddings, and argues a fortiori that private acts should be done discreetly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Micah reduced the principles to three: justice, loving-kindness, and walking humbly with God.
The Gemara explains each of the three principles: justice is law, loving-kindness is acts of kindness, and walking humbly includes attending to funerals and weddings.
The Gemara argues a fortiori: if the Torah requires discretion for public acts like funerals and weddings, then private acts certainly require discretion.

items.text: Isaiah and Amos reduce further, Habakkuk to one
items.text_en: Isaiah and Amos reduce further, Habakkuk to one
items.desc_en: Isaiah reduces to two (justice and righteousness), Amos to one (seek Me and live), but Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that this refers to the entire Torah. Instead, Habakkuk establishes the single principle: the righteous shall live by his faith.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Isaiah reduced the 613 commandments to two: justice and righteousness.
The gemara reports that Amos further reduced to one: seek Me and live.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects that Amos's verse 'seek Me' could refer to the entire Torah, not a single principle.
The gemara resolves that Habakkuk established the single principle: the righteous shall live by his faith.

items.text: Four decrees of Moses annulled by four prophets
items.text_en: Four decrees of Moses annulled by four prophets
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina states that Moses made four decrees on Israel, and four prophets later annulled them. Each decree is a verse from the Torah, and the annulling verse from a later prophet is cited: Amos, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Isaiah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina opens by stating that Moses made four decrees on Israel, and four prophets later annulled them, citing the first decree and its annulment by Amos.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina cites the second decree of Moses and its annulment by Jeremiah.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina cites the third decree of Moses and its annulment by Ezekiel.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina cites the fourth decree of Moses and its annulment by Isaiah.

items.text: Rav's fear of the verse 'you will be lost'
items.text_en: Rav's fear of the verse 'you will be lost'
items.desc_en: Rav expresses fear of the verse 'you will be lost among the nations'. Rav Pappa suggests it might mean a lost object that is sought, but Rav clarifies he fears the continuation: 'the land of your enemies will consume you'. Mar Zutra objects that this might be like eating cucumbers and gourds.

sub.desc_en: Rav opens by expressing fear of the verse 'וַאֲבַדְתֶּם בַּגּוֹיִם' (you will be lost among the nations).
Rav Pappa objects that the verse might mean a lost object that is sought, citing 'תָּעִיתִי כְּשֶׂה אֹבֵד בַּקֵּשׁ עַבְדֶּךָ' (I strayed like a lost sheep, seek Your servant).
Rav clarifies that his fear is from the continuation of the verse: 'וְאָכְלָה אֶתְכֶם אֶרֶץ אֹיְבֵיכֶם' (the land of your enemies will consume you).
Mar Zutra objects that the consumption might be like eating cucumbers and gourds, which is not harmful.

items.text: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Akiva on Rome's prosperity
items.text_en: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Akiva on Rome's prosperity
items.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Akiva hear the noise of Rome from afar. The others weep at the contrast between Rome's security and the Temple's destruction, but Rabbi Akiva laughs, explaining that if God rewards the wicked in this world, the reward for the righteous will be even greater.

sub.desc_en: The narrative sets the scene: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Akiva are walking and hear the noise of Rome from afar; the others weep while Rabbi Akiva laughs.

sub.text: The other rabbis' question to Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: The other rabbis' question to Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: The other rabbis ask Rabbi Akiva why he is laughing.
Rabbi Akiva responds by asking the others why they are weeping.
The other rabbis explain that they weep because the idolatrous Romans dwell securely while the Temple, God's footstool, is burned.
Rabbi Akiva explains that he laughs because if God rewards the wicked in this world, the reward for the righteous will be even greater, using a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument.

items.text: First episode: Sages weep, Rabbi Akiva laughs
items.text_en: First episode: Sages weep, Rabbi Akiva laughs
items.desc_en: The Sages see a fox emerging from the Holy of Holies and weep, but Rabbi Akiva laughs. He explains that if the prophecy of destruction (Uriah) is fulfilled, then the prophecy of restoration (Zechariah) will also be fulfilled.

sub.desc_en: The narrative describes the Sages and Rabbi Akiva ascending to Jerusalem, tearing their garments, and reacting differently upon seeing a fox emerge from the Holy of Holies.
The Sages ask Rabbi Akiva why he laughs, explaining that they weep because the place where the Torah warned that a stranger who approaches will die is now inhabited by foxes.

Rabbi Akiva explains that he laughs because if the prophecy of destruction (Uriah) is fulfilled, then the prophecy of restoration (Zechariah) will also be fulfilled, and if God punishes those who violate His will so severely, He will reward those who do His will all the more.

items.text: Second episode: Sages weep again, Rabbi Akiva laughs again
items.text_en: Second episode: Sages weep again, Rabbi Akiva laughs again
items.desc_en: The Sages see a fox leaving the Holy of Holies and weep, but Rabbi Akiva laughs. He explains that the fulfillment of Uriah's prophecy (destruction) guarantees the fulfillment of Zechariah's prophecy (restoration).

sub.desc_en: The narrator describes the Sages ascending to Jerusalem, tearing their garments at Mount Scopus, and then seeing a fox emerge from the Holy of Holies, causing them to weep while Rabbi Akiva laughs.
The Sages ask Rabbi Akiva why he laughs, and he counters by asking why they weep.
The Sages explain that they weep because the place where the Torah warned that any unauthorized person who approaches would die is now desecrated by foxes.

sub.text: Rabbi Akiva's answer to the Sages
sub.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's answer to the Sages
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva explains that he laughs because the fulfillment of Uriah's prophecy of destruction (Zion plowed as a field) guarantees the fulfillment of Zechariah's prophecy of restoration (elders sitting in Jerusalem's streets).
The Sages respond to Rabbi Akiva, saying 'Akiva, you have comforted us; Akiva, you have comforted us.'

items.text: Rabbi Akiva's explanation: linking Uriah and Zechariah
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's explanation: linking Uriah and Zechariah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva explains that the prophecy of Uriah (that Zion will be plowed) and the prophecy of Zechariah (that elders will again sit in Jerusalem) are linked. Since Uriah's prophecy was fulfilled, Zechariah's will also be fulfilled.

sub.text: Rabbi Akiva's response to the Sages
sub.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's response to the Sages
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva explains that he laughs because the prophecy of Zechariah is linked to the prophecy of Uriah, as the verse joins them together.

Rabbi Akiva cites the specific prophecies: Uriah's that Zion will be plowed, and Zechariah's that elders will again sit in Jerusalem, concluding that since Uriah's was fulfilled, Zechariah's will also be fulfilled, and the Sages acknowledge his comfort.
